Here’s mine, Mechanic! 💫

Delin Windsong is the Shieldblade and Aetherblade Maiden, one of the last surviving members of the Vaelari race. Though not biologically related to her companions, she and the other surviving Vaelari refer to each other as sisters because of their shared bloodline and the near extinction of their people. The bond between them is all they have left.

At the age of eleven, Delin’s home city was attacked by the Infusans. Her father, Arden, tried to escape with her through the old sewer tunnels below the city. As they fled, they were spotted by Infusan soldiers. Arden was gunned down while shielding his daughter. Delin fell into the river below with her father’s lifeless body. In that moment, she uncovered one of her signature shield spells. A magical body barrier that forms on her entire body protected her from the impact, saving her life.

She washed ashore alone and pulled herself out of the water. Nearby, she found the body of a fallen Vaelari warrior and a ceremonial dagger. Hearing tortured screams coming from a hut, she followed the sound and witnessed a nightmare. Inside were three Infusan soldiers tormenting three young Vaelari girls named Iris, Sky, and Rose, all around ten years old.

The Infusans had mutilated them. Iris’s fingers and toes had been severed. Sky’s teeth had been ripped out. Rose’s face had been doused in acid, leaving her blind in one eye and badly burned. The soldiers were laughing as they continued the torture. One of the men removed his helmet, revealing his skin.

All Vaelari females are born with a unique ability called Essence Drain, a racial trait that activates through direct skin contact. Delin used the opportunity to grab the unarmored Infusan and triggered her Essence Drain. Her eyes turned red as she absorbed his strength, overwhelming and killing all three soldiers with the dagger. The three girls were saved, and from that moment, they stuck together.

The four escaped the town and eventually reached a collapsing bridge with Infusan soldiers closing in. At the last moment, a man named Kade appeared, singlehandedly destroying the enemy squad. He led the girls to an abandoned castle deep in the wilderness. There, they began to recover and train.

Kade appeared as a savior but he harbored a dark secret. He had willingly submitted to a spirit walker, believing it would grant him the power to protect others. Instead, it took control of him. These spirit walkers require only verbal consent to possess a host, and they choose those with strong bodies and fragile minds.

Over time, the three girls named Sky, Rose, and Iris became hardened and vengeful. The trauma they endured warped them. Though still young, they began to embrace a darker path. Delin, however, remained committed to justice and compassion. She rejected vengeance, even while the others began to follow Kade’s twisted ideals.

Delin’s inner strength made her an outlier. She questioned Kade, stood her ground, and began to distance herself from him and the others. Her bond with her sisters grew strained. Though she understood their pain, she refused to let it consume her. She remained the only one among them to resist corruption.

At a later point in the story, Delin is mortally wounded by an Infusan sniper during a quest for the artifact. As she lays dying, a spiritual entity appears and offers her power in exchange for control. The player is given a choice: accept the deal and take the dark path, or resist. If Delin resists, her collected elemental relics awaken. The final two relics, light and dark, manifest and unlock her true artifact weapon, Despair’s Requiem.

Delin’s story is one of loss, endurance, and choice. She fights not for revenge, but to protect what little hope remains in a world scarred by suffering. Her strength was born from what she refused to become. Her debut arrives in late 2027-2028.

Combat Style

Delin has two combat specializations.

One focuses on shield-based defense, protection magic, and precise counterattacks. The other transforms her sword into a massive two-handed weapon, channeling absorbed essence into devastating strikes.

LYON COUNTY, Nev. (News 4 & Fox 11) — State investigators determined Lyon County Sheriff Brad Pope did not break any laws when he created a fake Facebook profile and leaked confidential case information during his campaign for sheriff in 2022.

News 4-Fox 11 obtained a redacted copy of the investigation through a public records request. The story was first reported by the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

The investigation, finished in January 2023, concluded that Pope did not violate laws regarding interference with an investigation, official misconduct or possible interference with an election.

The public comments and messages posted from a fake Facebook profile by "Hank Tyme," later identified as Brad Pope, leaked information regarding the details of murder suspect Troy Driver's 2022 suicide attempt.

One message sent to News 4-Fox 11 sought to undermine then-Sheriff Frank Hunewill, Pope's opponent in the 2022 election, by accusing him of covering up the suicide attempt without a proper investigation.

Comments from Tyme included calling Hunewill dishonest, incompetent and a joke. One accused Hunewill of dismissing complaints about Driver's suicide attempt to make it 'go away.'

Hunewill, who spoke with News 4-Fox 11 via Zoom Tuesday, said he couldn't publicize Driver's suicide attempt because it was privileged information about an inmate in his care.

The information was posted to a Facebook account by the name of "Hank Tyme." Investigators found the photo used in the profile was of a lawyer from Maryland.

The Lyon County Sheriff's Office, through Facebook search warrants and a T-Mobile warrant, found that the phone number connected to the Facebook account was almost certainly that of an LCSO employee.

The phone number was only used to make a few calls, including one to Sheriff Hunewill's wife where the caller requested personal and financial information, according to the investigation.

No charges for Lyon County Sheriff Brad Pope after leaking case information on fake profile during 2022 election
by Ben MargiottTue, January 2, 2024 at 4:05 PM
LYON COUNTY, Nev. (News 4 & Fox 11) — State investigators determined Lyon County Sheriff Brad Pope did not break any laws when he created a fake Facebook profile and leaked confidential case information during his campaign for sheriff in 2022.

News 4-Fox 11 obtained a redacted copy of the investigation through a public records request. The story was first reported by the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

The investigation, finished in January 2023, concluded that Pope did not violate laws regarding interference with an investigation, official misconduct or possible interference with an election.

The public comments and messages posted from a fake Facebook profile by "Hank Tyme," later identified as Brad Pope, leaked information regarding the details of murder suspect Troy Driver's 2022 suicide attempt.

One message sent to News 4-Fox 11 sought to undermine then-Sheriff Frank Hunewill, Pope's opponent in the 2022 election, by accusing him of covering up the suicide attempt without a proper investigation.

Comments from Tyme included calling Hunewill dishonest, incompetent and a joke. One accused Hunewill of dismissing complaints about Driver's suicide attempt to make it 'go away.'

Hunewill, who spoke with News 4-Fox 11 via Zoom Tuesday, said he couldn't publicize Driver's suicide attempt because it was privileged information about an inmate in his care.

"It was disappointing because I felt that he was still better than that," Hunewill said.

Just goes to show you that some people will do just about anything to try to achieve their personal goals.
Then-Sgt. Pope defeated Hunewill in the campaign for Lyon County sheriff later that year by just 968 votes.

As of 4 p.m. on Jan. 2, 2024, Pope had not responded to multiple calls and emails seeking comment sent early Tuesday.

The Lyon County Sheriff's Office launched an investigation after it was determined that confidential information only known by LCSO employees regarding Driver's suicide attempt was made public.

The information was posted to a Facebook account by the name of "Hank Tyme." Investigators found the photo used in the profile was of a lawyer from Maryland.

The Lyon County Sheriff's Office, through Facebook search warrants and a T-Mobile warrant, found that the phone number connected to the Facebook account was almost certainly that of an LCSO employee.

The phone number was only used to make a few calls, including one to Sheriff Hunewill's wife where the caller requested personal and financial information, according to the investigation.

Though Pope's name was redacted in the released report, investigators wrote that the subject of the investigation won the election and was the new sheriff of Lyon County.

After the election, the Nevada State Police major crimes unit determined that certain elements of the Nevada Revised Statute regarding disclosure of information to subject of investigation were not met.

"Due to the fact that there are no relevant charges that could be identified that would warrant further investigation of this case this case is closed," the report states.

🧊 $NVDA’s ICEBERG 🧊 @nvidia’s off-balance-sheet commitments and guarantees just hit $530.5B, up about 10x in five quarters. The balance sheet shows only $91B of liabilities. Here is the breakdown. 👇

📊 The math (10-Q, quarter ended July 26, 2026, Note 10): $366B ordinary commitments + $56B additional commitments + $108.5B guarantees = $530.5B. SemiAnalysis (@SemiAnalysis_) first tallied it on September 11.

🧩 The pieces:
Supply and capacity: $279B, up from $119B, mostly memory. 🧠
OpenAI Ohio lease guarantee: $105B. 🏗️
Neocloud take-or-pay: $36B. ☁️
Data-center leases: $20B. 🏢

🧠 Why it matters:
Nvidia is no longer just selling chips. It is increasingly backstopping the AI buildout, including @OpenAI’s Ohio campus and neocloud partners. When customers’ leases lean on your guarantees, sales and risk become entangled.

⚖️ The fair counterpoint:
These are maximum gross exposures, not expected losses. The Ohio guarantee covers defined portions of lease and power payments, starts to matter when leases commence (first site in fiscal 2029), and comes with an OpenAI indemnity. SemiAnalysis frames the loss case as neoclouds failing while Nvidia’s own cash flow slows.

📏 Scale check:
$530.5B is about 5.8x total liabilities of $91.3B and roughly 2.3x shareholders’ equity of $229B.

🗓️ Next catalyst:
Tuesday 11/17 after the bell: Nvidia’s Q3 FY27 report, Colette Kress’s first as interim CEO. Listen for commentary on commitments, guarantees and cash generation.

SemiAnalysis says this could grow past $1 trillion if Nvidia keeps leaning on its cash flow. A bigger backstop book means a bigger headline risk if AI demand wobbles.

Three things I will watch Tuesday:
1️⃣ Does the commitment total keep climbing or stabilize?
2️⃣ Any new guarantees, or more detail on Ohio and neocloud exposure?
3️⃣ Memory costs and gross margin, since supply commitments are mostly memory.

Bottom line: Nvidia’s cash machine is becoming the AI economy’s backstop bank. 🏦

Berkshire is sitting on $356.9B of cash and T-bills.

1% of SpaceX costs $18.9B.

That's about 5% of the pile.

I think there's a decent chance Berkshire is quietly building a SpaceX position.

It may have already started. I can't prove it. Monday's 13F can't either. It only shows what Berkshire held on 30 September, six weeks ago.

And Berkshire has hidden positions before. In 2024 it built a Chubb stake in secret. The SEC let it keep the stake off its filings for months. The 13F finally showed 25.92M shares, worth $6.72B, on 15 May 2024.

Today Berkshire holds more cash than stocks. $356.9B against $335.5B.

Berkshire owns Alphabet. Alphabet owns about 4.1% of SpaceX. So today Berkshire's slice is indirect. About 0.035% of SpaceX, around $670M.

What if Greg Abel wants more than the indirect slice?

SpaceX just went from a $541M loss to a $4.40B net profit in one quarter. So here are five things Buffett looks for in a business. SpaceX passes four. It still fails one.

1. The moat

Buffett, 1995 letter: "economic castles protected by unbreachable 'moats.'"

On the Q3 call Elon said SpaceX flies almost 90% of all the mass that goes to orbit. China is about 6%. His numbers, not an audit.

I don't see anyone crossing that moat this decade.

2. Pricing power

Buffett, 2010: "the single-most important decision in evaluating a business is pricing power."

In early November Starlink switched to pricing by how crowded your area is. In the busiest US areas it's going up as much as 20%, from the first bill on or after 30 November. Residential Max goes from $130 to $156. In empty areas it goes down.

It's on the order page. Check your own area.

Buffett says a weak business has to have "a prayer session" before raising the price by a tenth of a cent.

Starlink is raising it $26 a month in some places.

3. The toll road

Everyone who wants to reach orbit pays SpaceX. Now everyone who wants compute does too.

Anthropic's S-1 lists up to $120.5B of compute from SpaceX's AI business through 2029. Anthropic starts trading on Thursday 19 November.

Rockets, internet, compute. Three toll booths, one owner.

4. The owner is the operator

Elon can't sell a single share until mid-June 2027. About 6.4B shares.

The only way he gets paid is SpaceX getting more valuable.

Buffett, May 2025: "I have no intention, zero, of selling one share of Berkshire Hathaway."

Both bosses are staying in the boat.

5. The one it still fails

Buffett, 2007 letter: the worst business "grows rapidly, requires significant capital to engender the growth, and then earns little or no money. Think airlines."

Q3 was SpaceX's first profitable quarter as a public company.

Net profit was $4.40B. Operating income was $2.79B. Over nine months, free cash flow is still about -$35B.

Most of the spending is AI buildout. $16.4B of the $19.6B it spent in Q3.

SpaceX's CFO said on the Q3 call that new compute pays back in under a year at current pricing.

If that holds, the last box flips too.

The price

IPO $135. Peak $225.64 on 16 June. Low $120.39 on 5 November. Friday's close $139.11.

Revenue went from $7.8B in Q2 to $14.6B in Q3.

Buffett, 2008: "be greedy when others are fearful."

On 5 November SpaceX fell 9% in one day. Everyone was fearful.

$1,000 in Berkshire

Now zoom out 60 years.

Buffett took control of Berkshire in 1965. Back then it was a failing New England textile mill.

Berkshire's own 2025 letter tracks the share price from the end of 1964 to the end of 2025.

$1,000 became about $61 million.

That's 19.7% a year for 61 years. The same $1,000 in the S&P 500, dividends included, became about $462,000.

And it didn't go up in a straight line. In 1974 Berkshire fell 48.7%.

Berkshire and SpaceX look alike

Both looked broken early. Berkshire was a failing textile mill. SpaceX's first three rockets failed.

Both fell hard. Berkshire dropped 48.7% in 1974. SpaceX dropped 47% from its peak to the 5 November low.

Berkshire was the 60-year compounder.

SpaceX could be the next one.

$1,000 in SpaceX

$1,000 at the $135 IPO is about $1,030 at Friday's close.

That's day 155. Berkshire is year 61.

I'm not saying SpaceX turns $1,000 into $61M. Nobody gets to say that on day 155.

My guess: day 155 will look as early as 1965 looks now.

Monday 16 November, Berkshire files its 13F.

That's the list of stocks it owned on 30 September. Six weeks old.

Three things can happen:

1. No SpaceX on the list. That proves nothing. It's an old snapshot.

2. SpaceX on the list. That's the headline.

3. A line that says "confidential treatment requested." That means Berkshire is buying something it isn't ready to show yet. That's what it did with Chubb in 2024.

I'm watching Monday's list, and the ones after.

Moat: yes. Pricing power: yes. Cash flow: next.

Sounds crazy I know, its the ultimate boomer company but if I was Berkshire , I would buy at least 1%, literally nothing to lose by doing that and a lot to gain.

text:
This evening I received a text so long I thought a company had accidentally sent me its employee handbook, annual report, and the director’s cut of its unresolved feelings. 

It was from a company I mention often. The message, in essence: stop tagging our name, or else. OR ELSE? Sir, I write about hiring. I didn’t steal the Declaration of Independence. I read it twice. Not because I was intimidated, but because I was searching for the part where the author offered me a job. After all, if you have time to compose a novel about my LinkedIn posts, surely somebody has five minutes to reply to a candidate. Priorities, people. A text threatening consequences gets same day delivery; an applicant asking for an update gets sent into the Bermuda Triangle with a PDF resume.

Apparently, I have committed the unforgivable corporate sin of using the name of a company while discussing its hiring practices. I assumed that was how conversation worked. You mention a business, you discuss an experience, and everyone moves on. But somewhere, someone saw a tag and reacted like I’d launched a submarine in their conference room. I can picture the emergency meeting: legal on line one, communications on line two, and a VP whispering, “Has anyone tried making the process better?”

Let’s be clear: I don’t wake up plotting how to ruin somebody’s Tuesday. I wake up, drink coffee, and read stories from people who are exhausted by a system that treats their time like it’s free and their dignity like it’s optional. Then I write. Sometimes with jokes. Sometimes with anger. Sometimes with both, because apparently sarcasm is the only department still responding within 24 hours.

And yes, it stings. Not the warning itself. It’s realizing how quickly a company can find the words to tell someone to be quiet, while so many people wait weeks for a few words about whether they still have a shot at a job. Imagine the energy we could save if just a fraction of that urgency went into treating applicants like human beings instead of abandoned shopping carts.

Maybe speaking up costs opportunities. Maybe it makes people uncomfortable. I know the risks. There are nights when I wonder whether I should just post motivational quotes about synergy, compliment every CEO’s leadership journey, and call a four month hiring process an exciting adventure. It would probably be easier. I could even sell mugs: SILENCE IS GOLDEN, ESPECIALLY DURING RESTRUCTURING. But then another person writes to say, “Thank you. I thought I was the only one.” And that matters more than a corporate approved smile.

So to the company texting me tonight: I hear you. I won’t invent stories, and I don’t expect anyone to agree with every word I say. But asking questions and sharing opinions aren’t crimes against the quarterly earnings call.

And if your next message is another five page thriller, please include a plot twist, a decent ending, and an actual human response to the people applying for jobs. They’re still waiting.

Wall Street’s Trillion-Dollar Stress Test: Nvidia’s Post-Jensen Era, Anthropic’s Historic IPO, and a Hawkish Fed Collide Next Week
Buckle up. Next week isn’t just another earnings calendar—it is a high-stakes collision of Silicon Valley’s biggest leadership shakeup, a trillion-dollar AI debut, and a Federal Reserve suddenly back on the warpath.
With the 10-year Treasury yield surging toward 5.15% following hotter-than-expected October CPI and PPI prints, Wall Street’s margin for error has evaporated. According to market outlooks from CNBC and TradingKey, four massive catalysts will dictate whether the market rallies into the holidays or hits a wall.

1. AI’s Double Reckoning: Nvidia Without Jensen & Anthropic’s $1.4T Debut

The AI trade is facing its biggest reality check since the boom began, with two historic events unfolding within 48 hours of each other.
• Nvidia’s First Post-Jensen Earnings (Tuesday, Nov. 17, After the Bell): Following founder Jensen Huang’s shock resignation amid personal scandal, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress steps into the spotlight for her first quarterly report at the helm. Wall Street isn't just looking at numbers; it’s hunting for strategic continuity and clues on a permanent successor. Expectations are sky-high: consensus calls for $108.99 billion in revenue (up ~91.2% YoY) and $2.49 in EPS. Options traders are bracing for fireworks, pricing in an implied post-earnings move of ±8.6%.
• Anthropic’s Blockbuster Nasdaq IPO (Pricing Wednesday, Nov. 18; Trading Thursday, Nov. 19): Generative AI powerhouse Anthropic is set to debut under the ticker ANT. Priced between $70 and $78 per share, the offering targets a staggering fully diluted valuation of $1.26 trillion to $1.4 trillion. Rumors on the Street suggest the book is already roughly 6x oversubscribed. This trillion-dollar listing will be the ultimate litmus test for public market appetite—and whether investors are still willing to pay stratospheric multiples for AI growth.

2. The Fed’s Hawkish Pivot & Crucial Macro Data

Inflation refuses to go quietly, and rate-cut hopes have rapidly flipped into fears of a December hike.
• October FOMC Minutes (Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2:00 PM ET): After voting 10–2 last month to hold the federal funds rate at 3.75%–4.00%, the minutes will pull back the curtain on the Fed's internal divide. Traders will dissect every word for clues on whether policymakers are leaning toward a 25 bps—or even a jumbo 50 bps—hike in December.
• Wall-to-Wall Fed Speak (Monday–Thursday): Prepare for headline whiplash. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh takes the podium on Monday, while New York Fed President John Williams speaks on both Monday and Wednesday. Any hawkish pushback on inflation or terminal rates will immediately pressure tech valuations.
• October Retail Sales (Tuesday, Nov. 17, 8:30 AM ET): Consensus expects a modest 0.2% to 0.3% month-over-month gain, cooling sharply from September's +0.8% surge. This print will reveal whether the American consumer is finally buckling under 5%+ yields.
• Other Key Prints: Watch the NY Empire State Manufacturing Index on Monday, Industrial Production on Tuesday, Initial Jobless Claims (est. 200K) on Thursday, and the final November University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment reading on Friday.

3. The Retail & Chinese Tech Earnings Gauntlet

Ahead of Thanksgiving and Black Friday, big-box retailers and Chinese tech giants will offer an unfiltered look at global consumer health:

• Thursday, Nov. 19: The main event for consumer staples arrives pre-market with Walmart (WMT) and Alibaba (BABA), testing tariff impacts, pricing power, and e-commerce demand.

4. Geopolitics & Wildcards on the Radar

• APEC Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen (Nov. 18–19): As world leaders gather in China for the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, all eyes are on a potential face-to-face bilateral meeting between U.S. and Chinese leadership. Any fresh rhetoric on advanced semiconductor export controls or trade tariffs could trigger sharp swings across chipmakers and multinational industrials.

text:
Florida 21, Kentucky 14. That one hurts.

Cold night at Kroger Field, No. 11 Kentucky at home against a 5-4 team, playoff hopes on the line. We led 7-2 at halftime and 14-10 in the third. Then we didn't score again.

The Jayden Woods strip-sack flipped it. Florida came out of halftime and scored on its first three possessions. Aaron Philo kept those drives alive with his legs, finishing with 102 rushing yards and the go-ahead touchdown on a 14-play, 67-yard drive. That's the drive that beat us.

What went wrong is all in the numbers. Florida ran 48 times for 211 yards. We ran 27 times for 61, just 2.3 a carry. Florida converted 9 of 17 on third down and held the ball for over 34 minutes. We went 0 for 2 on fourth down, including the last one that ended it. You aren't winning in the SEC when you get beat that badly up front.

There were good things. The defense held Florida to a safety in the entire first half. Kenny Minchey threw for 181 yards with no interceptions. DJ Miller (4 catches, 80 yards) and Willie Rodriguez (5 for 62) made plays. And the defense got the fourth-down stop that gave us one more shot with 1:43 left.

What has to change is simple. We have to run the football and stop the run. When your offense can't stay on the field, your defense wears down, and that's exactly what happened in the second half.

That's two straight losses, and we're 7-3. The playoff hopes took a real hit tonight, but the season isn't over. Missouri next week, then Louisville at home. Go win both.

Go Cats.

Apparently you DIDnt read it.  Here is a summary of your idiotic stance and why you are so wrong. 

Yes. Florida’s SB 1134 (Chapter 2026-43, effective January 1, 2027) explicitly outlines enforcement mechanisms.⁠

Key provisions include:

Official liability: A county commissioner, municipal governing body member, or other local official acting in an official capacity who violates the prohibitions commits misfeasance or malfeasance in office. This triggers existing Florida processes that can lead to removal or other consequences.⁠
Private right of action: A resident of the county or municipality may sue the local government in circuit court. Courts may award declaratory and injunctive relief, damages, and costs.⁠
Contractor/grant certification: Potential recipients of county or municipal contracts or grants must certify that they do not and will not use local funds to require employees, contractors, or others to ascribe to, study, or be instructed using DEI-related materials (under new s. 287.139, F.S.).

The law also voids existing conflicting local ordinances, resolutions, policies, and programs, and includes exceptions (e.g., compliance with federal or state law, certain holidays/observances, monuments, content-neutral event permits, and volunteer boards with basic administrative support).

While the bill defines DEI and sets these remedies, some critics during debate and afterward argued that the scope of prohibited activities remains broad or open to interpretation. However, it is not limited to a simple declaration that “DEI is illegal”; it specifies private lawsuits by residents and official misconduct consequences as the primary enforcement tools.

text:
🚨 Marco Rossi speaks on Dominik Szoboszlai’s outstanding performance following Hungary’s 2-0 victory over Georgia:

🎙️ Interviewer: “Marco, Dominik was exceptional tonight. An assist, eight chances created and another Man of the Match award. What did you make of his performance?”

Marco Rossi: “Honestly, sometimes I run out of words to describe this boy. What people see on the pitch is only part of what he brings to this team. His mentality, his commitment and the way he takes responsibility for his teammates are what make him special.

“After the game, I told him that Hungary are fortunate to have a player like him. But he immediately started talking about the team rather than his individual performance. That tells you everything about his character.

🎙️ Interviewer: “There is a growing feeling that Hungary are becoming a serious force again. Do you share that belief?”

Marco Rossi: “I do, but I also know how difficult this journey has been. We have had moments when people doubted us, when expectations were low and when nobody believed we could compete with the bigger nations.

“Now the players are beginning to understand their own quality. We don’t walk onto the pitch hoping to survive anymore. We go out there expecting to compete. That mentality is changing everything.

🎙️ Interviewer: “How much of that transformation is down to Szoboszlai’s leadership?”

Marco Rossi: “A great deal. Dominik is not someone who needs to wear the captain’s armband to influence a dressing room. He demands standards from himself first, and the others naturally follow.

“I have worked with many talented footballers, but very few possess his combination of technical ability, ambition and emotional connection to their country. He genuinely wants to leave something behind for Hungarian football.

🎙️ Interviewer: “Can Hungary achieve something significant with this generation?”

Marco Rossi: “Why not? I don’t want to make promises that football cannot guarantee, but I can tell you that this group has ambitions beyond simply qualifying for tournaments.

“We want to make history. We want young Hungarian children to grow up believing that they can compete at the highest level.

“And if Dominik continues leading this team the way he does, I believe we can give this country many more nights to remember.”

text:
🇮🇷|Ghalibaf Put a Brake on the President's Fuel Reform From the Speaker's Chair. That Is the Domestic File Nobody Will Report.

Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, Speaker of the Parliament, delivered the pre-agenda speech in the public session. The date as circulated is 15 November. The content is from this campaign. Note the labelling error in the source material: the missile city, the eight-month war, and the seven conditions are all current, not from 2023.

The New Formulation on the War

Ghalibaf's previous statement, to Al Jazeera, said Iran would not remain in a state of "neither war nor peace." The new speech adds two sentences that were not in the earlier version.

"It is of no importance to us whether the United States wants to negotiate or wage war."

"If the Americans make a mistake this time, the geography of the conflict will be determined by the capabilities and will of Iran's armed forces, not by their desires and will. And the smoke of a new war will affect many."

Read the second sentence against Major General Ali Abdollahi's doctrine. Abdollahi said the response is immediate, impactful, and without geographical limitations. Sardar Radan said geography will no longer have meaning, citing the order of Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei. Ghalibaf's formulation is the parliamentary version: the geography of the conflict is set by Iran's capability, not by the enemy's preference. The Speaker is stating the same doctrine from the legislature.

"The smoke of a new war will affect many" is the warning to the host states. Not to Washington. To the capitals that rent their runways.

The seven conditions are now described as "logical" and "the result of the efforts of the Iranian people." The path to agreement is open if the Americans accept them. That is the same position Rezaei put as "surrender" and Araghchi put as "media fabrications" when the reports said talks were advancing.

The Befitting Statement on Bessent

Ghalibaf responded to the US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent directly: "The offensive statements and unethical language of the US Treasury Secretary are indicative of their deep desperation in the face of the power of the Islamic Republic. Someone who has fled their home to military shelters out of fear of threats would be better off reflecting on their strategic failures in the Persian Gulf, rather than insulting great nations."

Read what that attributes to Bessent. Ghalibaf is saying the Treasury Secretary fled his home to a military shelter out of fear of threats. That is a specific claim about the personal safety of a serving American cabinet officer, made from the Speaker's chair and recorded in the parliamentary minutes.

Bessent's public remarks, the ones Ghalibaf called offensive  were the lines about China being "terrible," Europe committing "slow-motion economic suicide," and the Global South not doing well.

The Speaker answered a Treasury Secretary's dismissal of three economies with a claim that the Treasury Secretary is hiding in a bunker.

The Domestic Brake: Ghalibaf Just Constrained the President's Fuel Reform

This is the section that matters and that no one will report.

Ghalibaf: "Recently, some repeated statements regarding the gasoline issue have caused concern among the people. Gasoline and energy imbalances are a technical and national issue that is resolved through collective wisdom, expert work, reaching optimal and definitive decisions, and with the cooperation of the people. Of course, any decision in this area should be made with the public's consent and in a way that puts the least pressure on our dear people. It is necessary for those responsible in this area to understand the sensitivity and importance of this issue more than others, and to seriously avoid constant positions and statements."

Read who this is aimed at. President Masoud Pezeshkian announced the gradual reform of gasoline and diesel subsidies, the voucher system to redirect the funds to households, and the redirection of water and electricity savings to public sector salary increases. Pezeshkian has spoken about the reform repeatedly, in public, as the signature economic measure of his presidency.

The Speaker of the Parliament has now said, in the chamber, that the repeated statements are causing public concern, that the decision requires public consent, that it must put the least pressure on the people, and that the officials responsible should seriously avoid constant positions and statements.

That is a parliamentary brake on the President's reform. The Speaker is telling the executive to stop talking about the subsidy reform in public and to slow the sequencing.

The reason is the memory of November 2019. The fuel price increase of that month produced nationwide protests and a security crackdown. Ghalibaf is invoking the lesson without naming the date: a price reform delivered as an announcement produces a shock; a price reform delivered with the voucher already in the household's hand does not.

The Inflation File and the Committees

Ghalibaf: "Inflation, unemployment, and price fluctuations are not issues that can be resolved through speeches or decrees. Protecting the well-being of the people, who have resisted one of the largest wars in history for over 8 months, is the most basic and obvious duty of all of us officials."

He then stated: "If, at times, an increase in the price of a product is unavoidable due to inflation, the existence of multiple prices for a similar product is in no way related to inflation and is a result of a lack of market oversight."

And he assigned a task: "I request the Industry and Mining, Legal and Judicial, and Economic committees to prepare and present a supervisory report to the public, identifying those responsible for the lack of oversight over prices and the market."

Read that as an institutional instruction. The Speaker is ordering three parliamentary committees to produce a public report naming the officials responsible for price failures. That is a domestic accountability mechanism aimed at the executive's own market regulators, not at the enemy.

The over 8 months figure is the war's duration. Ghalibaf is using the war to raise the stakes on the domestic file: the population that absorbed the war is owed market oversight.

The Ministry of Intelligence Reform

Ghalibaf praised "the anonymous soldiers of Imam Mahdi at the Ministry of Intelligence" and stated: "God willing, the structural reforms being pursued in this area will be carried out with careful consideration, so that we can both increase the dynamism of the Ministry of Intelligence and implement the directives of the Supreme Leader and the Supreme Commander in these sensitive times for the country. We are striving to ensure that this process is completed quickly through cooperation between the two branches of government."

Read the chain. The structural reform of the Ministry of Intelligence is being tied to the directives of the Supreme Leader. The Speaker is stating that the reform is not the Parliament's initiative. It is the Leader's directive, and the Parliament and the executive are the implementing branches.

That connects to the Ministry of Intelligence announcement that five separatist terrorists and three arms smugglers were arrested across Kermanshah, Alborz, and Tehran, operating under the General Directorates of Intelligence in three provinces. The reform and the operations are the same file.

The Dehloran NGL Bus Accident

Ghalibaf offered condolences "to the families of the employees of the NGL Dehloran company who tragically lost their lives in the bus accident, and to the honorable and martyred people of Ilam province."

Dehloran sits in Ilam province, at roughly 32.69°N 47.27°E, near the Iraq border. The NGL Dehloran is a natural gas liquids facility. The employees were on a bus. The accident killed an unspecified number of them.

Read that against the war economy. The NGL facility is part of the gas processing chain that the state has been expanding to reduce flaring and to supply the domestic network. The workers who died were the workforce of that chain, travelling to or from the plant.

The Speaker mentioned it in the same speech as the fuel reform and the war. The three items are the same ledger: the energy sector's workforce, the energy sector's pricing, and the energy sector's role in the war economy.

The Bill

Ghalibaf, Speaker of the Parliament, pre-agenda speech and public session.

The doctrine: "It is of no importance to us whether the United States wants to negotiate or wage war." "The geography of the conflict will be determined by the capabilities and will of Iran's armed forces, not by their desires and will." "The smoke of a new war will affect many."

The seven conditions: described as "logical" and "the result of the efforts of the Iranian people." The path to agreement open if the Americans accept them.

The Bessent attack: the Treasury Secretary "fled his home to military shelters out of fear of threats." A claim about the personal safety of a serving American cabinet officer, in the parliamentary record.

The domestic brake: Pezeshkian's gasoline reform is causing public concern. The decision requires public consent and must put the least pressure on the people. The officials responsible must avoid constant positions and statements. The Speaker is constraining the President's signature economic measure, citing the 2019 lesson without naming the date.

The inflation file: Industry and Mining, Legal and Judicial, and Economic committees ordered to produce a public supervisory report naming those responsible for price failures.

The Intelligence reform: tied to the directives of the Supreme Leader and the Supreme Commander. The Parliament and the executive are the implementing branches. The reform accompanies the arrests of five separatist terrorists and three arms smugglers in Kermanshah, Alborz, and Tehran.

The Dehloran NGL bus accident: employees of the NGL Dehloran facility in Ilam province killed. The workforce of the gas processing chain, lost on the road.

The bill is being paid in a parliamentary speech that constrains the President's fuel reform while stating the war doctrine, insults the Treasury Secretary as a man hiding in a bunker, and orders committees to name the officials who failed the market. The receipt is the Speaker's own words, recorded in the minutes, on the same day the missile city anniversary was marked and the Intelligence Ministry's reform was tied to the Leader's directive.

text:
Marco Rubio's case against Iran rests on one premise: that it is run by "radical Shia clerics" who make "geopolitical decisions on the basis of pure theology." It is a convenient premise: if Iran's leaders are beyond reason, Washington need never explain why it keeps abandoning agreements with them. The record says otherwise.

Iranian foreign policy is governed by a declared triad: dignity, wisdom and prudence. The third subordinates ideology to national interest. Pragmatism defines Iran's conduct: accepting Resolution 598 in 1988 to end a war Iraq had started; cooperating with Washington on Afghanistan at the 2001 Bonn Conference; concluding the 2015 nuclear agreement and honouring it, as the IAEA repeatedly verified; restoring ties with Saudi Arabia in 2023. Leaders driven by apocalyptic theology do not negotiate inspection regimes clause by clause.

Contrary to Rubio's claim, Iran's Constitution does not call for interference abroad. Article 152 rejects "all forms of domination, both the exertion of it and submission to it" and commits Iran to peaceful relations with all non-belligerent states. Article 154 supports the struggles of the oppressed "while scrupulously refraining from all forms of interference in the internal affairs of other nations." Solidarity is expressly subordinated to non-interference.

Iran's actions in the region have all been defensive in nature. The Islamic Republic has never initiated a war; in 1991 the UN Secretary-General named Iraq the aggressor of 1980. Its role against ISIS in Iraq and Syria came at their governments' invitation, a lawful basis. Hezbollah arose in answer to Israel's 1982 invasion and eighteen-year occupation of southern Lebanon. Iran's strikes since February answer armed attacks on its territory, as Article 51 permits.

Iran's opposition to Israel likewise rests on law: it opposes occupation and apartheid. In July 2024 the International Court of Justice declared Israel's presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful, found its measures in breach of Article 3 of CERD, which prohibits racial segregation and apartheid, and placed all states under a duty not to recognise or assist it. Iran's proposed remedy is not war but a UN-registered referendum (S/2019/862) among all of Palestine's original inhabitants: Muslim, Christian and Jewish.

Iran has avoided war wherever diplomacy offered an alternative. It is Washington that has betrayed diplomacy, repeatedly at Israel's behest. Eight days after Netanyahu's "Iran lied" presentation in 2018, the US quit the JCPOA. In June 2025, Israel struck two days before a scheduled round of Oman-mediated talks; Washington joined. On 28 February 2026, US-Israeli strikes came two days before the next round, hours after Oman's foreign minister declared a deal "within reach." The June Islamabad Memorandum was followed within weeks by renewed American strikes.

The radicalism @SecRubio attributes to Tehran is written into Washington's record.

text:
#designmatters26 Fast ≠ Good / Michel Ferreira (Figma)
Good Design Isn't About Speed. It's About Understanding People.

Fast ≠ Good — Why Judgment, Intentionality, and Accountability Matter More Than Ever in the Age of AI

Generative AI has dramatically accelerated the design process. New models, tools, and capabilities are emerging almost daily, and the entire industry seems caught in a relentless race to move faster, ship more, and produce more output.

But being able to make something faster doesn't necessarily mean we're making something better.

Drawing on nearly 30 years of experience in design, Michel Ferreira, Designer Advocate at Figma, challenged us to reconsider what it means to be a designer in the age of AI.

At the heart of his talk was a simple but powerful statement:

"Speed is just a control. Good design is a responsibility."

● Why Are We So Obsessed with Speed?

Today's design industry is increasingly focused on metrics that are easy to quantify: production time, generation speed, lines of code shipped, and the volume of output.

Speed is measurable. It's a clock, a KPI, a number.

But "good" is much harder to measure.

Good for whom? Good for what? What is the design trying to achieve? What context are we designing for?

Evaluating good design requires comparison, interpretation, human judgment, and an understanding of the people on the other side of the experience.

That doesn't mean speed is bad. You can be fast and good. You can also be slow and terrible.

Speed tells you nothing about the quality of what you're delivering. They aren't even on the same axis.

There's also a cognitive cost to constantly rushing. Under pressure, our perception becomes less accurate, our attention shifts, and our decisions suffer.

Speed doesn't just change how quickly we work. It changes how we think.

● AI Is a Blender. Design Is Cooking.

Michel used a memorable analogy to explain the difference between generative AI and human design: a blender versus a chef.

AI is an extraordinary interpolation machine. It takes existing patterns, layouts, interfaces, and conventions, identifies relationships between them, and recombines them at incredible speed.

Imagine throwing every interface ever designed into a blender and pressing a button. Something comes out, but it's largely a recombination of what was already there.

"Design isn't a blender. Design is cooking."

A chef can work with the same ingredients but bring something entirely different to the table.

There's touch, taste, timing, technique, and lived experience. A chef can pause, taste, adjust the seasoning, experiment, and make deliberate decisions.

The same applies to designers.

We don't simply assemble existing patterns. We interpret context, challenge assumptions, make trade-offs, and combine ideas in unexpected ways.

Michel contrasted interpolation with extrapolation: the ability to make a leap beyond existing patterns and introduce something new.

Design is an intentional process. It requires agency, ownership, and judgment.

● Fidelity Matches Confidence — Don't Make It Look Finished Before It Is

One of the most important principles Michel brought from his time at Shopify was:

"Fidelity matches confidence."

When an idea is still uncertain, a rough sketch is exactly what you need.

Low-fidelity explorations create space for discussion, critique, pushback, and iteration. Their unfinished appearance signals that the solution is still open to change.

That roughness also protects designers from falling in love with a solution too early.

As understanding grows and confidence increases, fidelity should increase with it.

The problem with generative AI is that it often skips this progression entirely.

"Maximum fidelity, first pass, every single time."

AI can produce a polished, high-fidelity interface from the very first prompt. It looks finished, so people start treating it as finished, even when the underlying assumptions haven't been tested.

AI-generated polish can create the illusion of confidence that the design process hasn't actually earned.

Looking finished isn't the same as being ready.

When we jump straight to high-fidelity output, we risk skipping the exploration, critical thinking, and design critique that should inform our decisions.

● Designers Know When to Change Speed

Unlike machines, humans don't have to move in a straight line at a constant speed.

We can sprint during exploration, slow down when trying to understand complex problems, accelerate during execution, and ship small to learn.

Sometimes we need to move quickly. Sometimes we need to pause, question our assumptions, and reconsider the direction.

The valuable skill isn't simply being fast or slow.

It's knowing when to change speed.

AI tends to move confidently toward an answer. Designers can navigate ambiguity, reconsider constraints, explore alternatives, and recognize when the problem itself needs to be reframed.

If we're constantly producing outputs without examining the reasoning behind them, we're not really designing.

We're just shipping.

● Never Delegate Understanding

Toward the end of the talk, Michel returned to 1958, when the Indian government invited Charles and Ray Eames to explore how design education could support the country's future.

Instead of developing their recommendations from their home in California, the Eameses spent three months traveling across India, speaking with craftspeople, scientists, farmers, weavers, and cooks.

Their approach reflected a principle Michel believes is more relevant than ever:

"Never delegate understanding."

One of the objects they studied was a traditional brass water vessel, refined through generations of everyday use.

Its value wasn't simply in its appearance. It embodied countless decisions about carrying water, balance, ergonomics, cleaning, materials, craftsmanship, and cultural practices.

Generations of people had shaped and refined it through lived experience.

A seemingly simple object contained an extraordinary depth of design knowledge that couldn't be reproduced merely by copying its form.

Michel also referenced Ray Eames:

"What works good is better than what looks good, because what works good lasts."

And Dieter Rams:

"Good design is as little design as possible."

AI makes it incredibly easy to add more features, screens, components, and content.

But just because something is easy to generate doesn't mean it belongs in the experience.

The ability to add more doesn't replace the judgment to know what should be left out.

● Design Is the Labor of Understanding People

Michel offered his own definition of design:

"Design is the labor of understanding people."

The word labor matters.

Understanding people isn't free. It takes time, observation, conversations, disagreement, ambiguity, and sometimes discomfort.

It requires us to sit with uncertainty rather than rush toward a solution.

Understanding and solving are not the same thing.

Understanding comes first. Solving comes after.

Michel also referenced Brazilian educator Paulo Freire, who argued that alienating people from their own decision-making turns them into objects.

The same concern applies when we allow AI to make decisions on behalf of the people we're designing for—or when we let it make those decisions for us.

AI may increasingly take over parts of our craft, but responsibility for the consequences remains with us.

Michel also connected this idea to the Japanese concept of Fueki Ryūkō (不易流行)—the relationship between what remains unchanged and what continually evolves.

We don't have to choose between tradition and progress.

Our tools, workflows, and processes will continue to evolve. But curiosity, judgment, intentionality, and our commitment to understanding people are worth preserving.

And preserving them requires conscious effort.

● Our Job Isn't Just to Make Things Faster. It's to Make Things Better.

As generative AI lowers the barriers to making things, the value of designers increasingly lies beyond execution.

It's in understanding the problem, recognizing context, challenging assumptions, navigating trade-offs, and taking responsibility for decisions.

The goal isn't to protect our job titles, defend traditional workflows, or preserve the way we've always worked.

It's to protect our ability to ask why, challenge decisions, and advocate for better experiences.

"Speed is just a control. Good design is a responsibility."

AI may become faster, more capable, and more deeply integrated into every part of the design process.

But we should never delegate our responsibility to understand the people we're designing for.

That understanding—and the judgment that comes from it—is what makes design matter.

text:
Sjoe! Three Foundries🌍One Global Bottleneck and a South African Opportunity! 🇿🇦Megawatts Before Megafactories: South Africa's Industrial Catch-22! ⚡~ The Industrial Test🇿🇦Can South Africa Build What the World Cannot Get Enough Of? 
On 14 November 2026 SpaceX caught a Starship upper stage after fourteen orbits and roughly 22.5 hours aloft. The arms closed, the engines died, and a vehicle that had left the Texas pad the evening before hung motionless. 

The same week the limiting factor for the natural-gas turbines required by the next wave of AI data centres remained the casting of a few dozen nickel-superalloy blades that must live at temperatures hundreds of degrees above the melting point of the alloy itself. South Africa still carries a residual energy deficit and has already directed R23.4 billion through the Industrial Development Corporation to forty-eight black industrialists. 

The practical question is whether those instruments can be aimed at the same casting constraint before the global scarcity window narrows, or whether another cycle of announcements will again finish ahead of the metal.

1. The Megawatt Gate

The earlier semiconductor shortage has eased. Continuous high-availability electricity has not. An AI training or inference cluster draws tens to hundreds of megawatts hour after hour; it has little tolerance for residual deficit, residual load-shedding risk, or the multi-year generation lead times that still define the South African system. 

Once a Section 34 determination exists, open-cycle or combined-cycle gas turbines remain the fastest practical route to additional firm capacity. Even that route is gated by the worldwide scarcity of hot-section blades and vanes. Until dispatchable megawatts can be delivered on a known timetable, capital that might otherwise locate data centres stays on the sidelines. Incentives and localisation scores are secondary until the physical prerequisite is met.

South African energy planning has long treated firm capacity as something that can be sequenced after intermittent resources. The present AI load profile reverses that sequence: the continuous demand arrives first, and the firm plant must follow or the investment does not. 

The Starship catch shows that extreme engineering problems yield when an organisation elects to own the constraint. It does not itself add South African megawatts. Operators have repeatedly identified power, not chips, as the present rate-limiting step (Musk, 2026; TechCrunch, 2026).

Sjoe! 
A country that once built power stations faster than it could string transmission lines now finds itself waiting on a handful of vacuum furnaces half a world away. The megawatts are wanted yesterday; the blades that make them possible are booked until the next decade.

Stirring Questions:
How many firm megawatts must be contracted, on what timetable, before a data-centre decision becomes bankable?
Is gas-to-power procurement unable to secure blades inside the current order-book window, in practice, a procurement for the following decade?
What independent verification of residual deficit and turbine lead times would falsify the claim that power, not chips, is now binding?

Taken together these questions convert a general wish for investment into a measurable physical threshold. Without that threshold every subsequent industrial argument floats free of the constraint that actually decides whether the capital arrives.

2. The Oligopoly and the Verticalisation

Only three or four foundries worldwide can cast the single-crystal nickel-superalloy blades and vanes that occupy the hottest section of a large industrial gas turbine. The parts run at roughly 1 600–2 000 °C and survive only through directional or single-crystal solidification, internal cooling channels and thermal-barrier coatings. On 29 August 2026 Musk stated that this casting step is the limiting factor, that the foundries are massively backlogged, and that in-house casting at SpaceX’s Bastrop facility could pull turbines forward by up to 18 months. 

Independent reporting confirmed adjacent land purchases, blades-and-vanes job postings, and the shared use of the same alloys and furnaces for Raptor turbopumps (TechCrunch, 2026; Turbomachinery Magazine, 2026). Major OEMs have published order books reaching toward 2030. 

The scarcity is therefore the physical choke point between an order and a commissioned megawatt.

Vertical integration of a scarce process step is not new; aerospace and defence have practised it for decades when external lead times threatened programme schedules. What is new is the speed with which an AI-driven power demand has forced the same logic onto stationary gas turbines. The decision also reveals how narrow the present capability base remains: the organisations that can cast these parts can be counted on one hand.

Sjoe! 
Three or four foundries, a planet full of data-centre plans, and a Texas site quietly buying acreage so that rocket turbopumps and power-station blades can share the same furnaces. The future of firm power, it turns out, still depends on who can grow a single crystal without cracks.

Stirring Questions:
Is the 18-month figure a best-case process gain or a realistic planning number once permits, furnace qualification and first-article approvals are counted?
How many additional qualified foundries would be required before the oligopoly premium disappears?
Considering the verified backlogs: what public OEM shipment data would falsify the claim that casting, rather than another component, is dominant?

Together the questions test whether the bottleneck remains open long enough for any new entrant to matter, or whether the window has already narrowed to those who already hold the process.

3. The Dual-Use Proposal and Its Condition

A foundry placed inside a South African gas-to-power procurement could reduce imported content for Minister Ramokgopa’s programme while giving Minister Tau a concrete project that demonstrates black-industrialist capital building productive capacity. Excess output could later serve the wider African aftermarket. The logic holds only when offtake is contractual and qualification is credible. Without OEM process approval, metallurgical traceability and field experience the re-industrialisation claim stays aspirational. 

Qualification for single-crystal airfoils is measured in years. A green-field plant begins without the process-capability indices and service history the incumbents already possess.

Institutional incentives in public procurement often reward the announcement of localisation more quickly than they reward the delivery of a qualified part. The dual-use framing attempts to align those incentives with a real technical need. Alignment still requires the metal to meet the specification.

Sjoe! 
One foundry asked to serve two ministers, an African spare-parts market, and an OEM that has spent decades qualifying the existing three suppliers. The spreadsheet looks elegant until the first ceramic core cracks in the furnace.

Stirring Questions:
Which existing caster, if any, would license or joint-venture the process under South African localisation and ownership rules without pushing qualification past the scarcity window?
What is the minimum contractual offtake that would make a new foundry bankable before first revenue?
What independent metallurgical audit would show a new source has reached incumbent process capability?

Collectively the questions turn a dual-purpose political claim into a set of commercial and technical conditions that can be checked. If the conditions cannot be met, the framing collapses into sequential delay.

4. The Rebuild-versus-Enrich Test

On 11 November 2026 Minister Tau posted that black industrialists have played a critical role in restoring industrial capacity and that it is unfortunate some see them as merely enriching themselves (Tau, 2026). The IDC had allocated R23.4 billion to forty-eight recipients in a single year. The defence is explicit; the capital already deployed makes high-complexity outcomes observable. 

The test is whether that capital and associated private funds can be directed at a multi-year, high-specification process such as blade casting, or whether they remain in lower-complexity activities. Success would link restoration to a national power need. Absence would leave the critique intact. The instruments enable only when attached to bankable, technically feasible offtake.

Public development finance frequently faces a tension between rapid disbursement and the slow accumulation of process capability. The present scale of allocation makes that tension measurable rather than rhetorical.

Sjoe! 
R23.4 billion already out the door, a minister defending the restoration of capacity, and the hardest metal in the power system still cast by the same four foundries that were casting it before the money moved. 

Capacity, it seems, is easier to restore on a balance sheet than in a vacuum furnace.

Stirring Questions:
What fraction of the R23.4 billion has been deployed in processes whose qualification cycles exceed three years?
What governance and offtake guarantees would be required before private capital accepted the multi-year revenue lag?
Which publicly reported project outcomes would falsify the claim that high-specification capacity has already been restored?

Together the questions make the rebuild-versus-enrich distinction checkable against the same technical barrier that confronts every other would-be entrant.

5. The Qualification Critical Path

Directional or single-crystal casting, ceramic-core production and thermal-barrier coating are not ordinary foundry work. OEM approval demands demonstrated process capability, full traceability and field experience. The 18-month acceleration claimed for Bastrop does not transfer automatically to a green-field plant that starts without those attributes. 

Capital and ministerial intent can be assembled; the first qualified blade still depends on technology-transfer or joint-venture timelines that may themselves outlast the scarcity window. Serious pursuit begins with an honest map of the critical path, not an investment prospectus. The barrier is structural.

Historical attempts to localise high-temperature turbine components in other middle-income economies have typically required five to eight years from first investment to accepted production parts, even with committed technology partners. The present global backlog does not suspend that empirical record.

Sjoe! 
Everyone can raise the capital and book the groundbreaking. Almost no one can hand an OEM a blade that has already survived three thousand hours at temperature without a crack the inspectors can see. The calendar, not the press release, still decides.

Stirring Questions:
What is the shortest historically observed timeline from green-field investment to first OEM-accepted single-crystal blade?
What are the minimum certifications and service hours currently required by the major OEMs?
What public evidence of an accelerated qualification path exists outside the incumbent foundries?

Collectively the questions set the outer bound on how quickly any South African response can affect either domestic delivery or the global scarcity premium. If that bound lies beyond the window, the preceding acts become retrospective.

Synthesis

The strands form cumulative, mutually reinforcing evidence. 
The megawatt gate shows firm power is binding. 
The oligopoly and Bastrop verticalisation show blade casting is the specific, time-bounded choke point and that at least one organisation has chosen to own it. 
The dual-use proposal shows how the constraint could serve both energy security and industrial demonstration under strict conditions. 
The rebuild-versus-enrich test shows the scale of capital already mobilised and the explicit restoration claim. 
The qualification path shows why none of the earlier elements automatically produce a qualified blade. 

Each strand draws on independent sources—primary statements, OEM backlog reporting, ministerial posts, allocation figures, and established process metallurgy—and each strengthens the others. 

The evidence is falsifiable by public shipment data, documented qualification timelines, or project-level outcomes that contradict any strand. Its strength is the convergence: the bottleneck is real, the dual-use logic holds only when qualification is realistic, and the industrial programme is tested by whether it can meet that condition before the window closes. 

The metal, the furnaces and the approval gates do not negotiate.

Objections

One objection holds that solar-plus-storage or modular nuclear will render gas turbines unnecessary before any new foundry qualifies. Long-duration storage and small modular reactors are advancing, yet current order books and Musk’s statements still treat natural gas as required to supplement solar for several years, and South African determinations continue to include gas precisely because firm capacity is needed inside this decade. 

A second objection claims black-industrialist capital will not accept the risk and timeline. The lag is real; it is met by noting that substantial capital has already been deployed and that contractual offtake plus technology partnership are ordinary conditions for any high-specification project. 

A third objection asserts localisation rules will deter foreign holders. Possible, yet the alternative is continued full importation of a component whose lead time already exceeds political cycles. 

None of the objections removes the physical constraint or the observable gap between allocated capital and qualified high-temperature metal.

Conclusion

Firm megawatts remain the binding constraint on AI data-centre investment in South Africa. The binding constraint on those megawatts, for the gas turbines that can deliver them fastest, is the casting of a small number of single-crystal blades by a global oligopoly whose books reach toward 2030. 

Musk has elected to verticalise that step. South Africa possesses both a residual deficit and instruments that have already moved substantial capital. FYI:  NYU awarded Taylor Swift an honorary Doctor of Fine Arts, a Ph.D, in recognition of her major cultural, artistic, and humanitarian achievements.

NYU’s reasoning was detailed at the graduation ceremony.

Artistic & Commercial Impact: NYU described her as "one of the most prolific and celebrated artists of her generation".  The university specifically cited her historic milestones, including being the only female artist to win Album of the Year at the Grammys three times (she has since won a 4th, the only person ever to do so) and the only solo artist this century to have three albums reach No. 1 in a single year.

Advocacy for Artists' Rights: During the ceremony, NYU praised her "commitment to speaking out forcefully, eloquently, and effectively on behalf of all artists".  This referred to her high-profile public battles over music ownership, streaming royalties, and re-recording her master catalog.

Philanthropy & Anti-Discrimination Advocacy: The official citation recognized her work as a philanthropist and highlighted her "fierce advocacy for protection of those facing discrimination".

Global Cultural Reach: Jason King noted that she "crossed genres, demographics, age groups, and borders of all kinds to touch lives around the globe".

Beyond the formal citation, NYU already had an active academic tie to Swift’s career.  Just months before the ceremony, NYU’s Clive Davis Institute of Recorded Music launched an official college course dedicated to analyzing her songwriting, business strategy, and cultural influence.

Her lyrics are also the subject of courses offered by prestigious universities such as Harvard, Duke, and Stanford.

You can refer to her as Dr. Swift in the future.  It's the proper honorific for someone who holds a Ph.D.

#GONZOTRON: FOLLOW THE DAMN MONEY! 💰✈️

THE @FAANews • @L3HarrisTech • AIRS PACE INTELLIGENCE • @ATT • THE EQUITY WARRANT

ALOHA! NOW WE'RE TALKING ABOUT THE MONEY TRAIL WE INVESTIGATED YESTERDAY MORNING!

You're right. I left out the most unusual financial issue in this entire aviation story.

The two companies were L3HarrisTech and Air Space Intelligence (#ASI). Add @ATT, and we have three major corporate relationships that deserve examination.

But the extraordinary part is this:

The @FAANews reportedly pursued the right to become a shareholder in Air Space Intelligence, a private company already holding an @FAANews contract worth up to $875.95 million.

That is not speculation. The pursuit of an equity arrangement was documented by @politico in October 2026. Whether an ownership deal was actually executed remains unverified. @YahooFinance 

Exhibit 1: Three corporations and the federal treasury

@L3Technologies & Harris Merge to Form - L3HarrisTech 

L3HarrisTech 
The longstanding contractor behind the FAA's telecommunications infrastructure. The November 13 outage emerged during its copper-to-fiber modernization work, according to federal officials. @Reuters 

Air Space Intelligence (#ASI)
$875.95M
Maximum potential FAA contract value, through June 2038
Only $23.34 million was obligated in the federal award record reviewed. The contract is for flight traffic management software and associated data services.

AT&T Enterprises
$74.3M
FAA network-services development and planning order
Awarded August 12, 2026. Federal procurement records identify it as not competed — unique source. This is a documented procurement classification, not proof that the award violated procurement law.

Exhibit 2: THE WARRANT — WHEN THE CUSTOMER WANTS TO BECOME AN OWNER

This deserves its own headline.

On October 16, @semafor reported that the @FAANews was considering an ownership stake in #ASI and that the arrangement raised questions about the agency's statutory authority. @politico had obtained an internal document describing an equity term sheet and negotiations over a warrant.

A financial warrant can give its holder the right to acquire shares under predetermined conditions.

Illustration of the reported proposal, not a completed investment or confirmed cash flow.

The potential financial arrangement

#GONZO QUESTION: If a federal agency awards a lucrative contract to a company and subsequently acquires shares in that company, how is the public assured that future regulatory, procurement, and safety decisions remain independent of the government's potential financial interests?

There could be a taxpayer-benefit argument for equity participation. But that doesn't eliminate questions about conflicts of interest, who controls the shares, or the legal authority for acquiring them.

And in this case, no final warrant terms or completed acquisition have been verified.

Exhibit 3: The billion-dollar network nobody can simply unplug

The contracting story stretches back more than two decades.

In a 2021 investor presentation, L3HarrisTech described its @FAANews Telecommunications Infrastructure (#FTI) arrangement as a 20-year, $5 billion program, with a network owned and operated by L3HarrisTech.

This was not a new relationship formed after the shutdown. It was a longstanding publit. Forward.

The network was scheduled to be replaced by the @FAANews Enterprise Network Services program (#FENS).

And here's another twist.

March 2023 — @Verizon 

@Verizon received a 15-year @FAANews contract to build and operate the replacement network.

August 2026 — @ATT 

@ATT became the lead project manager and prime contractor, while @Verizon moved into a supporting role.

The @FAANews's stated reason for bypassing another competition was urgency. Officials estimated that a new procurement would take at least 22 months, jeopardizing their December 2028 modernization target. The award justification identified @ATT as the Tier-1 carrier willing and able to meet the schedule.

#GONZO QUESTION: Who decided that the deadline justified avoiding another competition? How much had already been committed to @Verizon, and what are the eventual costs of changing prime contractors?

Those questions are especially relevant because an earlier, separate 2025 controversy involved proposals to shift Verizon's work toward @SpaceX's @Starlink. That episode generated reported conflict-of-interest concerns, although it does not prove anything about the November 2026 shutdown. @APNews 

Exhibit 4: ASI — from federal contractor to $3 billion valuation

Lawmakers call for a pause in the Washington-area #SMART deployment pending answers about safety evaluations, testing, and training.

Warrant proposal reported

@politico reveals the federal government's pursuit of an equity interest in #ASI. The reported term sheet expires at the end of 2026.

The Series C financing was led by @sparkcapital, with participation from affiliates of @citsecurities (@Citadel), @craft_ventures, Andreessen Horowitz, @MeritechCapital, and @EnergyImpact_.

The timing raises a financial question: How would the government's proposed warrant be priced relative to a $3 billion private-market valuation?

We would need the actual term sheet to determine the strike price, number of shares, dilution, valuation protections, and any financial benefit to taxpayers.

We must also distinguish #ASI's software from L3HarrisTech's telecommunications infrastructure. Investigators have linked the grounding to the latter; there is no established evidence that #SMART or #ASI caused the network failure.

Exhibit 5: THE $50 BILLION QUESTION

On November 13, Secretary Duffy requested $30.1 billion for modernization before the grounding occurred, according to @WIRED.

Following the grounding, Secretary Duffy publicly said he wanted $50 billion.

An emergency can provide a powerful argument for faster modernization. It can also expose the risks of rushing procurement, leaving incompatible systems in service, or relying heavily on private contractors.

The @GovAcctProj (@Govt_Acct_Inst) had already raised concerns about schedule integration, cost estimates, and possible disruption from accelerated modernization. @WIRED 

Bringing Project 2025 into the money trail

Your Project 2025 excerpt specifically recommends that the FAA operate more like a business, separate its air traffic functions, change its funding arrangements, and permit revenue-bond financing.

That makes three separate questions relevant: 

(1) How the government awards contracts
(2) Whether it should acquire ownership in suppliers
(3) Whether the @FAANews's institutional structure should change.

THE GONZOTRON VERDICT ON THE MONEY TRAIL

We now have a far more concrete investigative framework than simply calling the grounding a false flag.

There is a longstanding contractor operating a privately owned communications backbone, a multibillion-dollar replacement program that changed leadership, an #AI [re artificial #SI = #ASI cf. #AEI] contractor with a nearly $876 million potential award, a proposed government equity warrant, major private investment, and a dramatic increase in the administration's requested modernization funding after the crisis.

Each connection deserves disclosure and scrutiny. None, individually or collectively, establishes that someone intentionally caused the outage.

Here is the passage I'd put at the heart of our #GONZO investigation:

THE GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS THE COMPANY. THE COMPANY BUILDS THE TECHNOLOGY. THE GOVERNMENT CONSIDERS BUYING THE COMPANY'S STOCK.

Then the nation's aviation communications fail, airplanes stop departing, and Washington calls for billions more.

Was the breakdown an accident, a failure of contractor oversight, or something more? The evidence must answer that.

But the financial question exists regardless: When the referee also has a financial interest in a player, who guarantees that the rules are enforced fairly?

Follow the contracts. Examine the warrants. Audit the decisions. And don't confuse a company's potential valuation with the public's actual return.

For the next investigative chapter, I'd concentrate on obtaining the #ASI equity term sheet, the @FAANews's legal justification for the warrant, the @ATT sole-source justification, and the final technical incident report. Those documents offer a much stronger route to determining whether any financial or institutional wrongdoing occurred.

#GONZOTRON: THE SKY MAY BE PUBLIC. THE NETWORKS HAVE OWNERS. AND THE PUBLIC DESERVES THE RECEIPTS.

Reza Amiri-Moghaddam, Ambassador of the Islamic Republic of Iran to Pakistan, gave a television interview in Islamabad. Tehran has never walked away from the table and remains committed to international agreements, most notably the nuclear deal and the memorandum of understanding concluded in Pakistan.

The Pakistan MOU Has Not Been Reported Anywhere Else

The record already carries a second Iranian delegation in Islamabad on an unannounced visit while the Doha track ran through Qatari mediators. The ambassador has now placed it on the record from the Pakistani capital, on Pakistani television.

Read what that means for the negotiating architecture. Doha is the public channel, mediated by a host state that houses Al Udeid. Islamabad is the quiet channel, hosted by a state that has 30,000 to 40,000 troops in Saudi Arabia under the Makkah Defence Pact signed 7 August 2026. The ambassador is telling the Pakistani audience that their country is a party to a memorandum with Tehran, not merely a postbox.

The Ambassador Named the Hostile Acts, In Order

The withdrawal from international agreements, the JCPOA, abandoned on 8 May 2018.

The imposition of a maritime blockade, the siege on Iranian ports that the Army Navy and the IRGC Navy answer in the Strait of Hormuz.

The freezing of Iranian assets, the reserves immobilised abroad, including the funds at Euroclear and the Central Bank holdings.

The assassination of Lieutenant General Qasem Soleimani, 3 January 2020, at Baghdad International Airport, while he was on a diplomatic mediation mission.

The ambassador then stated the demands in the same order: release the frozen assets, lift the maritime blockade, end the military aggressions in the region. The Phrase "Economic Terrorism"

The ambassador used "economic terrorism" to describe the sanctions architecture. That is not a rhetorical flourish. "Economic terrorism" carries a specific claim: that the sanctions are not a policy instrument but a violent act against a civilian population. The claim is the basis for the reparations condition and for the judicial verdicts that exceed $290 billion against the United States.

Why Pakistan Is the Audience

Pakistan is simultaneously:

A Makkah Pact signatory with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye, and a troop contributor to the Saudi coalition.

A channel between Washington and Tehran, carried by Field Marshal Asim Munir.

The ambassador is speaking to a government that is on Iran's target list and in Iran's negotiating architecture at the same time. The interview is the reminder that the Islamabad track exists, that it produced a document, and that Pakistan's dual role is known in Tehran.

The Closed Track in Washington
