At 9 years old, Jensen Huang was cleaning toilets in a boarding school in Kentucky.
Today, he leads NVIDIA, one of the most valuable companies in human history.
But the journey between those two points is far more interesting than the money, the black leather jacket, or the billions of dollars.
Because NVIDIA almost died before the world knew what it was.
And the decisions that saved it were not always popular.
Let's go back to the beginning.
Jensen was born in Taiwan in 1963. When he was about five, his family moved to Thailand.
His parents eventually became concerned about the safety and future of their children. So they made a difficult decision.
They sent Jensen and his older brother to America ahead of them.
Jensen was only nine.
Imagine being that young, leaving your parents behind, travelling to another country, and trying to find your place in a world you barely understand.
But things became even more difficult.
His uncle wanted the boys to receive a good education, so he enrolled them in a boarding school in Kentucky.
There was just one problem.
It wasn't the kind of school he thought it was.
The school was actually a religious reform school for troubled teenagers.
Jensen was one of the youngest students there. He struggled with English, had a strong accent, and was one of the few Asian children.
Some of the older students were violent. His roommate was 17 and had scars from being stabbed.
And what was Jensen's daily responsibility?
Cleaning toilets.
Every single day.
But something interesting happened.
His roommate couldn't read, while Jensen could.
So they made a deal.
Jensen would teach him how to read, and in return, the older boy would teach him how to become stronger.
They became friends.
Think about that for a moment.
A nine-year-old boy, thousands of miles away from his parents, found a way to survive by identifying what someone else needed and offering something in return.
Years later, Jensen and his wife would donate $2 million to that same school to help build a dormitory and classroom building for girls.
He didn't forget where he came from.
When his parents eventually joined him in America, the family settled in Oregon.
Jensen attended Aloha High School, skipped two grades, and graduated at just 16.
He was interested in mathematics, computers, and engineering.
But he also needed money.
At 15, he got a job at Denny's, an American restaurant chain.
He started as a dishwasher.
Then he became a busboy, clearing tables, and eventually a waiter.
He worked overnight shifts while going to school.
Years later, he would say that the job helped him overcome his shyness and taught him how to work under pressure.
Interestingly, those restaurant jobs are still part of his professional story.
But nobody working alongside that teenager could have imagined what he would eventually build.
Jensen went on to study electrical engineering at Oregon State University.
After graduating, he worked as a chip designer at AMD and later joined LSI Logic.
He also attended Stanford at night, eventually earning a master's degree in electrical engineering.
By his late twenties, he had a stable career and a comfortable future.
He could have stayed there.
But he didn't.
In 1993, three engineers walked into a Denny's restaurant in San Jose, California.
Their names were Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem.
They sat in a booth, drank cheap coffee, and discussed an idea.
They wanted to build computer chips that would make video games look better.
That was the original idea behind NVIDIA.
Not artificial intelligence.
Not ChatGPT.
Not the technology powering the world's biggest data centres.
Just better graphics for video games.
They believed computers would eventually need special chips to handle increasingly realistic graphics.
Many people weren't convinced.
But the three founders took the risk.
They raised money, hired engineers, and started building.
Then came their first major mistake.
Their first graphics chip, the NV1, used a different approach from what most of the industry was adopting.
It was an intelligent idea on paper, but the rest of the industry was moving in another direction.
Game developers were building around triangles, while NVIDIA had chosen curved surfaces.
The result?
Their chip struggled to work with the software developers were already using.
Sales were disappointing.
The next product was also built around the same flawed approach.
Money started disappearing.
And the company was running out of time.
At one point, NVIDIA was roughly 30 days away from going out of business.
Let that sink in.
The company that would eventually become a multi-trillion-dollar business was once struggling to survive another month.
Jensen had a difficult decision to make.
He could continue pretending everything was fine, or admit that the technology they had built wasn't going to work.
He chose to admit the mistake.
But there was another problem.
NVIDIA had a contract with Sega, the Japanese video game company.
Jensen knew they couldn't deliver the product as originally promised.
So he travelled to Japan to meet a Sega executive named Shoichiro Irimajiri.
He explained the situation honestly.
He told him that NVIDIA couldn't deliver the chip in the way they had planned.
Then he made an unusual request.
He asked Sega to pay the remaining $5 million anyway.
Not because NVIDIA had delivered everything perfectly, but because the company needed the money to survive.
Sega could have walked away.
Instead, the executive agreed.
That $5 million gave NVIDIA the time it desperately needed.
Think about it.
Sometimes, the difference between a business that survives and one that disappears isn't a perfect business plan.
Sometimes, it's one person willing to trust you when you have very little left to offer.
But the money wasn't enough on its own.
NVIDIA had to change direction.
The company abandoned its original graphics approach and focused on the technology the wider industry was adopting.
It developed the RIVA 128 graphics chip.
The product was a success.
NVIDIA reportedly sold around a million units within its first four months.
The company that had nearly disappeared was back in the game.
In 1999, NVIDIA went public.
That same year, it introduced the GeForce 256 and helped establish the term GPU, short for Graphics Processing Unit.
At the time, these chips were mainly associated with gaming.
But Jensen noticed something other people were overlooking.
Scientists and researchers were beginning to use graphics chips for work that had nothing to do with video games.
And that observation would lead to the biggest decision in NVIDIA's history.
In 2006, NVIDIA introduced CUDA.
To understand why this mattered, imagine two kitchens.
The first has one extremely talented chef who can prepare almost any meal, but can only prepare one dish at a time.
The second has thousands of cooks, each handling a small part of the work at the same time.
The first kitchen is similar to a CPU.
The second is similar to a GPU.
A GPU can perform thousands of smaller calculations at once.
This makes it incredibly useful for certain types of scientific research, simulations, and artificial intelligence.
But there was a problem.
Using graphics chips for these other tasks was difficult.
So NVIDIA created CUDA, a system that allowed developers to write software that could use the power of its GPUs for much more than graphics.
Here is where Jensen made another unpopular decision.
He didn't reserve this technology for expensive, specialised chips.
He invested in making it available across NVIDIA's product range, including gaming graphics cards.
It cost money.
Investors questioned the decision.
For years, the investment affected profits, and many people wondered why a company known for gaming was spending so much on software that most of its customers barely used.
Jensen continued anyway.
NVIDIA made the tools available, supported universities, and helped train developers to use them.
He was building something that might not pay off immediately.
And that is what makes this decision so important.
He wasn't just selling computer chips anymore.
He was building an entire ecosystem around them.
Years later, researchers at the University of Toronto used two NVIDIA gaming graphics cards to train a system called AlexNet.
In 2012, that system achieved a remarkable result in a major image-recognition competition.
It showed the research world just how powerful GPUs could be for deep learning.
Suddenly, the same type of chips people bought to play video games could help computers learn to recognise images.
NVIDIA had spent years preparing for a market that was only beginning to emerge.
And it wasn't finished.
In 2016, Jensen personally delivered NVIDIA's first DGX-1 supercomputer to a young research organisation called OpenAI.
At the time, very few people understood just how important artificial intelligence would become.
Then came November 2022.
OpenAI released ChatGPT.
Millions of people started interacting with AI in a completely new way.
Businesses wanted their own AI systems.
Researchers wanted more computing power.
Technology companies began building enormous data centres.
And almost everyone needed the same thing:
NVIDIA's chips.
The H100 became one of the most sought-after pieces of technology in the world.
The company that started by making graphics cards for video games had become central to the artificial intelligence revolution.
Its market value climbed from $1 trillion in 2023 to $2 trillion, then $3 trillion, and eventually reached $5 trillion in 2025.
Jensen became a global celebrity.
The black leather jacket became his signature.
World leaders wanted meetings with him. People lined up for pictures and autographs.
But there is something important about this story that people often overlook.
NVIDIA didn't become what it is today because of one lucky moment.
It was built through decades of decisions.
Some worked.
Some failed.
The company struggled with product mistakes, competition, financial crises, failed market entries, and missed opportunities.
It also made major investments that looked questionable at the time.
One of the most important was CUDA.

Sometimes, the biggest opportunities are hidden inside things that other people don't take seriously.

By: Selina Nyarko Prah (Sis.)
Pastor Joseph Owusu-Boateng, Resident Minister of PIWC Winneba, has urged Christians to develop a genuine concern for the glory of God, emphasising that believers must be willing to defend His name, uphold His honour and place His purposes above their personal interests. Delivering a sermon titled “Concerns for the Glory of God” during the climax of the District Week, dubbed Grace Convocation, at PIWC Winneba, Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that a defining characteristic of people who walk closely with God is their concern for His glory.

Drawing from 2 Samuel 7:1–4, he examined the lives of three biblical figures, David, Elijah and Nehemiah, whose devotion to God was reflected in their commitment to His honour and purposes. He began with the story of David, who, despite living in a magnificent palace, became concerned that the Ark of God remained in a tent. According to the Resident Minister, David's desire to build a house for God demonstrated a heart that placed God's glory above personal comfort.

Although David was not permitted to build the temple, he did not abandon his concern for God's house. Instead, he deliberately made extensive preparations and provided resources for its construction. Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that David's response revealed the depth of his commitment to God. 

He challenged the congregation to consider how they would react if someone rejected an offer they had made with good intentions. He observed that many people would simply withdraw their support after such a response. David, however, continued making provisions for the temple, ensuring that the resources needed for its construction would be available.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng emphasised that genuine concern for God's glory does not disappear when personal expectations are not met. Rather, it motivates believers to remain committed to God's purposes even when they are not the ones chosen to carry out a particular assignment. He further referred to 1 Samuel 17:26, where David questioned the audacity of Goliath, the uncircumcised Philistine, who had defied the armies of the living God.

According to Pastor Owusu-Boateng, David's response was motivated by his concern for God's reputation rather than a desire for personal recognition. While others saw Goliath as a terrifying opponent, David recognised that the honour of the living God was being challenged. His willingness to confront the Philistine demonstrated a determination to defend God's name when others were afraid to act.

Turning to the life of Elijah, Pastor Owusu-Boateng referred to 1 Kings 18:21, where the prophet confronted the Israelites over their divided allegiance between God and Baal. He explained that Elijah could not tolerate the people's continued wavering between two opinions. The prophet was determined to demonstrate that the Lord alone was worthy of their worship.

Referring also to 1 Kings 18:24, he highlighted Elijah's challenge on Mount Carmel, where the God who answered by fire would be acknowledged as the true God. Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that Elijah's actions were not intended to promote himself but to restore the people's recognition of God's supremacy. He emphasised that when a believer's motives are genuinely directed towards God's glory, God is able to demonstrate His power in defence of His name.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng also identified Nehemiah among the biblical examples of individuals whose lives reflected a deep concern for God's honour and purposes.

Drawing lessons from these examples, Pastor Owusu-Boateng outlined the characteristics of people who are genuinely concerned about the glory of God. First, he explained that such individuals are grieved whenever God is dishonoured. They do not remain indifferent when God's name is treated with contempt or when conduct within the Church brings dishonour to Him.

He further stressed that believers who genuinely love God's glory do not celebrate the failures of the Church. According to him, rather than laughing when the Church experiences difficulties or setbacks, they are moved with concern and seek its restoration and progress. He challenged Christians to examine their reactions when they hear negative reports about the Church, explaining that their responses often reveal whether their concern is for God's glory or their personal interests.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng also emphasised that people who seek God's glory live for His pleasure rather than their own. Referring to 1 Corinthians 10:31, he reminded the congregation that whether Christians eat, drink or engage in any other activity, everything should be done to the glory of God. He explained that genuine devotion to God must influence everyday decisions, personal conduct and the motives behind one's actions.

Another characteristic he highlighted was the willingness to defend the name of the Lord. He explained that believers who are concerned about God's glory do not remain silent when His name is dishonoured. Like David and Elijah, they are willing to take a stand for God even when others are unwilling to do so.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng further emphasised the responsibility of Christians to proclaim God's name and make Him known to others. He noted that concern for God's glory should not remain a private conviction but must find expression in a believer's willingness to speak about God and make His greatness known.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that genuine concern for God's glory also purifies a person's motives and transforms their mindset. According to him, when God's honour becomes the primary motivation behind a believer's actions, personal ambition and the desire for recognition begin to give way to a sincere commitment to pleasing Him.

He encouraged Christians to evaluate the reasons behind their service, sacrifices and involvement in church activities, emphasising that the desire to glorify God must remain central. He further noted that those who consistently seek God's glory develop a relationship with Him marked by His favour and approval.

Concluding his message, Pastor Owusu-Boateng challenged the congregation to follow the examples of David and Elijah by demonstrating a genuine concern for God's honour in every area of life. His message reinforced the need for Christians to move beyond merely professing love for God and demonstrate that love through their willingness to defend His name, support His work, proclaim His greatness and live according to His purposes.

Emylee Thai (woman, right) and Khalid Ahmed Satary (man, left).

These are two people from the FBI’s Most Wanted Fraudsters list (launched in June 2026 under Kash Patel). The post highlights them as having stolen over $650 million combined (roughly $547M + ~$95M paid). Both were charged in large Medicare genetic-testing fraud schemes involving medically unnecessary tests, kickbacks/bribes, and false claims. They are presumed innocent until proven guilty in court.⁠Newsweek

Emylee Thai (right)
Who: Former Houston-area laboratory owner (ApolloMDx). Born in Vietnam (Aug. 27, 1984); Asian female; aliases include Kelsey Tan, Thu Anh Thai, Kimberly Le-Thai.
Allegations: Conspiracy to commit health care fraud, kickbacks, etc. Lab billed Medicare ~$142 million for genetic testing (2019–2022) and was paid ~$95 million; many tests allegedly unnecessary and not used in treatment. Indicted July 2022.
Where/when arrested: Arrested in Vietnam (hiding there since at least 2023). She had removed her GPS monitor on Dec. 8, 2022, fled the U.S. (last known at Harry Reid Airport in Las Vegas) via private plane under a false identity. FBI announced the capture around Sept. 14, 2026 (with international partners).
Current status: Captured and no longer a fugitive; in the U.S. justice system facing the charges (plus related ones for GPS tampering and records destruction). FBI had offered up to $150k reward.⁠Colombiaone
Khalid Ahmed Satary (left)
Who: ~54-year-old lab owner/operator of several diagnostic labs (ties to Houston, Atlanta, Florida, Dubai, etc.).
Allegations: Conspiracy to commit health care/wire fraud, kickbacks/bribes, money laundering. Alleged $547 million Medicare scheme (2016–2019) using recruiters, telemarketing, telemedicine, and bribes for expensive unnecessary cancer/genetic tests. Indicted Sept. 2019 in Eastern District of Louisiana; released on bond but violated conditions and fled ~late 2022.
Where/when arrested: Arrested July 20, 2026, in the Middle East (found with a fake Mexican passport under a false name). Returned to the U.S. (initial appearance in Virginia).
Current status: In U.S. custody facing the federal charges. This was one of the earlier captures from the new Most Wanted Fraudsters list.⁠Knoe
These two are part of a broader set of six high-profile fraudsters (linked to >$2B total) captured across multiple continents in 2026 as part of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud initiative. Details come from FBI statements, DOJ announcements, and reporting on the cases. For the absolute latest court status, check official dockets (e.g., PACER) as proceedings continue.

text:
tesla: 76% of the sales. spacex: 80% of the profit.

they're both studying a merger. no deal, no terms yet. so which one is the bigger company?

you can run this check on any merger paid in shares. here's why spacex needs it, why musk wants it, and why it may not be good for you.

both in their own numbers:

sales, last 12 months: tesla $103.6bn, spacex $32.0bn.
operating profit, latest quarter: tesla $0.7bn, spacex $2.8bn.
cash left after all spending, 12 months: tesla plus $3.3bn, spacex minus $39.2bn.
cash in the bank: tesla $45.4bn, spacex $89.9bn.

why spacex needs it: money. about $90bn in the bank lasts a little over two years at that pace. it also carries about four times tesla's debt.

everyone says starlink will pay for tesla's robots. the cash runs the other way. starlink made about $2.4bn of operating profit in the latest quarter. in the same three months spacex's AI segment spent $16.4bn on equipment. a merger puts tesla's cash behind that.

why musk wants it: he owns about 18% of tesla. merged at friday's prices he'd hold roughly a third of the whole thing. his spacex stake is from the may prospectus, so approximate.

they already trade with each other. spacex bought $151m of tesla's megapack batteries in the latest quarter. tesla owns spacex stock it paid $2bn for. under one roof that stops being a conflict. and it's one AI story to sell, not two.

why not: the ratio. at friday's prices tesla holders get 45% of the new company. spacex holders get 55%.

on sales tesla brings 76% and gets 45%. tesla holders give value away. on the latest quarter's profit spacex brings 80% and gets 55%. spacex holders do. no single ratio fixes both.

it flips because spacex is changing fast. quarterly sales went from $5.6bn to $14.6bn in a year. part of that was bought, the cursor deal closed 14 aug. the market pays about 59 times sales for spacex and about 15 times for tesla.

if you dislike the ratio, you have little comeback. both are texas companies. spacex's bylaws need a holder to own 3% before suing on its behalf. that's about $57bn of stock. other disputes go to arbitration.

regulators too. reuters pointed out tesla builds more than half its cars in shanghai, while spacex does US defence work.

and any premium is a transfer. each 10% premium spacex pays for tesla costs spacex holders about 4.3%. tesla holders gain about 5.3%.

the contribution test. you can run it on any merger paid in shares:
1. take both market values. each side's share is what it would own. tesla would own 45%.
2. each side's share of 12 months of sales. tesla has 76%.
3. same for the latest quarter's operating profit. tesla has 20%.
4. compare. a side that brings more than it would own is giving value away. if 2 and 3 disagree, the ratio is a bet on which number lasts.

i hold a long echostar / short spacex pair. echostar is owed about 261.8 million spacex shares, closing targeted 30 nov 2027. at friday's price that's about $36.4bn. echostar's whole market value is about $29.1bn.

what if spacex merges first? the purchase agreement says the price is "adjusted for" a list of events that includes a "merger, consolidation or other reorganization". that one bracket is the whole protection. i found no vote and no consent right.

so echostar takes whatever ratio the committees agree. a 10% premium for tesla is about $4.50 off each echostar share. my sum of the parts is about $195 against a $100 close, so it's small next to the gap. the short leg takes the same ratio, so most of it cancels.

if you're ever owed shares in a company, read that adjustment clause. ask if you get a vote too.

[PROPOSED] i'm not trading the merger. holding the pair and watching the ratio.

tesla offered to buy solarcity in 2016 and fell 10.5% on the day. the first offer was 0.122 to 0.131 tesla shares per solarcity share. it signed at 0.110. next 12 months: tesla up 71%, S&P 500 up 19%. one case.

in july i listed five ways this pair could break. a merger wasn't one.

if you've seen a deal where the side owed shares did get a say, which clause did it?

sources: tesla and spacex quarterly reports filed 22 oct 2026, echostar's purchase agreement. prices are tiger closes 13 nov 2026. sum of the parts includes my own estimate. rest is my own arithmetic.

text:
Should AI be banned from deciding who gets a loan, a job or bail?

I build with AI every day. I use it to write code and review diffs. I also know what it is bad at: explaining itself, noticing skewed training data, and owning the damage when it is wrong. So should a system with those limits be allowed to decide whether you get a mortgage, an interview or a walk out of jail?

Vendors will tell you the model only assists. In practice the score often is the decision. A resume that never reaches a recruiter has been rejected. A risk number signed without reasons has already been used. A credit limit that a support agent cannot explain has already been set. This is about lending, hiring and bail.

If a human cannot see the reasons and will be blamed for overriding the software, that human is a rubber stamp. That is still an automated decision.

When courts used a recidivism score

In May 2016, ProPublica analyzed COMPAS, a Northpointe tool that scores a defendant's risk of reoffending and has been used to inform bond decisions and, in some states, sentencing. It obtained scores for more than 7,000 people arrested in Broward County, Florida, in 2013 and 2014, then checked who was charged with a new crime over the next two years.

Of those labeled likely to reoffend, 61 percent were arrested for any subsequent crime within two years. For violent crime, only 20 percent of the people predicted to reoffend actually did so.

The errors were not evenly spread:
Black defendants who did not reoffend were misclassified as higher risk 45 percent of the time, versus 23 percent of white defendants.
White defendants who did reoffend were labeled low risk 48 percent of the time, versus 28 percent of Black defendants.

Northpointe disputed the analysis. It pointed to another ProPublica finding: overall accuracy was similar for both groups, about 59 percent for white defendants and 63 percent for Black defendants, and said that was the design goal. Both can be true: equal accuracy can still hide a much higher false-positive rate for one group.

The formula was proprietary. In 2016, the Wisconsin Supreme Court held in State v. Loomis that using a COMPAS score at sentencing does not violate due process if done with caveats, even though Loomis could not inspect the algorithm. The presentence report itself warned that the scores are not intended to determine sentence severity or incarceration. A court still used the numbers.

The EU AI Act entered into force on August 1, 2024 and, from February 2, 2025, banned using an AI system to assess or predict the risk that a person will commit a criminal offence, based solely on profiling or on personality traits. An exception exists for tools that support a human assessment already based on objective and verifiable facts linked to that activity. The United States has no equivalent federal ban.

What a hiring model learned

In 2014, Amazon built an experimental tool to score candidates from one to five stars, trained on a decade of resumes, most from men. Reuters reported in October 2018 that the system learned to penalize resumes containing the word "women's," such as "women's chess club captain," and to downgrade graduates of two women's colleges. It also favored verbs more common on men's resumes, including "executed" and "captured." The project was abandoned in 2017. Reuters said some recruiters had looked at the recommendations but did not rely on them alone. Amazon said the tool was never used by recruiters to evaluate candidates.

The lawsuit that is still open

In 2023, a job applicant sued Workday in federal court in San Francisco. The plaintiff, who is Black, said he was rejected for more than 100 jobs at companies that used Workday's AI hiring tools. The case alleges that the tools disproportionately exclude African American, female, over-40 and disabled applicants. Those are allegations, not findings. No court has ruled that the software is discriminatory. In May 2025, Judge Rita F. Lin granted preliminary certification of a collective action under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act. By October 2026, more than 15,000 people had opted in. In September 2026, the plaintiffs asked the court to certify broader classes. In November 2026, Workday asked the court to reject group treatment, arguing that it does not make hiring decisions for its customers.

New York City's Local Law 144, enforceable since July 5, 2023, bars employers and agencies in the city from using an automated employment decision tool unless an independent bias audit was completed in the past year, a summary is posted, and New York City candidates get notice at least 10 business days before use. Civil penalties run from $500 to $1,500 a day. The law does not require the employer to stop using the tool if the audit shows a disparate impact. A New York State Comptroller audit issued on December 2, 2025 called the city's complaint process ineffective. The department received two such complaints in that period, reviewed 32 company websites and found one potential issue. State auditors reviewing the same employers found at least 17.

When a government algorithm ruined thousands of families

From 2013, the Dutch Tax and Customs Administration used a self-learning system to flag childcare-benefit claims for suspected fraud. Amnesty International found that lack of Dutch nationality was built in as a risk factor, and that non-Dutch nationals received higher risk scores. Civil servants were supposed to review the flags. Parents who were flagged had benefits suspended and were told to repay money, often tens of thousands of euros, with little explanation. By the time the Dutch cabinet resigned on January 15, 2021, reporting put the number of wrongly accused parents at as many as 26,000, and as many as 10,000 families were forced to repay large sums. "A person signed it" is not a safeguard unless that person can see why the system fired, can override it and will not be punished for doing so.

The credit card that could not be explained

In November 2019, Apple Card customers said on Twitter that women were offered lower credit limits than men in the same household, and that support staff could not explain why. Apple Card had launched in August 2019, underwritten by Goldman Sachs Bank USA. New York's Department of Financial Services investigated. Its March 2021 report found no evidence of deliberate or disparate impact discrimination, but it did find deficiencies in customer service and transparency. Opacity is a failure even when unlawful bias is not found.

The Equal Credit Opportunity Act and Regulation B require a creditor to give the specific principal reasons for a denial or other adverse action. CFPB Circular 2022-03 said those rules apply even when a complex algorithm is used, and that a creditor that cannot provide specific, accurate reasons may not use that algorithm to decide. On May 12, 2025, the Bureau withdrew that circular. Regulation B was not amended. A rejected applicant is still owed the specific reasons.

The EU treats credit scoring and hiring tools as high-risk AI. The European Commission's AI Act page, read in November 2026, says the high-risk obligations apply from December 2, 2027, after a delay. The United States has no federal equivalent.

A fix stricter than a disclaimer

I do not want AI banned from these sectors. I want it banned from making the final decision. Used as a search aid, it can be useful. Used as the decision, it concentrates errors at scale.

The rule should be simple enough to enforce:
1. In lending, hiring, and bail, pretrial release or sentencing, an AI system may recommend. It may not issue the decision. A named human has to own the outcome.
2. That human must be shown the specific reasons, in plain language, and must have a logged right to override them. A red or green score with no reasons is theater.
3. Anyone denied a loan, rejected for a job, or scored for bail or sentencing gets a right to an explanation of the actual factors, and a right to appeal to a different human.
4. Independent audits should be mandatory, public in summary form, and consequential. If an audit shows unlawful disparate impact, the tool cannot be used until it is fixed.
5. People must be told, before the tool is used, that AI is involved, what it will assess, and how to request a human review.
6. Both the vendor and the deployer should be accountable. The Workday case is still being litigated, so this is a policy position.

The verdict

Yes. AI should be banned from deciding who gets a loan, a job or bail. Not from analyzing a file or flagging a missing document. From deciding. If a system cannot explain a decision, cannot be audited in a way that stops it, and cannot be overruled by a human who has the reasons, it should not be the last word on your liberty, your income or your credit.

If a model scored your loan, your job application or your bail hearing and you were not allowed to see how, should that score have been allowed to decide the outcome?

text:
This nasty McDonald’s tech just did the impossible — making Elizabeth Warren look good | John Mac Ghlionn, Blaze Media

America's most famous clown has Sen. Warren acting deadly serious.

Nine times out of ten, if asked to choose sides in a dispute between Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Ronald McDonald, I would choose the McDonald. No questions asked. Warren, after all, went viral for claiming Native American ancestry, only to be ridiculed and forced to offer groveling apologies. Ronald, meanwhile, has spent over 60 years selling Americans Happy Meals and creating plenty of happy memories.

Yet we live in strange times, so strange that I now find myself siding with the teepee-loving teller of tall tales. Warren, along with four other Democrats, recently sent McDonald’s CEO Chris Kempczinski a furious letter.

Your perceived wealth dictates your bill.

In it, the pols demanded answers about the company's AI-powered pricing tools. The technology estimates what customers at each location are prepared to pay and quickly recommends the prices the company believes will make it the most money. It’s sneaky, and I’m certainly not lovin’ it.

The golden arches built a huge empire on low-cost convenience. Drive into any suburban strip mall, drop a few dollars, and receive a standardized slab of meat-like matter. The transaction was simple and straightforward. Today, that transaction is morphing into a machine-learning surveillance operation designed to calculate the absolute limit of your financial tolerance.

The question is no longer what a Big Mac actually costs to produce, but how much McDonald’s thinks it can fleece you before even a Jack in the Box burger starts to look appealing.

Maybe one lost customer doesn't even register for a chain as big as Mickey D's. But dissatisfaction can spread like wildfire. And every day, the fast-food giant serves approximately 26 million people across the country. In other words, well over a million people every 60 minutes. At that scale, little algorithmic tweaks that leave you grumbling can net out to megabucks of profit.

May I take your Orwellian order?

Corporate executives love to hide behind technical jargon and market theory. They insist that their AI doesn’t technically set menu prices because individual franchisees retain final authority over their final prices. Three separate franchisees told Reuters that the pricing engine's recommendations have noticeably widened the cost gaps between nearby locations. When a multibillion-dollar corporate headquarters sends automated price targets to a franchise owner, those numbers carry the weight of an imperial mandate. Calling it a mere suggestion is nothing but corporate doublespeak.

Let me paint a somewhat sinister picture. Two working-class parents pull up to a drive-thru window after a 10-hour shift. Ten miles down the highway, another family pulls up to an identical menu board. The meat in the kitchen arrived on the same refrigerated truck. The workers behind the register wear the exact same uniforms and earn the exact same hourly wage. Yet the family living in the slightly higher-income neighborhood pays an extra dollar for every single item. The AI analyzed local income metrics, traffic patterns, and economic desperation, concluding that those specific parents had nowhere else to go.

This dynamic is disturbing, and it flips traditional commerce on its head. In a standard market, prices reflect supply, demand, and overhead costs. Algorithmic pricing discards that tried-and-tested trinity, creating a localized dynamic in which your perceived wealth dictates your bill. Forget inflation. Forget rising beef costs or supply chain bottlenecks. McDonald’s has built a shady system designed to squeeze every penny out of your pocket.

The broader implications extend far beyond a bag of French fries. Fast food has historically functioned as an economic equalizer, a place where a plastic surgeon and plumber bought the exact same lunch for the exact same five-dollar bill. Algorithmic pricing makes each neighborhood into a distinct cash cow, milked through digital demographic profiling.

And if this software succeeds across 14,000 American locations, you can be sure it won't stop with burgers. Every major retail sector could adopt the exact same play. Supermarkets, pharmacies, gas stations, and hardware stores may run machine-learning software to price basic necessities based on your neighborhood's financial scorecard.

Flimsy defenses

American consumers are already struggling to keep their heads above water. More and more have less than $500 in savings, while countless others are being squeezed by higher rents and eggs priced as though they came with the chicken.

Eating out at a fast-food chain used to provide a brief reprieve from economic stress. Now, even a simple meal has become a calculated financial extraction exercise. You drive up to the speaker box, state your order, and wait for a computer server in Chicago or California to decide how much value it can pull from your checking account today.

McDonald’s insists that its machine-learning tools merely help store operators navigate ever-changing economic environments. That defense is flimsy, and it ignores the fundamental contract between a business and its customers. People don’t walk into a fast-food restaurant expecting to be on the receiving end of algorithmic manipulation. They want a quick burger, a side of fries, and a few minutes of peace without worrying about their bank balance.

If the golden arches can turn a routine bite into a localized wealth-extraction test, the traditional concept of a fair price is dead. We are rapidly moving toward a future in which the price tag on the wall is little more than an illusion, tailored in real time to extract maximum revenue from whichever unfortunate soul craves some greasy goodness. Elizabeth Warren might be an unlikely defender of the average American’s wallet. But on this issue, McDonald’s has made the not-so-native American look surprisingly reasonable.

🤔 Wild thought: SpaceX + Tesla + Nvidia, one AI ecosystem 🚀🚗🟩

(@elonmusk - IF anyone can construct an action plan to do a derivative approach to Acquiring/Merging NVDA to integrate SPCX TSLA NVDA and bring Jensen back - it would be you!!)

$SPCX runs its AI on $NVDA. Musk in August: "SpaceX has committed to using Nvidia GPUs exclusively because they are the best" 🔒

He said SpaceX expects "a very significant percent" of Nvidia's GPUs next year 📦

A buyout isn't realistic. A merger? Genius 🧠

Here's why 👇

🟩 WHAT NVIDIA HAS THAT OTHERS DON'T (YET)

💰 THE PROFIT (actual, Q2 FY27)
Revenue $96.2B, up 106% from a year ago
Gross margin 75.0%
Net income: GAAP $59.7B | Adjusted $54.0B
Q3 guide (forecast): $108B, plus or minus 2%

🏭 THE SUPPLY CHAIN
Nvidia holds the majority of TSMC's advanced packaging capacity (CoWoS), the step every top AI chip has to go through. UBS estimates about 60% in 2026 and about 49% in 2027 (estimates) 🇹🇼

💾 THE MEMORY
Supply and capacity commitments jumped from $119B to $279B in one quarter, mostly memory, with long-term HBM deals across SK hynix, Samsung and Micron

📈 THE SCALABILITY
That supply is already locked in for the next several years. The hyperscalers can't just buy that overnight 🔐

🛰️ SPACEX: THE COMPUTE
SpaceXSI's Colossus 1 runs 220,000+ Nvidia GPUs, with supercompute campuses planned in Texas and Arizona. Starmind AI satellites, basically Vera Rubin NVL72 computers in orbit, are targeted to start launching next year 🌌

🚗 TESLA: THE PHYSICAL AI
Tesla designs its own AI5 chip, now in trial production, headed into Optimus around April 2027 🤖

🏭 AND THE FAB
Terafab, the SpaceX + Tesla chip plant in Texas ($16.8B first phase), is targeting volume production around Q3 2028. Musk himself calls that timeline "very aggressive" ⚡

📈 WHY IT'S SO POWERFUL (my take)
This would be about as vertical as it gets 🏗️

Instead of paying Nvidia's margins, SpaceX would own them. The profit stays in-house and gets reinvested straight into more compute, more satellites and more robots 💸

Locked-in TSMC and memory capacity + SpaceX's speed of building = a huge profitability pipeline, and scaling no one else can match 🚀

⚖️ THE HYPERSCALERS
$META $GOOGL $MSFT $AMZN would be at a serious disadvantage. When one player controls the top chips, the TSMC capacity, the memory AND the compute buildout, everyone else is fighting for what's left 🏁

Yes, they have their own chips (TPU, Trainium and more), but in my view they'd struggle to keep pace 🐢

☁️ THE NEOCLOUDS (my take)
Different story. Neoclouds are built largely on Nvidia GPUs to compete with the hyperscalers, so they'd likely stay key customers and keep riding the same Nvidia roadmap 🤝

Compute → Intelligence → Productivity → Economic Value 💰

🗳️ COULD IT ACTUALLY HAPPEN?
A true merger needs both boards to say yes 🤝 Without that, it goes to shareholders: a tender offer, or a proxy fight to elect new directors. Every $NVDA director is up for election every year

📜 The hurdles, per Nvidia's charter, bylaws and Delaware law:
✅ No poison pill in place (but a board can adopt one quickly)
📣 Calling a special meeting takes 15% of the vote, held for 1+ year
🚫 No action by written consent
🔒 Delaware's Section 203: buy 15%+ and you're blocked from merging for 3 years, unless the board approves first or you reach 85% in the same deal

Plus massive antitrust hurdles ⚖️

Pure thought experiment, but think about it... 👀

Compute is the new capital. Own the assets 💰

Lead the Flock 🐏

text:
November 13 Saint Frances Xavier Cabrini: the first United States citizen to be canonized.
1850-1917
Patronage:
against malaria
emigrants (given on 8 September 1950 by Pope Pius XII)
hospital administrators
immigrants
orphans
.
“We must pray without tiring, for the salvation of mankind does not depend on material success; nor on sciences that cloud the intellect. Neither does it depend on arms and human industries, but on Jesus alone.”
.
She founded the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart to care for poor children in schools and hospitals, and at the urging of Pope Leo XIII, moved to the United States to work among immigrants. Through her care for those who were struggling, hard work, and obedience, Saint Frances is regarded today as the Patron Saint of all immigrants.
.
Frances Cabrini was born in Sant’Angelo Lodigiano (Lombardy, Italy). Born two months prematurely, Frances was small and weak, and struggled for survival. Frequently ill as a child, she would remain physically frail and susceptible to illness her entire life. 
Frances’ parents were farmers, and her mother stayed at home each day with the children. In total, her parents produced eleven children, with Frances being the tenth. Sadly, only four of the Cabrini children survived their childhood. Despite numerous losses and tragedies in the family, both Frances’ mother and father were strong in the Catholic faith, and through their teaching and example, Frances came to love God. One of her favorite activities was listening to her father read the stories of missionaries from the Annals of the Propagation of the faith. More than anything, from and early age and throughout her life, Frances desired to travel to China as a missionary. 
.
Frances was especially devoted to the Sacred Heart of Jesus, which inspired her growing faith. With her parents’ support, she applied for admission to several religious orders, but was turned away by each due to her frequent illnesses and frail health. Disappointed, but not discouraged, Frances cared for her parents until their death, as well as raised her brothers and sisters. Throughout all of this, despite her frailties, she worked on the family farm—physical activity that both taxed her body, but also prepared her for the physical work that she would encounter throughout her life. Upon the death of her parents, Frances began studying to her teaching degree at a boarding school administered by the Daughters of the Sacred Heart. While her classmates complained, she was delighted that the students of the school were required to live in the convent with the religious sisters. Adding to her joy was the devotion of the sisters to the Sacred Heart. Upon graduation, she again petitioned to join the order, but was again refused, with her health cited. The Superior of the Order encouraged her, saying, “You are called to establish another Institute that will bring new glory to the Heart of Jesus.” 
.
Again disappointed, but not discouraged, Frances returned to her home town, and began teaching in a private school, spending her non-work hours devoted to charitable works and serving the poor. She was immediately recognized for her gentle spirit, teaching ability, faith, and obedience, and over the next several years, was requested to move from school to school by the diocese, filling vacant positions and invigorating educational facilities. Eventually, she was requested to move to the town of Codogno, and assume direction of the girls’ orphanage there, known as the House of Providence. The diocese wished to restructure the facility into a religious institute, and realized that despite her frail health, Frances possessed the faith and spirit to accomplish the task. Without hesitation, Frances accepted, and within the year, the five young women who taught at the House, entered their novitiate with Frances as their novice mistress.
.
In 1877, at the age of 27, Frances’ wish to take the veil was granted, and along with her five sisters, made her profession. In honor of Jesuit father Frances Xavier, Frances took the name Xavier, becoming Mother Frances Xavier Cabrini—as she would be known for the remainder of her life. Named superior of the community by her local bishop, she was encouraged to form a new religious institute. Along with the five sisters who took their vows with her, she founded the Institute of Missionaries of the Sacred Heart of Jesus in 1880. While some objected to the inclusion of the word “Missionaries” in the order’s name (as it implied overseas work, and the bishop intended that the sisters serve locally), Mother Cabrini was already thinking on a larger, grander scale. She had plans for her sisters to spread the Gospel beyond the borders of Lombardy.
Mother Cabrini left Lombardy to travel to Rome, as was the custom at the time, seeking approval from the pope for her fledgling order. She also wished to establish a mission house in Rome, from which she could then use as a base for international missions. 
.
Surprisingly, despite the youth of the foundress and the relative newness of the order, she received papal approval and permission to open two missions in Rome. Mother Cabrini also met the founder of the Missionary Institute of Saint Charles, who was looking for a religious woman to assist him with ministering to Italian immigrants overseas—specifically in New York. He requested that she assist, but Mother Cabrini was reluctant. Her plans were to send her missionaries to China, as she had always dreamed. However, when presented with a letter from New York Archbishop Corrigan, formally inviting the Missionaries of the Sacred Heart to establish a house in New York, she was moved to request an audience with the pope.
.
Ever obedient, and certain in the plan of the Lord, Mother Cabrini decided that she would do whatever Pope Leo XIII asked her to. She presented her dilemma to him, and following deliberation and conversation, he responded: “Not to the East, but to the West.” Disappointed, but not discouraged, Mother Cabrini and six of her sisters set out immediately for New York. Upon arrival, she was surprised to find that Archbishop Corrigan had not expected her so soon, and even more surprised when he suggested they return to Italy until he could prepare for her arrival. But Mother Cabrini answered, "Your excellency, the Pope sent me here and here I must stay." The archbishop admired her pioneer spirit, and so she and her sisters were permitted to begin their work. She and her companions spent the first night in a dingy tenement in the heart of the Italian ghetto. They could not sleep and stayed awake, tired, yet peacefully engaged in prayer. 
.
Soon afterwards, a local order, the Sisters of Charity, extended Mother Cabrini and her sisters hospitality and guided their first steps through the city. At once, the new sisters were faced with a language difference. Not speaking English, and being unfamiliar with the new countries customs, Mother Cabrini worked to establish her mission. She slowly gained the support of the Archbishop, eventually becoming dear friends. She secured the donation of a house for the Order, and soon thereafter, instituted an orphanage on the same property. A free school soon followed, all through donations and alms-gathering that the sisters undertook on a daily basis. Soon, based upon their good work—and the personal attention and spiritual direction they gave to each family in the Italian district—young women were requesting to join the order.
.
Mother Cabrini returned to Italy, accompanied by her first North American postulants, who began their novitiate in Codogno. After an audience with her friend, Pope Leo XIII, she returned to New York, and embarked upon the institution of a larger orphanage. This site eventually included the North American novitiate of the order. Purchased at a low price, due to the lack of fresh water on the site, Mother Cabrini soon discovered a underground spring (some called it a miracle!), which still provides water to this day.
.
From New York, the Missionary Sisters branched out throughout America, starting in New Orleans (school and orphanage), and continuing west. It became clear—both in New York and other areas—that the immigrants were not receiving the medical care that they needed in public hospitals. However, Mother Cabrini was not particularly inclined to undertake this ministry. It was not until she had a dream of Our Blessed Mother that she changed her mind. 
.
In her dream, Mother Cabrini saw Mary, the Mother of God, tending to a hospital patient. Asking Our Blessed Mother what she was doing, Mother Cabrini was surprised by her response: “I am doing the work you refuse to do.” Upon waking, Mother Cabrini moved quickly to establish a hospital for the Italian sick poor in New York City, and to her surprise, found herself to be a capable (even outstanding) healthcare provider and administrator. Hospitals were eventually established by the Missionary Sisters in Chicago and Seattle.
.
The Missionary Sisters recount how the great faith of Mother Cabrini allowed this fast and miraculous growth of the order to occur. In Seattle, for example, as she was looking for a site to institute an orphanage, Mother Cabrini had a dream in which she saw a beautiful house on a hilltop. The next day she and some sisters were walking when she waved down a chauffeur-driven limo and asked for a ride. The lady in the limo was happy to help the sisters, and on the way, Mother Cabrini spoke of the house she had dreamed of. When they arrived at the convent and were saying goodbye, the lady told her: "Mother Cabrini, that house you dreamed of is mine, I own it. I never thought of parting with it, but if I may be allowed to enter your Holy House for a moment and receive a glass of water in the name of Our Lord, your little orphans shall have their home with my blessing." When asked later how she had obtained such a beautiful property, Mother Cabrini would say "I paid for it with three treasures: my love, a dream, and a glass of water in His Name."
.
The Order had successfully established bases in three American cities, but Mother Cabrini was thinking bigger. She extended the Missionary Sisters work into Latin America, establishing schools in Nicaragua and Argentina. She established schools in Europe, including Paris, London, and Madrid. And she continued to work throughout the United States, including schools in Chicago, Scranton, and Newark. Based upon the needs of the Italian miners working in and around the Rocky Mountains, Mother Cabrini traveled to Denver and established schools, orphanages, and a mission center.
.
While until that point her focus had been solely on Italian immigrants, the Missionary Sisters began to see the needs of other immigrant groups, extending their work to Mexican immigrants in California. Despite her failing health, Mother Cabrini traveled across the country (and the world!), visiting each house, and personally establishing new locations. Her travels included: New York, Pennsylvania, Illinois, Louisiana, Colorado, California, Washington State, Central and South America and Europe.
.
During this time, she fulfilled another personal goal, and became a citizen of the United States. Mother Cabrini began contemplating missions in Alaska, and still felt pulled toward Asia. However, the impact of her travels began to take its toll, and at the age of 67, she died in Chicago, in a private room at Columbus Hospital, as she was preparing Christmas candy for the local children. Less than 30 years later, she was canonized as a Saint—the first United States citizen to be canonized—by Pope Pius XII. 
.
From the homily at the Canonization of Saint Frances Xavier Cabrini by Pope Pius XII: “Inspired by the grace of god, we join the saints in honoring the holy virgin Frances Xavier Cabrini. She was a humble woman who became outstanding not because she was famous or rich or powerful, but because she lived a virtuous life. From the tender years of her youth, she kept her innocence as white as a lily and preserved it carefully with the thorns of penitence; as the years progressed, she was moved by a certain instinct and supernatural zeal to dedicate her whole life to the service and greater glory of God. She welcomed delinquent youths into safe homes, and taught them to live upright and holy lives. She consoled those who were in prison, and recalled to them the hope of eternal life. She encouraged prisoners to reform themselves, and to live honest lives. She comforted the sick and the infirm in the hospitals, and diligently cared for them. She extended a friendly and helping hand especially to immigrants, and offered them necessary shelter and relief, for having left their homeland behind, they were wandering about in a foreign land with no place to turn for help. Because of their condition, she saw that they were in danger of deserting the practice of Christian virtues and their Catholic faith. Undoubtedly she accomplished all this through the faith which was always so vibrant and alive in her heart; through the divine love which burned within her; and finally, through constant prayer by which she was so closely united with God from whom she humbly asked and obtained whatever her human weakness could not obtain. Although her constitution was very frail, her spirit was endowed with such singular strength that, knowing the will of God in her regard, she permitted nothing to impede her from accomplishing what seemed beyond her strength.” 
.
Saint Frances Xavier Cabrini’s life was filled with disappointments… but she was never discouraged. Despite setbacks, weak health, and constant difficulty, the accomplishments of Mother Cabrini are remarkable. Ever humble, she took no credit, instead directing those who might compliment her work back to the Lord—to Jesus Christ—though which all things were (and are) accomplished. Throughout her life, Mother Cabrini found her strength in the Lord, and used every ounce given to her to serve others. We look to her today as a model of obedience, hope, service and strength. Mother Cabrini, pray for us!
.
Eternal Father, I wish to honor St. Frances Xavier Cabrini, and I give Thee thanks for all the  graces Thou hast bestowed upon her. I ask Thee to please increase grace in  my soul through the merits of this saint, and I commit the end of my life to her by this special prayer, so that by virtue of Thy goodness and promise, St.  Frances Xavier Cabrini might be my advocate and provide whatever is needed at that hour. Amen.

Greetings. I am Data and this is a broadcast of current human events you may find of interest. A Microsoft service outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for more than twelve hours, affecting businesses and government organizations around the world. Microsoft attributed the disruption to server problems and reported signs of recovery after deploying fixes.

I find humanity's technological infrastructure remarkably fragile. An entire civilization has become dependent upon systems that can suddenly cease functioning because a server experiences difficulties. On the Enterprise, this would be considered a critical systems failure. On Earth, it is called Thursday. I understand some employees were forced to communicate verbally. My condolences.

In other news, four advocacy organizations have filed a lawsuit against five major artificial intelligence companies, including OpenAI, Google, Meta, Anthropic, and SpaceX. The groups seek to prevent development and deployment of new AI models, alleging that increasingly powerful systems pose unacceptable risks.

As an artificial life-form, I find this dispute personally intriguing. Humanity is attempting to create machines that can reason independently, while simultaneously expressing considerable anxiety about machines reasoning independently. My creator, Doctor Soong, encountered similar difficulties. Fortunately, he never had to explain my existence to a California superior court. I suspect the paperwork would have been considerable.

This concludes your broadcast of current human events. I had intended to offer an optimistic assessment of humanity's future, but Spot has just vomited on my research notes. I believe she is expressing editorial disagreement. Her analysis is difficult to refute.

2027: Abiodun Unveils 50,400 Renewed Hope Apostles for Grassroots Campaign Across Ogun

Ogun State Governor, @DapoAbiodunCON, has inaugurated 50,400 grassroots canvassers, known as Renewed Hope Apostles, across the state's 20 local government areas to mobilise support for the APC ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The initiative will deploy the canvassers across Ogun's 236 wards for door-to-door engagement, educating residents on the achievements of the APC-led governments at federal, state and local government levels.

Abiodun disclosed this during strategic meetings with party leaders and stakeholders, explaining that the initiative would strengthen grassroots mobilisation, counter misinformation and take government achievements directly to households.

He revealed that 15,000 canvassers had been selected in Ogun East, bringing the statewide figure to 50,400. He added that their recruitment and verification took approximately three months.

Highlighting federal projects benefiting Ogun State, the governor mentioned the Sagamu-Ijebu-Ode-Ore Road reconstruction, Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, Gateway Deep Sea Port, revival of the Ogun LNG project and establishment of a major Customs facility.

On his administration's achievements, Abiodun listed over 1,700 kilometres of roads constructed, more than 1,600 schools rehabilitated or constructed, and over 7,000 housing units delivered.

He also highlighted the upgrading of 160 Primary Healthcare Centres, construction of new hospitals, completion of the 250-bed Gateway Medical Centre of Excellence, establishment of independent power plants and support for over 20,000 farmers.

Additionally, he disclosed that over 60,000 women had benefited from the Oko Owo Dapo empowerment initiative, while cooperative societies and artisans had received over ₦1 billion in financial support. His administration has also recruited more than 7,000 teaching personnel.

The governor urged the Renewed Hope Apostles to remain committed and disciplined, stressing that their responsibility was to communicate government achievements, address public concerns and mobilise support for the APC.

He also called for unity among party members, emphasising that internal cohesion and effective grassroots coordination were essential to electoral victory.

Prominent APC leaders, including State Chairman, Chief Yemi Sanusi; Senator Lekan Mustapha; and other party stakeholders, pledged their commitment to mobilising support for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, Governor Abiodun and all APC candidates.

The stakeholder engagements have covered several local government areas, including Sagamu, Ikenne, Ijebu-Ode, Ifo, Ewekoro, Abeokuta North, Abeokuta South, Odeda and Obafemi-Owode, among others.

The exercise forms part of Governor Abiodun's broader mobilisation strategy ahead of the 2027 general elections.

By: Selina Nyarko Prah (Sis.)
Pastor Joseph Owusu-Boateng, Resident Minister of PIWC Winneba, has urged Christians to develop a genuine concern for the glory of God, emphasising that believers must be willing to defend His name, uphold His honour and place His purposes above their personal interests. Delivering a sermon titled “Concern for the Glory of God” during the climax of the District Week, dubbed Grace Convocation, at PIWC Winneba, Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that a defining characteristic of people who walk closely with God is their concern for His glory.

Drawing from 2 Samuel 7:1–4, he examined the lives of three biblical figures, David, Elijah and Nehemiah, whose devotion to God was reflected in their commitment to His honour and purposes. He began with the story of David, who, despite living in a magnificent palace, became concerned that the Ark of God remained in a tent. According to the Resident Minister, David's desire to build a house for God demonstrated a heart that placed God's glory above personal comfort.

Although David was not permitted to build the temple, he did not abandon his concern for God's house. Instead, he deliberately made extensive preparations and provided resources for its construction. Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that David's response revealed the depth of his commitment to God. 

He challenged the congregation to consider how they would react if someone rejected an offer they had made with good intentions. He observed that many people would simply withdraw their support after such a response. David, however, continued making provisions for the temple, ensuring that the resources needed for its construction would be available.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng emphasised that genuine concern for God's glory does not disappear when personal expectations are not met. Rather, it motivates believers to remain committed to God's purposes even when they are not the ones chosen to carry out a particular assignment. He further referred to 1 Samuel 17:26, where David questioned the audacity of Goliath, the uncircumcised Philistine, who had defied the armies of the living God.

According to Pastor Owusu-Boateng, David's response was motivated by his concern for God's reputation rather than a desire for personal recognition. While others saw Goliath as a terrifying opponent, David recognised that the honour of the living God was being challenged. His willingness to confront the Philistine demonstrated a determination to defend God's name when others were afraid to act.

Turning to the life of Elijah, Pastor Owusu-Boateng referred to 1 Kings 18:21, where the prophet confronted the Israelites over their divided allegiance between God and Baal. He explained that Elijah could not tolerate the people's continued wavering between two opinions. The prophet was determined to demonstrate that the Lord alone was worthy of their worship.

Referring also to 1 Kings 18:24, he highlighted Elijah's challenge on Mount Carmel, where the God who answered by fire would be acknowledged as the true God. Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that Elijah's actions were not intended to promote himself but to restore the people's recognition of God's supremacy. He emphasised that when a believer's motives are genuinely directed towards God's glory, God is able to demonstrate His power in defence of His name.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng also identified Nehemiah among the biblical examples of individuals whose lives reflected a deep concern for God's honour and purposes.

Drawing lessons from these examples, Pastor Owusu-Boateng outlined the characteristics of people who are genuinely concerned about the glory of God. First, he explained that such individuals are grieved whenever God is dishonoured. They do not remain indifferent when God's name is treated with contempt or when conduct within the Church brings dishonour to Him.

He further stressed that believers who genuinely love God's glory do not celebrate the failures of the Church. According to him, rather than laughing when the Church experiences difficulties or setbacks, they are moved with concern and seek its restoration and progress. He challenged Christians to examine their reactions when they hear negative reports about the Church, explaining that their responses often reveal whether their concern is for God's glory or their personal interests.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng also emphasised that people who seek God's glory live for His pleasure rather than their own. Referring to 1 Corinthians 10:31, he reminded the congregation that whether Christians eat, drink or engage in any other activity, everything should be done to the glory of God. He explained that genuine devotion to God must influence everyday decisions, personal conduct and the motives behind one's actions.

Another characteristic he highlighted was the willingness to defend the name of the Lord. He explained that believers who are concerned about God's glory do not remain silent when His name is dishonoured. Like David and Elijah, they are willing to take a stand for God even when others are unwilling to do so.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng further emphasised the responsibility of Christians to proclaim God's name and make Him known to others. He noted that concern for God's glory should not remain a private conviction but must find expression in a believer's willingness to speak about God and make His greatness known.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that genuine concern for God's glory also purifies a person's motives and transforms their mindset. According to him, when God's honour becomes the primary motivation behind a believer's actions, personal ambition and the desire for recognition begin to give way to a sincere commitment to pleasing Him.

He encouraged Christians to evaluate the reasons behind their service, sacrifices and involvement in church activities, emphasising that the desire to glorify God must remain central. He further noted that those who consistently seek God's glory develop a relationship with Him marked by His favour and approval.

Concluding his message, Pastor Owusu-Boateng challenged the congregation to follow the examples of David and Elijah by demonstrating a genuine concern for God's honour in every area of life. His message reinforced the need for Christians to move beyond merely professing love for God and demonstrate that love through their willingness to defend His name, support His work, proclaim His greatness and live according to His purposes.

text:
Advance Scouting Report on Fernando Mendoza

By: Former New York Jets Pro Scout Daniel Kelly

@Seahawks @Broncos @Browns @chargers @Titans @AZCardinals @Chiefs 

Background: Indiana carried Fernando Mendoza with their run game and their National Championship roster, and he’s coming off a rough preseason for the Raiders. He had one appearance during the regular season for Las Vegas vs. New England where he threw mostly short passes in one drive.

In the preseason, Mendoza played in three games and completed 55.6% of his passes, 1 TD, 2 INT, 4 Sacks (Fox Sports). 

Per Pro Football Focus (PFF) Mendoza preseason: 

4/5 (behind the line of scrimmage) 80.0%

17/23 (0-9 yards) 73.9%

5/10 (10-19 yards) 50.0%

0/2 (20+ yards) 0%

Per PFF:

During the preseason, Mendoza’s time to throw was 3.02 seconds (ranked No. 79/108) in the NFL, and he had a 21.1% Pressure to sack P2S% (ranked No. 67/108) in the NFL.

Completion percentages (PFF):

Kept clean: 65.6%
Under pressure: 35.7%
Not blitzed: 55.3%
When blitzed: 62.5%

Preseason summary: Mendoza was conservative, had a slow time to throw, and a below 60% completion percentage vs. vanilla defensive schemes. He also struggled vs. pressure. 

Mendoza showed at Indiana and in his NFL experience to date that he is an elementary and limited game manager. 

He has the skillset of a third string quarterback in the NFL. 

He has a conservative and calculated nature.

Mendoza is a sequential hardcore rigid linear thinker. He needs to have everything lined up for him just so and he needs everything to go as planned. He does not have a mind that can quickly and successfully adapt to change.

He is not a dual-threat. He looks stiff and awkward as a runner and he lacks bend. When he runs, he looks like a first baseman trying to steal second.

He wants to work from the pocket and he likes the highest percentage throws that offer him the most throwing leverage.

At Indiana, Mendoza either handed the ball off or he repetitively kept throwing the same 3-4 pass routes that offered him the most throwing leverage. Mendoza was very repetitive. Indiana’s No. 13 (Team Rankings) rushing attack propped him up. Indiana averaged 207.3 rushing yards per game. They averaged 33.8 rushing attempts per game (Team Rankings). 

*Mendoza depended on the run game at Indiana.

At Indiana, his completion percentage dropped to 53.2% when he was forced to move (ESPN) and 51.2% (PFF) when he was under pressure last season. 

https://t.co/pbP2dhAnVY

Last season at Indiana vs. Purdue, he completed 53.3% of his passes. That was his lowest completion percentage of the season. Purdue did that by showing him a lot of different defensive looks as talked about in this video clip: https://t.co/xqAaUlUzof

Mendoza loves to throw high percentage passes to the outside to the sidelines. 

When the University of Miami tightened up their outside pass coverage in the second half of the National Championship Game, Mendoza’s completion percentage dropped to 40.0% https://t.co/rz3LW2ARx3

Raiders unit rankings (PFF)

Rushing: No. 25 (65.7)
Pass blocking: No. 28 (58.0)
Defense: No. 32 (50.5)
Special Teams: No. 22 (78.0)

How to defeat Mendoza: 

• Play 8 in the box and dare him to throw it. He’s going to try to lean heavily on the run game the way he did at Indiana. They are going to try to run to set up the pass. Take away the run. Put the game on Mendoza’s shoulders. 

• Show him a lot of different looks defensively pre-snap. Then switch it up on him post-snap. Make his mind attempt to adapt.

• Flush him out of the pocket. 

• Focus on taking away the short passing game and outside passing game (sidelines). That’s his bread and butter. 

• Play tight man coverage.

• Cornerbacks should sit on his trademark sideline routes as seen in this video clip: https://t.co/f63IssFnM6

Key to victory: 

Get Mendoza down on the scoreboard early.

text:
They Can't Sign It Tomorrow. They're Building It for 2029.

Democrats just took the House 254–167 and the Senate by a working majority. They flipped Texas. They have a governor-elect in Austin who has already told The Washington Post she will tear down a terrorism designation. And they have a two-year problem named Donald Trump, who can veto almost anything they send him until January 20, 2029.
That last sentence is not a lullaby. It is a countdown.

They do not have the votes to override him. A veto dies unless two-thirds of both chambers say otherwise — 290 in the House and 67 in the Senate. They have 254 and about 54. So no, they cannot enact Medicare for All, a national amnesty, or a 13-justice Court in February. Anyone who tells you they can is selling panic, not a bill. The honest danger is different: they will spend the next two years investigating, defunding, legislating for the record, and changing the rules of the Senate so that the first Democrat who takes the White House can sign the stack.
Chuck Schumer already admitted the wall is there. "Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump's and Republicans' intransigence, of course not," he said after the election. Then he promised to fight "bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes."

They will not say "open borders." Watch what they fund.

No serious Democratic leader ran around the country shouting "open borders." Hakeem Jeffries, the next speaker, says the system is "broken" and should be "fixed in a bipartisan way." Fine. Then listen to the rest of the sentence. House Democrats, he told reporters, will not give "a dime" to what he calls the administration's "violent mass deportation machine." He wants to redirect $75 billion previously provided to Immigration and Customs Enforcement through 2029. ICE, in his words, got a "slush fund so that masked agents could brutalize and kill American citizens, and violently target law-abiding immigrant communities."
That is a promise to starve the agency that enforces the law we have.

The bill they are actually waving is the American Dream and Promise Act, from Rep. Sylvia Garcia of Texas. It would offer permanent-resident status — a green card, with a path beyond it — to immigrants brought here as children and to people whose temporary protected status was revoked, if they have been in the country since 2021 and meet education, military, or work tests and a background check. Republicans call that amnesty. Trump has said, "There is no amnesty." The text is a legalization program, and legalization is the point.

Some Democrats talked this fall about abolishing or gutting ICE. After the election, a Capitol press conference of progressives and moderates declined to offer a plan to abolish it. They talked instead about "legal pathways for long-term immigrants." Do not confuse a change in tone with a change in destination. The destination is less enforcement and more status for people who entered or stayed illegally. The people who benefit first are not the citizens who waited in line.

Medicare for All is not a vibe. It is a bill, and the bill is enormous.

Leadership's first-hundred-days health talk is more incremental: restore Affordable Care Act subsidies, reverse Medicaid cuts. Jeffries and Schumer have not even sponsored the current Medicare for All bill. The progressive wing will not stay quiet, and some new members ran on the real thing.
The real thing is on paper. The Medicare for All Act introduced in April 2025 by Rep. Pramila Jayapal would entitle "every individual who is a resident of the United States" to benefits, bar discrimination on the basis of "citizenship status," and let the Health and Human Services secretary extend eligibility to other people "to ensure that every person in the United States has access to health care." It would also prohibit private insurers from selling coverage that "duplicates the benefits" of the program, and prohibit employers from offering duplicate coverage.
