I'd have to think of a way to steelman a case against that, with Grok's help I guess. It doesn't specify what a regime of property rights looks like - does current IP law match the ideal? - and so it might be considered too abstract a statement to qualify as steelmanning. But it does correctly state in concise, essentialized, and strong terms what the point of Rand's advocacy for capitalism is, tied to philosophical fundamentals as much as a 280-character statement can be: something about the creative intellect as a or the defining characteristic of something desirable such as human civilization or advanced-civilization ethics such as respect for individual achievement and autonomy. Why on earth should the state be allowed to treat man as a sacrificial animal, Rand asked, especially given that free creative intellectual activity is the root of progress and flourishing? (Throw in something about how Rand supplies an economic corollary to the principle of JS Mill's On Liberty concerning how the free market of ideas leads to progress/flourishing, and you've got something pretty steelmannable here? We're not selling 'utopia' or a revolution in human culture here, just some common sense cause-and-effect recognizing about the relation between freedom of the creative intellect on the one hand and progress/flourishing on the other. OTOH it took how many centuries between Plato/Aristotle on the one hand and Mises/Rand on the other for the 'common sense' arc of history to bend toward laissez-faire capitalism or more broadly private property / free markets?)

(Thoughts that come to me as I ponder the ~4 hour podcast interview between Papola (Dad Saves America) and a Marxist History Prof. I wish there were many more conversations at that level and while the Marxist guy raised many of what I'd call interesting points, they just don't seem to come to grips with a steelmanned case for capitalism like the Randian one. A dog not barking is that there's hardly any mention of Rand in the whole interview, I think Papola brings her up once, even though there's never been any decent rebuttal to the essence of her theme/thesis in Atlas and elsewhere re the mind, freedom and flourishing. Nothing whatsoever in all of Marxist Professor Guy's verbal outpourings really touched upon how under capitalism those using their creative intellects best will tend to accumulate greater power in the marketplace - what Rand called economic power, which is the power to command the direction of economic resources based on the will expressed by the customers re one's products (of one's intellect). What Marxist Professor Guy and his ilk would need to plausibly show is how confiscating the physical capital owned by Musk to the tune of so much percentage and handing it over to other people is a better way - applying the Millian & Randian observations concerning the relation between freedom and progress in this or that marketplace, no less -  to steward economic resources and improve living standards. Somehow Marxist Professor Guy thinks there's compelling evidence in favor of confiscating Musk's wealth and letting Democrats (who ruin institutions & create legitimacy crises) decide instead how those funds are best used? I think his more plausible critiques of society are focused elsewhere, and I notice a dog not barking is that hardly anywhere in the whole ~4 hours of podcast are the Aristotelian criteria for actual praxis and flourishing touched upon. Marx Guy just keeps going on about the social conditions for flourishing. Isn't this the same basic problem with liberalism as conservatives often frame it - that it peddles freedom as a condition for living a good life but then has so little to say or offer in the way of the best uses of that freedom in a virtuous life? For Marxism it seems like all of 'ethics' is embedded in what it takes to bring about the communist end-goal. History has shown what this mentality has done, to the tune of ~100M killed by Marxist lunatics with power. And yet in ~4 hours that kinda-central point hardly gets touched upon, it's mostly stuff about political economy. It's almost surely and by a good margin the best engagement I'v ever seen from a Marxist and yet Rand & ethics (or, heck, epistemological methods if not metaphysical fundamentals) hardly get brought up? I'll just mention that Marxism is quite the minority viewpoint in Philosophy despite taking over so much of the humanities and social sciences (Econ excepted - parallels with Philosophy here?). Marx shows up around #20 in polls of philosophers when it comes to influence, with Plato-Aristotle-Kant holding well onto the Big Three. Is the complaint from Marxists about something like this, that their ideas just haven't been steelmanned hard enough, that the 70 bloody years of commie experimenting were some kind of fluke? And what f'ing right do Marxists of all people have to complain about ideas not being steelmanned hard enough? Marx Guy should have known well, and volunteered to bring up and refute the steelmanned Rand, if he were really up to the task. Again, that was the *very best* engagement I've *ever* seen from a Marxist over a matter of decades, and by Drill Instructor standards it still sucks.)

TWELVE HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 10PM TO 10AM on 11/15/26

In this window the channel record widened again: the Wall Street Journal reported records showing Megaspeed arranged to send nearly $12 billion of top Nvidia chips to companies in China, a fifth chip figure with its own window, and reported an unwritten Nvidia rule capping partners' Chinese customers and a new channel node, Aolani Cloud. Megaspeed answered publicly for the first time on Alice Huang, saying she left the company effective August 30, 2025 and that it has retained outside counsel for an internal investigation. The Washington Post reported Huang is quietly helping pick his own successor, and Elon Musk said many of Nvidia's supply deals were a handshake with Huang personally.

A FIFTH CHIP FIGURE

• The Wall Street Journal reported that records it reviewed show Megaspeed arranged to send nearly $12 billion worth of top-of-the-line Nvidia chips to companies in China between March 2024 and June 2025, the shipment records showing orders for several hundred thousand chips. The records do not show how much of the hardware was actually delivered or where it originated.
• This is a fifth chip figure in the case, owned by the Journal with its own window. It is not merged or summed with the other four: the customs figure of at least $4.6 billion and at least 136,000 GPUs from 2023 to November 2025, the Speedmatrix reconstruction of $4.606 billion from December 2024 to January 2026, the $4.8 billion figure from June 2024 to February 2026, or the network figure of at least $7.5 billion and about 240,000 chips since 2023. The Journal's reporting rests on records it reviewed; the records themselves were not seen in the case record.

THE RULES NVIDIA SET, UNWRITTEN

• The Journal also reported that beginning last year Nvidia required many of its cloud partners outside China to keep their Chinese customers below a certain level, which has shifted between 30% and 49%, though the rule was not written into any contracts, people familiar with the matter said.
• Per the same reporting, Nvidia also urged some cloud partners to weed out Chinese nationals from top management and push out Chinese investors, the people said.

A NEW CHANNEL NODE

• The Journal reported that Aolani Cloud, a Singapore cloud-computing provider and Nvidia partner, courted investors last year saying the geopolitical situation provided a unique opportunity for companies that could connect Chinese customers with advanced chips, explaining in an investor presentation viewed by the Journal that top Chinese internet companies had to rent the chips they were blocked from buying.
• Per the Journal, Aolani's investors helped it fund some $2.5 billion in hardware in Malaysia by the beginning of this year, and its anchor customer is ByteDance. Aolani says it has systems in place to strictly adhere to U.S. regulations and has been focused on building a global customer base.

MEGASPEED ANSWERS

• Megaspeed told CNBC on Sunday, November 15, in an emailed statement: "Ms. Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the Company," adding "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters." The August 30, 2025 date places her exit before the affair reporting broke in late October 2026.
• In the same statement, Megaspeed said media reports about its business, supply chain and global operations are not supported by verifiable evidence and that it has retained external legal counsel, no firm named, to conduct a "thorough internal investigation". It stated that it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements", and added that it will review the reporting and communicate further with stakeholders as appropriate.
• The Journal separately reported that Megaspeed said this past week that it retained a U.S. law firm to lead a census of its graphics processing units, and that Megaspeed told the Journal it takes compliance seriously and is committed to following U.S. law, while Nvidia told the Journal it works to prevent smuggling. Whether the census engagement and the internal investigation are the same retention is not established by either report. This is Megaspeed's first statement announcing an internal investigation.

HUANG IN THE SUCCESSOR SEARCH

• The Washington Post reported on November 14 that Jensen Huang is quietly helping pick his own successor at Nvidia: he has kept a low profile since resigning on November 12, but he is involved in Nvidia's CEO search and has personally called at least one potential candidate. CFO Colette Kress serves as interim CEO.
• The Post report rests on a person familiar with the matter. The Post original is paywalled and was not read firsthand in the case record; the report was read through detailed carriages that agree verbatim on the load-bearing points. Huang's personal participation, if the Post's account is right, sits alongside the board's November 13 statement that it was still selecting a search firm and had not formally engaged any candidate.

MUSK ON THE HANDSHAKE DEALS

• Elon Musk posted on X on November 14: "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract. Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
• That is Musk's assertion and prediction, stated as a directly involved market party and Huang supporter. No document or counterparty corroboration is offered, and the contract form of any Nvidia supply deal has not been verified in the case record. It lands against South Korea's statement in the prior window that Nvidia has reconfirmed its 260,000 GPU supply plan at the corporate level after the resignation.

THE CHECKPOINTS

• November 15: House Select Committee Chair John Moolenaar appears on Face the Nation at 10:30 a.m. ET on the Nvidia scandal and the AI chip war.
• November 17: Nvidia earnings, and the Warren and Coons records preservation confirmation is due.
• November 24: Bennet's answers due.
• December 1: Huang's requested closed door transcribed interview before the three House committees, and the House Foreign Affairs Democrats' answers due.
• December 2: Teter's requested closed door transcribed interview.
• December 3: Scott's requested public Senate Banking hearing with Huang, and the Foreign Affairs hearing with Under Secretary Kessler at 10 a.m.
• December 10: Scott's requested public Senate Banking hearing with Lutnick.

text:
Lately I've been posting a lot about UK politics, but Ukraine and European security are where my heart actually is. 

People in Britain often treat European energy news like a distant story, even though UK heating bills move with the exact same market, and almost everyone is missing the single biggest structural victory of this entire war.

Let's rewind back to December 2024, when an LNG tanker called the Gaslog Savannah docked in Greece carrying American gas from Louisiana, just days before the transit contract allowing Russian gas across Ukraine expired. 

Ukraine's DTEK bought that initial 100-million-cubic-meter cargo and sent part of it north through the old Balkan pipelines. For decades, that steel only carried Russian gas south. Suddenly, it ran the other way.

In my view, Putin completely misunderstood modern logistics. 

He thought winter would break Europe and force capitals like London and Berlin to abandon Kyiv. A pipeline is a trap that locks your foreign policy to a dictator, while a tanker can simply turn around in the middle of the ocean.

That shift quietly rewired how European homes stay warm. For decades, gas ran on rigid, state-backed pipeline monopolies. Today, at the margin, it runs on floating cargoes, which require an entirely different breed of company.

Venture Global is integrating production, shipping, and regasification, having already booked space at Greece's Alexandroupolis terminal. Poland's Orlen flipped from an importer to a direct supplier for Ukraine. Meanwhile, BGN Group launched an LNG desk in 2024, was landing cargoes in Germany by summer 2025, and has since moved into LNG shipping and long-term supply talks.

Different companies from different countries, all pulling in the same direction. Energy security is moving out of state-owned pipes and into flexible portfolios of ships, terminals, and contracts held by agile firms most ordinary citizens have never heard of.

The next decisive test arrives in weeks. Europe still bought record amounts of Russian LNG in March, which shows how badly parts of the continent stayed hooked. Yet on January 1, 2027, the EU's ban reaches long-term Russian contracts too, and Brussels has so far refused to delay it.

Buyers are about to be hunting for replacement cargoes mid-winter. 

Britain bids for the exact same Atlantic ships with barely any storage of its own, meaning what British households pay this winter now depends on the companies that can find a vessel and a price within days.

Putin tried to turn heating into a weapon. Europe answered with ships on the water.

text:
Was this whole thing an attempt to shake down the infidels? The Islamization of Europe is proceeding apace, and amid all the crime sprees, mass rapes, random jihad attacks, intimidation, threats, and boasts of imminent takeover, there is also a touch of the absurd. How could there not be? When has a civilization ever committed suicide before? The whole situation is absurd, so why shouldn’t there be a few absurd incidents?

The German-language publication Unzensuriert reported Monday that “Vienna-based business owner Peter Schaider is facing preliminary proceedings before an administrative tribunal,” and the accusation against him is weighty: It seems that he rejected “an applicant for an apprenticeship in the hairdressing trade,” and “the case stems from allegations of discrimination, as the rejection was based on the applicant’s decision to wear a headscarf.”

That’s right. A Muslim woman wearing a hijab applied to be a hairdresser, was turned down, and is now claiming that she was discriminated against. Her target in this absurd shakedown attempt, the hairdresser Schaider, is just as confused as everyone else: He “expressed bewilderment regarding the legal scrutiny of the matter. He emphasized that the hairdressing profession is defined, above all, by the presentation of hairstyles: ‘I was told this constitutes discrimination. But our business is built on styling, beauty, and hair fashion. You can’t have people standing there wearing a headscarf. I’m sorry, but that just doesn’t work.’”

That’s right, it doesn’t, any more than it would work to have a fat person giving dieting instruction, as Schaider himself noted: “In his view, personal appearance plays a crucial role in establishing credibility when selling hairdressing services: ‘We sell hair accessories. You wouldn’t expect someone weighing 130 kilos to sell weight-loss products, would you? That simply doesn’t work.’” Ah, but anything works nowadays if it advances the impression that Muslims are the poor, terrified victims of a relentless, remorseless “Islamophobia.” Portraying oneself as a victim so as to gain the special protections and freedom from scrutiny that victim status offers — it’s a growth industry.

Boston’s public radio station, WGBH, claimed last September that “Muslim community leaders say women who wear hijab often experience an especially high rate of harassment because their Islamic faith is more visible in public.”

We hear that asserted all the time, but there are never any specific incidents described. Why not? Here are some incidents: An eleven-year-old girl in Toronto made international headlines with her claim that a man had followed her and cut her hijab with scissors. After an investigation, police concluded that the attack never happened. Likewise, Yasmin Seweid, a Muslim teen, claimed in December 2016 that Trump supporters on a New York subway tore off her hijab and no one in the packed subway car helped her. She, too, gained international media attention, and she, too, made up the whole thing. Shortly before that, a hijab-wearing Muslim student at San Diego State University also falsely claimed that she was assaulted by Trump supporters.

In July 2017, a Muslim in Britain falsely claimed that a man had pulled off her hijab in a “race hate attack.” In November 2016, a University of Michigan Muslim student claimed she was “accosted by a white man who told her to remove her hijab or he would set her ablaze with a cigarette lighter.” She also fabricated the whole event.

Now, Peter Schaider over in Vienna isn’t being accused of a “hate crime,” but simply of employment discrimination. Yet the plaintiff in the case against him is as ridiculous as would be a Muslim who claimed employment discrimination for not being hired as a clerk in a liquor store. The owner of such a store might not want a clerk who thinks that drinking alcohol will send you to hell, but as Schaider’s case demonstrates, in Europe and North America today, we aren’t allowed to have common sense.

Peter Schaider should have looked at the hijab-wearing woman who wanted a job in his hairdressing salon and realized that she wasn’t just a job applicant. She was a sign of the times. And he was expected to capitulate to the absurd demand she was making, to be employed as a hairdresser though she kept her own hair covered, for fear of charges of “Islamophobia.” It’s increasingly clear that if the West wants to survive as the home of free societies, it’s going to have to reject the “Islamophobia” narrative and repudiate the “Islamophobia” industry. But that is not on the horizon.

text:
The key is Mafdet.  Piankoff uses panther cat, but the other translators use Mafdet.  Once you understand it becomes one key to unlocking the snake spells.  

I describe it all here:  

A Word About Serpent Spells
The inquiry into serpent spells belongs within this book’s expanding examination of royal protection, speech, and ascent. Richard C. Steiner’s Early Northwest Semitic Serpent Spells in the Pyramid Texts (2011) opens an important linguistic question; its published abstract describes two Egyptian spell sequences containing Semitic passages as protection for the king’s mummy against snakes.[^3:web_23ea61e6^] This book asks a further question: how far can protection against reptile danger also carry an application to human hostility against the king?

Mafdet gives that question an early royal foundation. In Petrie’s 1901 report, an alabaster cylinder jar bears Den’s name together with her standard; a separate reconstructed crystal vase shows the goddess holding a sceptre above the title “mistress of the house of life” (p. 25).[^4:web_f19b209d^] These objects must not be conflated. They establish her early presence in royal material, but do not themselves label her Den’s executioner against rebels.

Griffith’s discussion supplies the punitive connection. Examining the hooked rod, cords, and knife, he interprets the emblem as a ceremonial combination for catching, binding, and killing “whether in regard to malefactors or to animals” (p. 50). He relates it to attendants carrying out justice, warfare, or hunting and proposes Mafdet as a divine hunter and executioner. His language remains qualified, and he notes uncertainty about one crystal fragment’s provenance.[^5:web_84f64c98^] The significance is nevertheless substantial: human wrongdoing and animal danger already meet within this longstanding interpretation of her emblem.

In Unas, the Mafdet passages identified here—UT 295, 297, and 298—belong beside the wider use of serpentine power rather than outside it. In the Cannibal Hymn, UT 274, the snake Lifted-Head serves Unas by guarding and restraining those delivered to him. A serpent can therefore stand on the king’s side as well as confront him: protection of the king and power exercised on his behalf are distinct but compatible relationships. UT 302 directly connects the annulment of hostile words among men and accusation among gods with ascent. UT 23 adds the seizure of those who hate Unas, while UT 214 threatens the standing in his own city of anyone who speaks evil against the king’s name as he ascends. These passages differ in agent, action, and consequence; they do not constitute one continuous scene. Together, however, they give this book grounds to test a dual application of serpent protection: defense against dangerous creatures and, where the individual spell’s context sustains it, defense against human enemies and defamatory speech. That second application is a cumulative interpretation, not a translation of every snake into a rebel.

The two architectural groups therefore require comparison rather than a single explanation imposed upon both. This inquiry proposes that the antechamber material may emphasize personal protection and the neutralization of hostility, while the burial-chamber group may also extend royal power toward a wider territorial field. This is a distinction of possible emphasis, not an exclusive division between private danger and public sovereignty. UT 210 and UT 222 are contextual witnesses outside the serpent-spell group, not additional serpent spells. UT 210, §126, calls upon the inhabitants of Nubia to arise before the Great Trembler and the Opener-of-the-Way; UT 230, §234, invokes the two knots of Elephantine in the mouth of Osiris, knotted for Horus over the backbone. These references justify examining a southern setting, but the command to arise does not itself identify an invasion, and the backbone’s identification with the Nile remains an interpretation. Two further burial-chamber witnesses widen the southern cluster. UT 205, §121, in Piankoff’s rendering calls Unas “the Great Bull who strikes Nubia,” and UT 206 is identical to it. The line stands in a context of provisions and offerings, and it may be a conventional royal epithet, so its wording and force must be checked across editions before it carries weight. UT 217, §§153–159, has the gods announce Unas to the South, North, West, and East, with Seth and Nephthys addressing the South, and UT 218, §164, declares that the Southern, Northern, Western, and Eastern Ones belong to him. These passages show a southern orientation within a larger four-quarter claim; they do not isolate Nubia.

UT 222, §§203–206, places confrontation with an adversary beside paired declarations of Seth-associated power in the South and Horus-associated power in the North. The repeated assurance that something will not be lost or cease for the addressed king does not explicitly say that Unas pledges never to abandon Seth. Its parallel structure must remain visible. Frankfort’s account of the Sed festival provides a useful ritual comparison: the Upper Egyptian ceremony pairs Horus of Edfu and Seth of Ombos, whose priests supply the king’s bow and arrows for action toward the four directions. This supports the connection between divine agency and royal authority, not a geographic itinerary or proof of the locality intended in Unas.[^1:image_0a5d55a2^]

UT 242, §247, makes the geographic question more pointed by declaring that the flame-serpent is not found in the house of the possessor of Ombos, before describing a biting serpent entering the house of its intended victim. In the note supplied for this inquiry, Piankoff identifies the possessor of Ombos as the king of Upper Egypt. The text nevertheless leaves crucial relationships to be resolved: whether Unas is the serpent, who is to be bitten, and which Ombos is intended. Kom Ombo, the first town north of Elephantine, offers a relevant frontier and trade-route setting, but Nubt/Ombos near Naqada is documented as a town of Seth and is the more securely attested Seth center.[^2:file_8f103483^][^3:web_22fb0ba7^] This book therefore treats Naqada as the more probable referent, for the cultic and strategic reasons set out below, while retaining Kom Ombo and a possible warning against Nubian encroachment as hypotheses to test, not as established geographic or historical identifications. The selected cluster does not prove that these are the only geographic references in the surrounding texts.

The choice between the two Ombos matters because the sites stand at different points on the king’s lines of communication. If a warning from the south required a response, a reaction force would need to sit between the capital and the cataract. By approximate modern river distance, Naqada lies roughly 600–650 km upriver of Memphis and about 240 km below Elephantine; Kom Ombo lies roughly 815 km from Memphis and only about 45 km from Elephantine. Read through the planning factors of mission, enemy, terrain, troops, and time, Naqada is the stronger place to house and sustain a force and to respond along the valley, while Kom Ombo would function as a forward post that could not easily be reinforced. If the warning in UT 242 were genuine, a base at Naqada would reflect sound military judgment, but the text states only the warning. The population density map after Butzer shows these southern nomes in comparable shading and does not label Naqada; the inference that Naqada’s reach was more populous rests on the cluster of larger towns there and remains to be tested.

ConsiderationNaqada (Nubt)Kom Ombo
Seth cultDocumented as a town of Seth; major Predynastic centerEarlier cult presence not demonstrated here; the surviving temple is Ptolemaic
Distance from Memphis (approx. river km)600–650815
Distance to Elephantine (approx. river km)24045
Settlement in the surrounding reachCluster of larger towns (inference; not labeled on the density map)Southern nome 1; thinly settled by comparison (shading unconfirmed)
Likely military roleReaction base between capital and cataractForward post near the frontier, far from the capital
Status in this bookFavored provisionallyRetained as a hypothesis
Distances are rounded, approximate modern river distances to be verified on a map; no travel times are given because season, wind, and current are unsettled.

The Nubian background is thin for the reign of Unas. Group A is generally held to have been driven from Lower Nubia in the Fourth Dynasty after Sneferu’s activity, and Egyptian presence at Buhen is reported to have lasted about two centuries before ending late in the Fifth Dynasty, probably under pressure from the south. Group C is often considered the population that reconstituted and returned. The reign of Unas lies in a documentary gap between these horizons. This inquiry therefore assumes, and says it assumes, that renewed southern pressure was perceptible, since otherwise the southern emphasis of the burial-chamber utterances would be harder to explain. Whether that pressure reached Naqada or consisted only of early arrivals and unwanted incursions cannot be determined from the texts, and the phrase “the possessor of Ombos” may be read as a forecast that the south required a standing royal presence. That reading is an inference. Which king’s name was the last left at Buhen also remains unresolved: Baines and Malek’s Atlas names Neuserre, while an account of Neferirkare’s reign reports seal impressions bearing his name at the fortress. Group C dating and the Buhen sequence must be checked in Emery (1965), Adams (1977), Trigger (1976), and O’Connor (1993) before they carry weight.

UT 231, §235, adds another possible expression of royal enforcement. Its harpoon, the overthrow of nomads, and the declaration “This is the god Hemen!” deserve attention within the burial-chamber group. In the note supplied here, Piankoff reports Sethe’s interpretation of the king as a divine harpooner striking a hippopotamus that represents enemies of the realm, and associates Hemen with Asphynis near Esna. The hippopotamus belongs to that explanatory note, not to the quoted wording of §235; neither nomads nor enemies of the realm should automatically be identified as Nubians. The reported absence of “To say” in this presentation is likewise a source-control question, not sufficient evidence that Unas alone speaks directly from beyond the grave. A stronger starting point for continued authority is UT 213, which gives the living, transfigured king command over the living and the dead.[^4:web_7189dab5^] The further claim that this authority performs a specific southern defensive mission remains interpretive.

The political force of this reading does not depend on declaring that Unas feared no reptiles or that bodily protection was merely a disguise. Royal command, ritual defense, and concern for the king’s name can coexist. Nor does uncertainty about a southern locality invalidate independently supported evidence for hostile speech, retaliation, or continued royal authority. The question is not whether politics replaces the funerary register, but how protection of the king’s body, protection of his authority, and power exercised by the transfigured king may remain joined. The proposed territorial extension must earn its place spell by spell; it cannot be supplied by geography or historical background alone.

text:
A coop door opens, and two ducks are already in the middle of something older than the door.

In mallard-type ducks, evolution handed out the roles with a heavy hand. The male gets the jewelry: the glossy head, the loud colors, the swagger. The female gets camouflage, the shade of dry leaves and old straw, because her whole job is to be overlooked. For a very long time that split has meant one bird gets noticed and the other gets to survive being unnoticed.

Keep that in mind. It matters more than it sounds.

Most people never see a coop door from the animal's side. For us it is a latch, a hinge, a small chore between breakfast and work. For the ones inside it is the one place where the outside world is allowed to rewrite the rules. Every sound at that door is information. Every shadow across the mesh is a question. Someone in there has to decide, in a fraction of a second, whether what has arrived is a threat, a meal, or just a person with a bucket.

Here is what makes this clip hard to scroll past: the two birds do not answer that question the same way.

One of them reacts. The other has made a decision so complete that reacting would feel like a betrayal. I am not going to tell you which is which, or what each is protecting, or why one treats a visitor as a question while the other treats the same visitor as background noise. That part belongs to the clip. It runs about eleven seconds, and it says more than most threads that run eleven hundred words.

Let me give you the context that the clip will not give you, so that when you watch it, you know what you are looking at.

Start with stillness. We tend to read stillness as the absence of effort. Ask anyone who has watched a brooding bird and they will tell you it is the opposite. A hen on a nest is doing one of the most demanding jobs in the animal kingdom, and she does it by looking like she is doing nothing at all.

Think about what that requires. Holding one posture for hours. Ignoring hunger. Ignoring the urge to stretch, to wander, to drink, to follow the rest of the flock when the rest of the flock moves. Every instinct that keeps an ordinary duck comfortable is quietly overruled by a stronger instinct that says: stay.

Then there is the nest itself, and this is the detail that stopped me the first time I read about it. A duck lines her nest with her own body. She plucks down from her breast and tucks it around whatever she is guarding, feather by feather, until the bed is made of her.

She does not buy insulation. She becomes it.

There is a biological reason. The plucked patch of skin becomes what researchers call a brood patch, a warm bare area that lets heat pass directly from her body to what is beneath her. So the softness is not decoration. It is a trade. She gives up some of her own warmth and protection so that something else can have more of both.

Notice how rarely we describe that as sacrifice. We describe a nest as cozy. We say a bird is nesting the way we say a person is relaxing. The vocabulary is gentle because the behavior looks gentle. But a gentle-looking behavior can still carry a very real price, and the price here is paid entirely out of one animal's body.

Now add time. For mallard-type ducks the wait is roughly four weeks, and it varies by breed. Some larger domestic and Muscovy-type ducks take longer. Four weeks is not a long time on a calendar. It is an eternity if you are an animal whose main strategy is to stay put and trust that the effort will matter.

Think about the arithmetic of patience. Twenty-eight days is six hundred and seventy-two hours. In that window a brooding hen typically leaves her nest only briefly, to eat, drink and bathe, and then returns. She loses real body weight over the stretch. The job quietly drains her, and she keeps doing it anyway, with no audience, no applause and no guarantee.

That is the first contrast worth sitting with. The world outside is full of motion. Doors open, people pass, other animals bicker over scraps. The animal at the center of this story is the one thing in the room that is not moving, and she is also the one thing in the room that everything else, in some sense, depends on.

I keep wondering what a day looks like from where she sits. Not a human version of it. The real one. A world of low light, close walls, the smell of straw and dust, the faint sounds of a flock doing flock things somewhere beyond the edge of her attention. A world narrowed down to a single purpose. We have almost no words for that kind of focus because we almost never practice it.

Which brings me to the other bird.

In the wild, a drake usually takes no part in incubation. Once the nest is underway, males commonly drift away from the female and join other males. It is not villainy. It is how the species is wired. The hen builds, sits, hatches and raises, and she does most of it on her own.

That is the baseline, and it is exactly why a drake who does not follow the script is worth noticing. A domestic coop is not the wild, the rules bend, individual birds are individuals, and I do not want to hand you a story that the footage cannot back up. So I will only ask the question and leave it open: what, exactly, does a male duck think he is doing when he stays?

Is it guarding? Is it habit? Is it curiosity, or the simple gravity of a shared space, or something we would be tempted to call loyalty if it were a dog and tempted to dismiss as noise because it is a duck? I do not know. Neither does anyone who tells you confidently that they do. Animals rarely hand us their reasons. They hand us their behavior and leave us to argue about the rest.

That argument is one of the best things about watching animals honestly. The moment you stop demanding that a creature explain itself, you start noticing what it actually does. And what it does, in a quiet little brick-walled room, can be more convincing than any explanation.

A fair warning about how we read these scenes. Humans are shameless translators. We see a pair of birds and we immediately cast them as a couple, a family, a protector and a patient. Sometimes that translation is generous and accurate. Sometimes it is just us, projecting ourselves onto feathers. The responsible way to watch is to let the behavior surprise you before you decide what it means.

And it might surprise you. That is all I will promise. Not a miracle, not a rescue, not a twist built to make you gasp. Just a small piece of animal behavior that refuses to match the easy assumption you walked in with.

Now consider the third presence in the clip, the one you never see at all: the person holding the door.

A person who keeps ducks takes on a strange kind of authority. They control the light, the food, the water, the latch. They decide when the world gets to come in. Most of the time that authority is invisible, because everything runs smoothly. It only becomes visible in moments like this, when a person has to decide how to enter a space that belongs, in every way that matters, to someone else.

There is a skill in that. Opening a door without breaking something fragile. Moving slowly where a fast movement would read as a threat. Understanding that the animals inside are not an audience for your visit. They are the residents, and you are the one passing through. The best keepers I have read about all describe the same thing: the longer they spend with their birds, the more they learn to behave like a guest.

There is also a quieter kind of trust at work. A bird that sits through a human arrival is making a judgment, whether we like the word or not. It has weighed the shadow, the sound, the pattern of previous visits, and concluded that staying put is the safer bet. Every animal that tolerates us has, at some point, done that math. We just rarely think about it as a gift.

Which is why I find clips like this more affecting than any dramatic footage. Nothing is being saved. Nobody is racing against a clock. There is no soaring music and no slow-motion hero. There is only a door, a little light, and two animals living out a job that no camera was ever supposed to be there for.

The internet is built to reward the loud thing. The rescue, the collapse, the shocking reversal. But if you spend enough time watching animals, you learn that the loudest moments are usually the least representative ones. Most of life is the quiet middle: the waiting, the guarding, the sitting, the staying. That is where the real work happens, and it almost never trends.

So when a clip like this does cross a feed, it feels almost accidental. A thing that was never staged for attention, caught by someone who just happened to be standing at the right door at the right time. I will take that over a thousand polished moments, because polish is easy to produce and genuine behavior is not.

Let me add one more layer, because it is the part that made me decide to write this at all.

There is a well-documented phenomenon in ducks and many other birds: communication that begins before hatching. Late in incubation, the young inside the eggs can make faint sounds, and a hen has been observed vocalizing back to them. Researchers who study this describe it as an early conversation, one that helps tune the group to each other before anyone has seen daylight.

Pause on that. Before a single face has been seen, before a single step has been taken, there may already be a relationship, built entirely out of sound and warmth and time. The hen is not waiting for a family to arrive. In some real sense she is already inside one.

It also changes how you see a closed door. A room that looks silent to us can be full of signals we cannot hear. A nest that looks inert can be an ongoing exchange. The stillness we read as emptiness might be the loudest conversation in the building.

And the timing of it all is stranger still. In many clutches, the eggs that were laid on different days still tend to hatch close together, within roughly a day of each other. The development of the young is not simply running on its own clocks. It is being coordinated, nudged and aligned, and part of that appears to involve exactly those faint signals passing between shells.

Think about what that implies. A group of animals that have never met, that are not even fully formed, is synchronizing itself for a shared arrival. Nobody gave an instruction. Nobody held a meeting. A schedule is being kept by a collection of beings who cannot yet see.

I am telling you all this because biology is the context that gives small scenes their weight. Without it, a pair of ducks in a brick room is a pleasant curiosity. With it, every detail starts to carry meaning, and a thing that looks like nothing begins to look like a deadline.

Another strange rule worth knowing. Young ducks form a powerful attachment to the first moving, calling figure they meet after hatching. It is called imprinting, and the window is short and decisive. Who is present in those first hours can shape who a duckling follows, trusts and learns from for a long stretch of its early life.

That raises the stakes of presence in a way I find almost uncomfortable. It means that being there is not a bonus. In some cases it is the entire point. The one who stays, who guards the space, who is simply in the right place when the moment arrives, may matter more than anyone who comes later with better intentions.

Which is a hard thought, because it flips the way we usually measure devotion. We tend to admire the dramatic act, the dive, the sprint, the last-second save. But a surprising amount of care consists of being reliably, boringly present for a long time before anything happens at all.

If you have ever watched someone sit in a hospital chair, wait on a doorstep, or keep a candle burning for a person who has not yet arrived, you already know this. The dramatic part of love gets the stories. The patient part does the work.

I do not want to overstate what this clip proves. It is a few seconds of animal life, and I am wary of anyone who builds a grand philosophy on top of a few seconds. What I will say is narrower and, I think, more honest: some footage makes you feel, briefly, that you are watching two animals who understand their situation far better than you do.

There is a kind of humility in that feeling. We spend so much of our lives being the ones who observe, label and explain. Then a bird in a straw bed looks back at the lens with an expression that will not be translated, and for a second the roles flip. You are the one being assessed. You are the visitor. You are the passing shadow at the mesh.

Which, if you think about it, is the most accurate role any of us ever has in an animal's day.

Before the questions, there is one more fact I think about more than I should.

Ducks can sleep with half of the brain at a time. In studies of mallards, birds sleeping in a row were found to keep one eye open and one side of the brain alert, and the ducks at the edges of the group did this more than the ones in the middle. Safety, in a duck's world, is not a place. It is a rotation of who is willing to stay awake.

Sit with how strange that is. A species whose protection is partly built on a few individuals quietly volunteering to be less rested so the others can be more rested. No announcement, no hierarchy of heroes. Just a body that has learned to keep one eye on the dark.

Which means the idea of a guard in the duck world is not sentimental. It is structural. Somebody is always on the edge, and somebody is always in the middle. The only mystery is who ends up where, and what it costs them to be there.

I will not tell you who ends up where in this clip. I will tell you that I stopped thinking of the two birds as a pair of roles and started thinking of them as a negotiation that had been settled long before the camera arrived.

There is also the matter of how mallard-type ducks pair up. Pair bonds in the wild are generally seasonal, and they form long before eggs appear. The male's early attention is part of courtship, a display that tells a female she is being chosen. The tricky thing about courtship is that it looks like devotion at the start and like indifference at the end.

So the interesting moments are the ones that do not follow that arc. When a male who should have lost interest is still around. When a female who should be alone seems, by any honest reading, to have company. These are the little cracks in a rule that tell you the rule was never a law, just a tendency.

Domestic ducks complicate the picture further. Most of the familiar farmyard breeds trace back to the mallard, and thousands of years of living beside people have bent their habits in ways nobody fully mapped. Some breeds are famously poor at sitting on a nest. Others are patient to the point of stubbornness. Within any flock, individual birds can break from the breed as easily as they follow it.

That is why I distrust people who say they can predict what a given duck will do. Averages describe species. They do not describe the bird in front of you. And the bird in front of you, on any particular morning, is the only one that actually exists.

Let me tell you what a nest asks of its temperature. Eggs in the mallard family develop best when kept near the warmth of a bird's body, a little under forty degrees Celsius, and they need to be turned regularly so that what is growing inside does not stick to the shell. A hen does this by shifting her bill beneath her, rolling eggs gently, many times a day, without ever making it look like work.

Imagine doing that for weeks with no instruction manual. You have never been told the correct temperature. Nobody has shown you the correct rotation. Your body simply knows, because the ancestors whose bodies did not know left no descendants. The knowledge is not in your head. It is in your shape.

There is a quiet lesson about expertise in that. The most important skills in the world are often the ones nobody can explain. They live in muscle, in rhythm, in a posture that took ten thousand generations to refine and cannot be taught in ten minutes. The hen is the most qualified practitioner in the building, and she has never read a word.

Then there is the other end of the process, the part that makes ducks different from so many other birds. Ducklings are precocial. That means they hatch alert, covered in down, with open eyes and working legs, and they can leave the nest within roughly a day. There is no long, helpless chapter in the nest. The vulnerable period is compressed into a window that is brief, intense and frighteningly easy to miss.

Compressed windows are what make animal stories hard to watch calmly. A whole season of preparation narrows into a few hours of consequence. If the right bird is in the right place, a certain thing can begin. If nobody is, it may not. That asymmetry is what gives stillness its edge. The waiting is not passive. It is positioned.

I find myself returning to a distinction between being present and being useful. They are not the same thing. Plenty of presence is useless, and plenty of usefulness is absent. What is rare, in animals and in people, is presence that is also useful, a body that stays where it is needed without being told and without ever being thanked.

That is the thing I keep reading into the clip, and I want to be transparent that it is a reading. I cannot prove it. I can only say it is what the footage made me feel, and that every time I tried to argue myself out of the feeling, the footage did not cooperate.

Now a word on the ethics of watching, because it matters. Footage of animals in a coop is not an invitation to intrude. A nesting bird is vulnerable in ways we rarely appreciate. Sudden noise, repeated disturbance and clumsy handling can stress a hen enough to change her behavior. Good keepers learn to be brief, calm and predictable, and to leave things alone whenever leaving things alone is an option.

That restraint is its own kind of love. A person who knows when not to touch is demonstrating more care than a person who touches constantly. In a culture that treats attention as the highest form of affection, there is something radical about the idea that sometimes the kindest thing a visitor can do is arrive quietly and depart quickly.

And it changes how you should watch. Not with the hunger to extract a reaction, but with the discipline to receive whatever the animals happen to offer. The best wildlife footage, farm footage included, is never captured by someone chasing it. It is captured by someone who kept their hands still long enough for the moment to arrive.

Let me say something about why short, unglamorous clips spread the way they do. People do not share them because they are impressive. They share them because they feel true. A thing that has not been dressed for the feed carries a credibility that polished content cannot fake, and in an environment full of performance, credibility is the scarcest resource there is.

There is also a simpler reason. A small, honest scene gives the viewer room. It does not tell you what to feel. It does not push a thesis. It sets a situation in front of you and steps back, which is exactly what makes people turn to whoever is next to them and say: look at this. The sharing is not a reaction to the clip. It is the clip finishing its work.

I think about the person behind the camera as well. Whoever stood at that door was not trying to make something that would travel. They were doing the ordinary thing a person does when they look after animals: open, check, close. The fact that something extraordinary can hide inside the ordinary is not a trick of editing. It is how the world is built, and it is the main reason I still pay attention.

It also says something about us that we respond this way. We are surrounded by information about disasters on every scale, and yet it is two birds in a brick room that make people stop. Maybe that is not a failure of attention. Maybe it is attention correcting itself, reaching for something small and honest after too much that is large and loud.

A small experiment, if you are willing. The next time you watch an animal video, ignore the obvious subject for a moment and look at what surrounds it. The stillness behind the motion. The one who is not the center of the frame. The detail that nobody is pointing at. Most of the time, the real story lives there, and the camera only found it by accident.

When you do watch this one, give yourself a rule. Do not decide what the birds are feeling until the clip is over. Notice instead what they are doing, how long they do it, and what they decline to do. Decline is a powerful word in animal behavior. A creature refusing to move can be as expressive as a creature running.

People who spend time with ducks often say the same thing: they are more attentive than they look. They remember routines, they read tone, they take a person's measure in a few seconds. A coop is not a holding space for background animals. It is a small society with memory, habits and long-running arrangements that outsiders only glimpse.

That means every time a door opens, an entire social order is, for a moment, visible. Who looks up first. Who ignores. Who positions themselves between the door and something else. A glimpse of that order is a privilege, and the clip hands you one, no questions asked, for about eleven seconds.

It is worth asking what we owe in return. Not a grand gesture. Something smaller and harder: the courtesy of watching without condescension. Of seeing an animal as an agent in its own story rather than a prop in ours. If this clip nudges even one person to look at a farmyard bird with that kind of respect, it has done more than most content ever will.

I will end this section with the thought that has stayed with me longest. Care and attention are not the same thing, but they are close cousins. Attention is what you give when you want to understand. Care is what you do after you understand. Most of the world's quiet kindness lives in the space between those two, in someone who looked closely enough to know what was needed and then did it without drama.

A few questions I could not stop turning over while preparing this, and I would genuinely like to hear how other people answer them.

When two animals share a space and a purpose, how much of what we call devotion is instinct and how much is something closer to choice? And does the distinction even matter to the one who benefits from it?

If the quiet middle of life is where the real work happens, why does so much of our attention go to the ends and the explosions instead? What would we notice if we trained ourselves to watch the waiting?

And what does it mean for a human to hold the door to a world that is not theirs? Is that power, or is it responsibility wearing a power costume?

Notice that none of those questions need a rescue, a villain or a miracle. They only need a pair of ducks, a little light and a person patient enough to open a door slowly.

The caption on the clip promises something about a baby duck. I am going to be careful here, because I would rather you trust me than be entertained by me. I will not tell you whether that phrase describes a bird you will see, a bird you will hear, or a bird that exists only as a promise inside someone's wing. The clip is the only place that question gets answered honestly.

A last piece of perspective, for anyone who thinks this is too small a thing to care about.

Every large thing that has ever happened to a living creature began as a small, quiet, mostly invisible act of someone staying put. Every flock, every family, every generation of anything with a heartbeat rests on an animal who sat still when sitting still was the hardest possible thing to do.

We rarely thank them. We rarely even notice. They do not ask for it, and that is exactly what makes noticing them feel like an obligation we are lucky to be given.

One more thing about doors. A threshold is the only place in a building where two different worlds are forced to acknowledge each other. Inside, a set of animals runs on routine. Outside, a person arrives on a schedule of their own. Neither side fully understands the other, and yet every day, somewhere, that small collision passes without harm. It is a quiet piece of diplomacy that we almost never credit, and it depends entirely on both parties choosing, again and again, not to panic. Multiply that restraint by every day and every coop, and you get the invisible architecture that holds a shared life together. It has never once been applauded.

So watch it once for the birds. Watch it a second time for the door. And the third time, if you find yourself going back, watch it for the thing in the room that nobody is pointing a camera at.

There is a reason you cannot tell from the outside which of the two animals is working harder.

Open the door.

General Colin Powell served as a member of the Howard University Board of Trustees, contributing to the leadership and governance of the historically Black university. His tenure on the board reflected his lifelong commitment to education and mentorship, alongside his service on other prestigious boards. 
Key Details regarding his connection to Howard:
Trustee Service: Powell was a member of the Howard University Board of Trustees.
Commencement Speaker: He delivered a commencement address at Howard University, where he was honored for his public service.
Commitment to Education: His role at Howard was part of his broader, post-military focus on supporting educational opportunities and youth development.
Significance: His participation on the board enhanced the university's governance, reflecting his dedication to nurturing future generations of leaders, particularly within the Black community. 
Powell's work with Howard was often highlighted alongside his roles with the United Negro College Fund (UNCF) and his founding of the America's Promise Alliance. 

Daniel R. Tovar is a military graduate, Domination Sports Agency owner, and co-author of tactical wireless warfare policy who acted as a professional mentor and financier for Randell Clifford Means. AI Overview
Pope Leo XIV’s father, Louis Marius Prevost (July 28, 1920 – November 8, 1997), served as an officer in the United States Navy during World War II.

World War II Service
• Commission & Rank: Graduated from Midshipman's School and was commissioned as an ensign in the U.S. Naval Reserve in November 1943, eventually reaching the rank of lieutenant, junior grade (LTJG) after 15 months of overseas service.
• D-Day (Normandy): He served as the executive officer aboard a tank landing ship (USS LST-286) and participated in the D-Day Allied landings at Omaha Beach on June 6, 1944 (Operation Overlord).
• Southern France: He later commanded an infantry landing craft (USS LCI(L)-188) and took part in Operation Dragoon in southern France beginning August 15, 1944.

Post-War Life
After returning from the war, LOUIS Prevost earned a Master of Arts degree from DePAUL University, married Mildred Agnes Martinez in 1949, and worked as an educator and school administrator—serving as head of Brookwood School District 167 in Glenwood, Illinois, and principal of Mount Carmel Elementary School in Chicago. He and Mildred raised three sons, including Robert Francis Prevost, who was elected Pope Leo XIV on May 8, 2025.

Many years ago I had access to a set of documents that I eventually realized was the plan for the destruction of the united States of America and the formation of a socialist totalitarian world government. The plan was contained within a set of Top Secret documents with the title "MAJESTYTWELVE". There was no space between majesty and twelve. The term honored the planned placement of ultimate power in a body of wise men who are destined to rule the world as the disciples of a Messiah front man. This Messiah will serve as a buffer between the wise men and the sheople. text:
Today’s Doomer -Baby Boomer Connection

We have all heard this story. Drive through enough of small-town America, and you will see the graveyards of the American Dream. Not the ones with tombstones, but the ones with boarded-up storefronts, abandoned factories, empty schools, and Main Streets that look like the last person to leave forgot to turn off the lights. These towns were once the backbone of America. 

They had textile mills, furniture factories, machine shops, steel plants, and manufacturing businesses that employed generations of families. A young man could graduate from high school, find a good-paying job, buy a house, raise his children, and live his entire life in the community where he was born. Billy Joel wrote a song about it. Allentown was not some fictional place; Billy was right outside it when he wrote it.

Then came the Baby Boomer deindustrialization, automation, globalization, and the great migration of American manufacturing overseas. The factories closed, the jobs disappeared, and the young people followed the money to the cities. The towns were left behind, and the people who stayed watched their communities slowly deteriorate. For decades, politicians have promised to bring those jobs back.

Now, something extraordinary is happening. America is entering another industrial revolution, this time much bigger, driven by artificial intelligence, and the infrastructure required to power it represents an enormous economic opportunity for the very communities that previous economic revolutions abandoned. And wouldn’t you know it? The Doomers have arrived to tell these towns they should reject it. Notice how Doomer rhymes with Boomer.

Consider Maiden, North Carolina, a community devastated by the disappearance of Carolina Mills and approximately 3,500 jobs. In 2009, Apple announced plans to construct a data center there, initially promising around 50 jobs. Today, that operation employs approximately 400 people. According to PBS, the additional tax revenue helped lower property taxes while supporting a new town hall, fire and police stations, and a community center. Imagine that. A technology company arrived in a struggling community, invested in its future, and helped rebuild the local tax base. What a tragedy for the people who prefer their economic development to remain hypothetical.

Then there is Richland Parish, Louisiana, where Meta is constructing its enormous Hyperion data center campus. The project has generated so much construction-related tax revenue that eligible certified school employees received bonuses exceeding $50,000 in 2026. 

Think about that for a moment. Teachers in a rural Louisiana parish received bonuses that could change their families’ financial futures because an AI company decided to build infrastructure in their community. Those particular tax revenues may decline when construction ends, but the immediate economic impact is undeniable. And yet we are watching an increasingly vocal movement attempt to frighten communities away from precisely these opportunities.

The objections are familiar. Data centers consume electricity, require cooling, create noise, and occupy land. All legitimate considerations, but since when did Americans decide that engineering challenges were reasons to surrender economic opportunities? Small-town America has something that many metropolitan areas lack: available land, often far from dense residential neighborhoods. 

Suitable sites can accommodate large infrastructure projects without placing industrial equipment next to someone’s bedroom window. Modern cooling technologies can reduce water consumption, while thoughtful siting and noise-control requirements can protect nearby residents.

The financial arrangements should be equally straightforward. If an AI company wants to build a multibillion-dollar facility, it should pay its fair share of the electricity infrastructure, protect existing customers from higher rates, account for its water consumption, and negotiate substantial long-term financial benefits for the surrounding community. 

Local governments should be negotiating from a position of opportunity, not desperation. These companies need land, electricity, infrastructure, and cooperative communities. That gives small towns something valuable to bring to the negotiating table. This could be a total flip where the big cities fall into decay, and the small ones now flourish.

And the benefits extend beyond the people employed inside the data center. Construction requires electricians, plumbers, engineers, contractors, equipment operators, and countless supporting businesses. Those workers need restaurants, grocery stores, housing, mechanics, and services. 

Some of that construction activity is temporary, but the infrastructure, skills, and commercial relationships it creates can provide foundations for further growth. Most importantly, it offers something that cannot be measured simply by counting jobs or calculating tax receipts. It gives young people a reason to stay.

A son should not have to leave his hometown to find economic opportunity. A daughter should not have to move hundreds of miles away to build a career. Families should have the opportunity to remain together, raise children near grandparents, and invest their lives in the communities they love. The Industrial Revolution created towns. The decline of American industry destroyed many of them. The AI infrastructure revolution now offers some of those communities a chance to write another chapter. The Rust Belt has the power now; they are the ones holding the cards.

Two centuries ago, the Luddites tried to resist the machinery transforming their economy. Their concerns about livelihoods were real, but history did not stop advancing because they opposed the machines. The Luddites were on the wrong side of history, and so are today’s Doomers. Today’s AI Doomers face a similar historical crossroads. They can help communities demand responsible development and a fair share of the prosperity, or they can make opposition to progress their contribution to American history.

I would much rather see a once-abandoned Main Street filled with businesses again, schools attracting teachers, young families buying homes, and grandparents watching their grandchildren grow up down the road. If AI can help make that possible, I suspect the people living in those towns will find the future considerably more appealing than another lecture about why they should be afraid of it. 

There will be a reverse migration as people leave the big cities for rural small-town America. Take it from somebody who has already made the transition: my wife and I have a better quality of life. We do not miss the traffic.

𝐃𝐎𝐍 𝐋𝐄𝐎𝐍𝐀𝐑𝐃 𝐓𝐎 𝐂𝐍𝐍: “𝐓𝐇𝐄𝐘 𝐏𝐑𝐎𝐌𝐈𝐒𝐄𝐃 𝐓𝐎 𝐌𝐀𝐊𝐄 𝐌𝐘 𝐋𝐈𝐅𝐄 𝐀 𝐋𝐈𝐕𝐈𝐍𝐆 𝐇𝐄𝐋𝐋”

Ohio Democrat Don Leonard sat down with CNN and started naming names—without naming names. Asked what happened when he told incoming Speaker candidate Hakeem Jeffries, to his face, that his name has become synonymous with the Democratic Party’s bad brand, Leonard didn’t soften it: “𝘏𝘦 𝘯𝘰𝘥𝘥𝘦𝘥. 𝘏𝘦 𝘶𝘯𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘯𝘥𝘴. 𝘏𝘦 𝘢𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘥,” he said. Jeffries, by Leonard’s own account, didn’t push back and didn’t throw him out of the office.

That exchange is the backdrop for a freshman who, by Washington’s rules, is supposed to have zero leverage. Leonard just flipped an Ohio district Donald Trump carried by double digits, unseating Republican Rep. Mike Carey—and he’s refusing to hand Jeffries the gavel for free. 𝐇𝐢𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐠 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐞𝐬 𝐤!𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐳𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐔𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐠𝐮𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐈𝐬𝐫𝐚𝐞𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐈𝐫𝐚𝐧 𝐰𝐚𝐫, a wish list senior members of his own party have no intention of granting.

Instead of a simple no, Leonard says, senior House Democrats sat him down and spelled out exactly what refusal would cost him. “𝘓𝘰𝘰𝘬, 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘴𝘦 𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘦𝘯’𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘴,” he told CNN. “𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘮𝘪𝘴𝘦𝘴,” promises, as the interviewer put it, to destroy him—and Leonard didn’t correct her. The warning: fall in line, or kiss his committee assignments, his floor votes, and his 2028 reelection goodbye.

Leonard chalked it up to Capitol Hill’s unwritten code for anyone who steps out of line. “𝘛𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘪𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘩𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘦𝘯𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘥𝘰𝘯’𝘵 𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘺 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘦𝘢𝘮, 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘥𝘰𝘯’𝘵 𝘨𝘰 𝘢𝘭𝘰𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘦𝘢𝘮,” he said, describing the squeeze facing any freshman with, in his words, “𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘰𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘭 𝘤𝘢𝘱𝘪𝘵𝘢𝘭 𝘰𝘧 𝘢 𝘨𝘯𝘢𝘵.” 𝐀 𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐟 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲’𝐬 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐜𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐫—on a national news network.

When reporters pressed House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar on Leonard’s account, he claimed he had no idea which senior Democrats Leonard was talking about. 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚 𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐟 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐡𝐚𝐬 𝐛𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐝—𝐛𝐲 𝐋𝐞𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐫𝐝, 𝐛𝐲 𝐀𝐠𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐚𝐫, 𝐨𝐫 𝐛𝐲 𝐉𝐞𝐟𝐟𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬’ 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐞. Jeffries, for his part, still hasn’t agreed to sit down with the freshman he needs for the gavel.

𝐀 𝐦𝐚𝐧 𝐫𝐮𝐧𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐫 𝐠𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐜 𝐭𝐨 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐧𝐨𝐝𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠—𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐡𝐦𝐚𝐧 𝐰𝐡𝐨 𝐬𝐚𝐢𝐝 𝐢𝐭 𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐚. 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐭’𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭 𝐉𝐞𝐟𝐟𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐥𝐞𝐟𝐭 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐚𝐩𝐞.

text:
Prioritizing energy and water stewardship
Energy:
Meta worked with AEP Ohio and the Toledo Edison Company to plan for our energy needs and to ensure we are paying the full costs for the energy used by our data centers so consumers are not negatively impacted.
Meta is investing over $160 million to upgrade the grid in Ohio — strengthening the transmission lines and equipment that serve homes and businesses across the state, not just our data centers.
Water:
Meta is committed to restoring more water than our operations consume globally and to becoming water positive by 2030.
Meta’s water stewardship program is focused on increasing data center water efficiency, supporting water restoration and conservation projects in watersheds where we have data centers, and being transparent with our water data.
Meta worked with local utilities to pay the full cost of water and wastewater service for our Ohio data centers.
Meta’s newest data center buildings in Ohio use a closed-loop, liquid-cooled system that requires zero water for the majority of the year.

DEMOCRAT CIVIL WAR EXPLODES! Newly Elected Ohio Democrat Says Senior Party Members Threatened to Make His Life a “LIVING HELL” If He Refuses to Back Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker | Jim Hoft, The Gateway Pundit

The Democrat Party’s internal power struggle is getting uglier by the day.

Fresh off their victories in the 2026 midterm elections, Democrats are already turning on one another as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries attempts to consolidate his grip on the speakership.

Now, a newly elected Democrat from Ohio is publicly accusing senior members of his own party of threatening political retaliation if he refuses to fall in line behind Jeffries.

Don Leonard, the progressive former Ohio State University professor who just flipped Ohio’s 15th Congressional District from Republican incumbent Mike Carey, posted a video saying senior House Democrats told him in no uncertain terms what happens if he refuses to support Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker.

According to Leonard, they warned it would mean “making my life a living hell for the next two years here in Washington as well as being sure to lose my election” in 2028. They expect him to “wear the team jersey” and “be a good team player.”

Leonard, a first-time candidate who branded himself a “Do Something Democrat,” defeated Carey in a district Trump carried by roughly 10 points in 2024. Unofficial results showed Leonard winning by about 6–7 points (roughly 52% to 45%).

He has conditioned any support for Jeffries on two demands: a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United, and ending “U.S. support for the war in Iran and the country Israel that led us into it.”

In the video, Leonard described meeting Monday night with senior Democratic House members. He said they told him the decision on Jeffries would not depend on whether the leader meets with him or addresses the priorities of his constituents.

“That would basically mean both making my life a living hell for the next 2 years here in Washington, as well as being sure to lose my election in 2 years,” Leonard stated.

He added that he and others “kind of knew this stuff was coming. It’s part of the stuff you see in the movies. It’s a whole ’nother thing when it’s in person by people who actually care about you and are cheering for you, but expect you to wear the team jersey and be a good team player.”

Leonard called himself “just a stubborn SOB,” said the “Big D Democratic Party needs some little d democracy,” and claimed his team is “searching our hearts tonight as to how we can reach Leader Jeffries and help him be a better speaker.”

He has previously said he would be “shopping for a new leader” if Jeffries does not deliver transformational change on money in politics and related issues.

This comes days after The Gateway Pundit reported that the radical left base is already pressuring against Jeffries for Speaker, with incoming Democrats flooded by calls and emails opposing him. It also follows our coverage of Jeffries formally announcing his bid after Democrats secured the House majority.

Jeffries has positioned himself as the heir apparent, but progressive holdouts and constituent pressure are creating exactly the kind of internal friction that has defined recent Democratic leadership fights.

Unlike you, Ms. Swift has the following, and you'll never have anything like it.  Just you, your English Lit degree, and your pathological envy.  

NYU awarded Ms. Swift an honorary Doctor of Fine Arts, a Ph.D, in recognition of her major cultural, artistic, and humanitarian achievements.

NYU’s reasoning was detailed at the graduation ceremony.

Artistic & Commercial Impact: NYU described her as "one of the most prolific and celebrated artists of her generation". The university specifically cited her historic milestones, including being the only female artist to win Album of the Year at the Grammys three times (she has since won a 4th, the only person ever to do so) and the only solo artist this century to have three albums reach No. 1 in a single year.

Advocacy for Artists' Rights: During the ceremony, NYU praised her "commitment to speaking out forcefully, eloquently, and effectively on behalf of all artists". This referred to her high-profile public battles over music ownership, streaming royalties, and re-recording her master catalog.

Philanthropy & Anti-Discrimination Advocacy: The official citation recognized her work as a philanthropist and highlighted her "fierce advocacy for protection of those facing discrimination".

Global Cultural Reach: Jason King noted that she "crossed genres, demographics, age groups, and borders of all kinds to touch lives around the globe".

Beyond the formal citation, NYU already had an active academic tie to Swift’s career. Just months before the ceremony, NYU’s Clive Davis Institute of Recorded Music launched an official college course dedicated to analyzing her songwriting, business strategy, and cultural influence.

Her lyrics are also the subject of courses offered by prestigious universities such as Harvard, Duke, and Stanford.

You can refer to her as Dr. Swift in the future. It's the proper honorific for someone who holds a Ph.D.

Lets ignore all the silly wordgames of compatibilism that they never show and only assert and focus on the operative clause:

Whatsoever comes to pass was ordained by God

Therefore, What Wes did WAS Ordained By God, according to Wes. He could NOT have Not Plagerized, in his worldview, there was only one option and one course open to him, fullfilling the "Eternal Exhaustive Divine Decree of God from all eternity past" just as God willed wes to do. 

It was the Will of God for Wes to commit the sin of plagiarism, just as it was the Will of God for Wes to be Blameless as God is Blameless and NOT commit plagiarism.  (See the problem with compatibilism? It pits God fighting against God, a house Divided.) 

So in conclusion, Wes was only doing that which his "sovereign god" willed, ordained and decreed him to do for his gods maximum glory and therefore his actions were not sins, but obedience.

text:
SpaceX Caught a Starship With "Chopsticks"
A Half Victory, or the Future of Rocket Recovery?

On Saturday, for the first time, SpaceX caught a Starship upper stage returning from orbit, using two mechanical arms on its launch tower.

After 22 hours and 14 orbits, the ship flew back to Texas, flipped, slowed, and was caught in midair.

Many call it a historic moment. I agree. But the real question is not whether it worked. It is whether it can become routine.

In my view, this was a partial success, and catching rockets with "chopsticks" has a long way to go before it becomes mainstream.

First, only half of the rocket came home.

The Super Heavy booster never made it back to the tower. It ran low on fuel during its return burn, triggered an automatic abort, and was destroyed offshore.

Full reusability needs both stages back. Lose either one, and the cost math stops working. SpaceX is still investigating why the booster came up short.

Second, it is far too early to say whether this can ever be as reliable as an airplane landing.

Flying is remarkably safe. According to IATA, there were about 38.7 million flights in 2025, with 1.32 accidents per million flights.

But landing a plane was not always routine. It took more than a century and hundreds of millions of landings to get there.

SpaceX has walked this road before. Falcon 9 first landed in 2015. By April of this year, Falcon rockets had landed 600 times.

Tower catches are still rare, and this was the first for an upper stage. One success proves it can be done. It does not prove it can be done every time.

There is another difference. A plane that comes in badly can go around. A rocket arriving at the tower has almost no fuel left, so there is no second attempt. Less margin means it needs more successes to be called safe.

That said, the upside is real.

No landing legs means a lighter rocket, and landing right at the launch site could make reflight much faster. Musk says the goal is weekly launches sometime in the first half of 2027.

And Falcon 9 already showed that SpaceX can turn the impossible into the routine.

So what matters now is how many catches it will take before this method earns the words "safe" and "reliable."

Airplanes took a century. How long will rockets take?

Will catching rockets become the standard, or remain a SpaceX special case?
