text:
🛰️ 100 FACTS ABOUT SPACE JUNK AND ORBITAL DEBRIS

🛰️ BY THE NUMBERS

𝟏. ESA estimates about 54,000 objects larger than 10 cm orbit Earth, including active satellites.

𝟐. About 1.2 million pieces between 1 and 10 cm are thought to be up there.

𝟑. ESA's models suggest around 140 million fragments between 1 mm and 1 cm.

𝟒. Space surveillance networks regularly track roughly 40,000 objects.

𝟓. The total mass of human-made objects in Earth orbit is well over 13,000 tonnes.

𝟔. More than 10,000 of the objects in orbit are working satellites, most launched in the 2020s.

𝟕. More than 650 break-ups, explosions and collisions have been recorded since 1957.

𝟖. Thousands of spent rocket stages still circle the planet.

𝟗. SpaceX's Starlink alone has more than 8,000 satellites in orbit.

𝟏𝟎. Starlink reportedly made well over 100,000 collision-avoidance manoeuvres in a single six-month period (Dec 2024 to May 2025).

🚀 WHERE IT COMES FROM

𝟏𝟏. The rocket core stage that launched Sputnik 1 in 1957 also reached orbit, arguably the first space junk.

𝟏𝟐. Dead satellites that can no longer be steered.

𝟏𝟑. Spent upper stages left in orbit after delivering their payloads.

𝟏𝟒. Leftover fuel and old batteries that explode years later, a major source of fragments.

𝟏𝟓. Fragments from collisions and anti-satellite weapon tests.

𝟏𝟔. Paint flecks peeling off spacecraft surfaces.

𝟏𝟕. Slag and aluminium oxide dust from solid rocket motors.

𝟏𝟖. Droplets of sodium-potassium coolant leaked by Soviet reactor-powered satellites.

𝟏𝟗. Project West Ford (1963) released about 480 million tiny copper needles for a radio experiment; some clumps remain.

𝟐𝟎. Lens caps, bolts and separation hardware released during deployments.

💥 BIGGEST DEBRIS EVENTS

𝟐𝟏. 2007: 🇨🇳 China's anti-satellite test on the Fengyun-1C weather satellite created over 3,000 trackable fragments, the worst single debris event.

𝟐𝟐. 10 Feb 2009: 🇺🇸 Iridium 33 and the defunct 🇷🇺 Kosmos 2251 collided at about 790 km over Siberia, the first accidental crash of two intact satellites.

𝟐𝟑. That collision produced more than 2,000 trackable fragments.

𝟐𝟒. 15 Nov 2021 (five years ago today): 🇷🇺 Russia destroyed Kosmos 1408 in an ASAT test, creating over 1,500 trackable fragments.

𝟐𝟓. The 2021 test forced the ISS crew to shelter in their docked spacecraft.

𝟐𝟔. 2019: 🇮🇳 India's Mission Shakti destroyed a satellite at about 300 km; most of the debris decayed quickly.

𝟐𝟕. 2008: 🇺🇸 the US shot down the failing USA-193 satellite at about 247 km (Operation Burnt Frost).

𝟐𝟖. July 1996: 🇫🇷 the French satellite Cerise was hit by an Ariane rocket fragment, the first confirmed collision between catalogued objects.

𝟐𝟗. 2024: a 🇨🇳 Long March 6A upper stage broke up after a Qianfan launch, reportedly creating hundreds of fragments.

𝟑𝟎. Oct 2024: the Intelsat 33e satellite broke apart in geostationary orbit.

⚡ SPEED & DANGER

𝟑𝟏. Debris in low Earth orbit moves at about 7 to 8 km/s, roughly 28,000 km/h.

𝟑𝟐. Average collision speeds in low orbit are around 10 km/s.

𝟑𝟑. At those speeds, even a 1 cm fragment can disable a satellite.

𝟑𝟒. An object larger than 10 cm can shatter a satellite completely.

𝟑𝟓. Impact energy grows with the square of speed, so tiny particles pack a huge punch.

𝟑𝟔. 1983: a paint fleck about 0.2 mm across chipped a window on Space Shuttle Challenger (STS-7).

𝟑𝟕. Shuttle windows were replaced many times because of debris and micrometeoroid pits.

𝟑𝟖. The ISS has made more than 30 debris-avoidance manoeuvres since 1999.

𝟑𝟗. 2021: a debris strike punched a hole in the ISS's Canadarm2 robotic arm; it kept working.

𝟒𝟎. 2016: a millimetre-sized particle damaged a solar array on ESA's Sentinel-1A, leaving a scar about 40 cm wide.

🏠 THINGS THAT FELL TO EARTH

𝟒𝟏. 1978: the nuclear-powered 🇷🇺 Soviet satellite Kosmos 954 crashed in 🇨🇦 Canada; the USSR later paid C$3 million.

𝟒𝟐. 1979: Skylab broke up over 🇦🇺 Western Australia; the town of Esperance fined NASA $400 for littering.

𝟒𝟑. 1991: the Soviet station Salyut 7 came down over 🇦🇷 Argentina.

𝟒𝟒. 1997: Lottie Williams of Tulsa, 🇺🇸 Oklahoma, was brushed by rocket debris, the only person known to be hit. She was unharmed.

𝟒𝟓. 2001: Russia's Mir station was steered into the South Pacific.

𝟒𝟔. 2018: 🇨🇳 China's Tiangong-1 made an uncontrolled reentry over the South Pacific.

𝟒𝟕. 2021: a Long March 5B core stage fell uncontrolled into the Indian Ocean near the 🇲🇻 Maldives.

𝟒𝟖. 2022: pieces of a SpaceX Dragon trunk landed on farms in 🇦🇺 Australia's Snowy Mountains.

𝟒𝟗. 2024: a chunk of an ISS battery pallet crashed through a house in Naples, 🇺🇸 Florida.

𝟓𝟎. Dec 2024: a metal ring of roughly 500 kg reportedly fell on a village in 🇰🇪 Kenya.

🧑‍🚀 ASTRONAUT LOSSES & CLOSE CALLS

𝟓𝟏. 1965: Ed White lost a spare glove during America's first spacewalk (Gemini 4).

𝟓𝟐. 1966: Michael Collins lost a camera during a Gemini 10 spacewalk.

𝟓𝟑. 2008: Heidemarie Stefanyshyn-Piper lost a tool bag on a spacewalk; it could be seen from Earth with binoculars.

𝟓𝟒. 2006: an old Russian spacesuit fitted with a radio, SuitSat-1, was released from the ISS.

𝟓𝟓. 2023: two astronauts lost another tool bag on an ISS spacewalk; skywatchers spotted it too.

𝟓𝟔. ISS modules use Whipple shields, thin outer bumpers that shatter debris before it reaches the hull.

𝟓𝟕. They are named after astronomer Fred Whipple, who proposed the idea in the 1940s.

𝟓𝟖. NASA moves the ISS when the chance of a collision exceeds about 1 in 10,000.

𝟓𝟗. Hubble's solar arrays, returned by astronauts, showed many tiny impact craters.

𝟔𝟎. NASA's LDEF spent nearly six years in orbit (1984 to 1990) and came back with thousands of impact marks.

🌍 ORBITS & LIFETIMES

𝟔𝟏. Vanguard 1 (1958) is the oldest human-made object still in orbit and may stay up for about two more centuries.

𝟔𝟐. Below about 400 km, debris usually falls back within a few years.

𝟔𝟑. Around 800 km, objects can stay up for decades to centuries.

𝟔𝟒. Above 1,000 km, debris can remain for centuries or longer.

𝟔𝟓. Geostationary orbit (35,786 km) has almost no drag, so junk there stays essentially forever.

𝟔𝟔. Retiring geostationary satellites are boosted to a "graveyard orbit" about 300 km higher.

𝟔𝟕. Solar maximum heats and expands the upper atmosphere, dragging debris down faster.

𝟔𝟖. Most objects that reenter burn up completely before reaching the ground.

𝟔𝟗. The busiest region is roughly 500 to 1,000 km up, home to most satellites and debris.

𝟕𝟎. Point Nemo, the ocean spot farthest from land, is used as a spacecraft cemetery for controlled reentries.

🔭 TRACKING & MONITORING

𝟕𝟏. The US Space Force maintains the main public catalogue of orbital objects, shared via https://t.co/cTKoDPSt2d.

𝟕𝟐. In low orbit, objects down to about 10 cm are routinely tracked; smaller ones are estimated statistically.

𝟕𝟑. In geostationary orbit, only objects roughly 30 cm to 1 m across are routinely trackable.

𝟕𝟒. The Space Fence radar on 🇲🇭 Kwajalein Atoll became operational in 2020.

𝟕𝟓. NASA's Orbital Debris Program Office was set up in 1979.

𝟕𝟔. ESA's DISCOS database records objects launched since 1957.

𝟕𝟕. Commercial firms such as LeoLabs now run their own debris-tracking radars.

𝟕𝟖. Laser ranging stations can measure the distance to some debris very precisely.

𝟕𝟗. 2002: astronomers found J002E3, a mystery object later identified as most likely an Apollo 12 rocket stage.

𝟖𝟎. March 2022: a stray rocket stage crashed into the Moon, leaving an unusual double crater.

🧹 CLEANUP & SOLUTIONS

𝟖𝟏. The Kessler syndrome, described by NASA's Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais in 1978, warns collisions could cascade.

𝟖𝟐. 2018: 🇬🇧 the UK-led RemoveDEBRIS mission tested a net and a harpoon in orbit.

𝟖𝟑. 2021: 🇯🇵 Astroscale's ELSA-d demonstrated magnetic docking for debris capture.

𝟖𝟒. 2024: 🇯🇵 Astroscale's ADRAS-J approached a spent H-IIA upper stage to about 15 m.

𝟖𝟓. ESA's ClearSpace-1 mission aims to capture and deorbit the defunct PROBA-1 satellite.

𝟖𝟔. Drag sails and tethers can speed up the fall of dead satellites.

𝟖𝟕. Ground- and space-based lasers have been proposed to nudge small debris.

𝟖𝟖. Engineers now "design for demise" so satellites burn up completely.

𝟖𝟗. 2024: 🇯🇵 Japan launched LignoSat, the first wooden satellite, partly to cut metal pollution on reentry.

𝟗𝟎. A 2023 NOAA-led study found about 10% of stratospheric aerosol particles contain metals from burned-up spacecraft.

⚖️ RULES & THE FUTURE

𝟗𝟏. The 1972 Liability Convention makes launching states liable for damage their space objects cause on Earth.

𝟗𝟐. The Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee issued mitigation guidelines in 2002.

𝟗𝟑. The UN endorsed space debris mitigation guidelines in 2007.

𝟗𝟒. The long-standing guideline: deorbit within 25 years after a mission ends.

𝟗𝟓. 2022: the 🇺🇸 US FCC adopted a stricter 5-year rule for satellites in low orbit.

𝟗𝟔. 2023: the FCC issued its first-ever space debris fine, $150,000 to Dish Network.

𝟗𝟕. 2022: the 🇺🇸 US pledged not to conduct destructive direct-ascent ASAT missile tests.

𝟗𝟖. A UN General Assembly resolution calling for such a moratorium passed with 155 votes in Dec 2022.

𝟗𝟗. ESA's Zero Debris approach aims to stop creating new debris by 2030.

𝟏𝟎𝟎. The ISS is set to be deorbited into the Pacific around 2030 using a SpaceX-built vehicle.

text:
Plus Bank pod decyzją UOKiK. Uwierzytelnienie PIN-em to za mało, by odmówić zwrotu
Solorz Business Daily · 15.11.2026

Prezes UOKiK 3 listopada 2026 r. wydał wobec Plus Banku, kontrolowanego przez Zygmunta Solorza, decyzję zobowiązującą nr RWR 8/2026. Urząd uznał za uprawdopodobnione, że bank odmawiał zwrotu pieniędzy po nieautoryzowanych transakcjach, sugerował klientom, że użycie PIN-u oznacza ich zgodę, i podawał nieprawdziwe limity reklamacji. Bank zobowiązał się zmienić procedury i ponownie zbadać odrzucone zgłoszenia. Kary finansowej nie orzeczono. Kwot zwrotów decyzja nie podaje, bo Urząd je utajnił.

Rozstrzygnięcie ogłoszono 4 listopada razem z podobnymi decyzjami wobec ING Banku Śląskiego, Banku Ochrony Środowiska i Nest Banku. To decyzja zobowiązująca z art. 28 ustawy o ochronie konkurencji i konsumentów: Plus Bank sam złożył zobowiązanie, a Prezes UOKiK je przyjął. Praktyki zostały „uprawdopodobnione”, a nie stwierdzone decyzją z karą.

Urząd zakwestionował trzy praktyki. Po pierwsze, bank nie zwracał kwoty nieautoryzowanej transakcji w terminie z art. 46 ust. 1 ustawy o usługach płatniczych, czyli najpóźniej do końca następnego dnia roboczego, choć nie miał podstawy prawnej, by zatrzymać pieniądze. Po drugie, w odpowiedziach na reklamacje informował klientów, że użycie PIN-u świadczy o autoryzacji operacji. We wzorze odpowiedzi, który cytuje decyzja, bank pisał, że „transakcja została autoryzowana po wprowadzeniu […] poprawnego numeru PIN”. Po trzecie, podawał nieprawdziwe informacje, że transakcji kartowych zgłoszonych po 120 dniach nie można uznać za nieautoryzowane i że nie da się reklamować więcej niż 15 transakcji. Te ograniczenia wynikały z procedur chargeback procesora kart, a nie z polskiego prawa, które daje klientowi 13 miesięcy na zgłoszenie.

Plus Bank musi wdrożyć nowe procedury najpóźniej sześć miesięcy po uprawomocnieniu się decyzji. Prawidłowe uwierzytelnienie nie może być jedyną podstawą do uznania, że klient sam autoryzował transakcję. Bank z urzędu ponownie rozpatrzy negatywne odpowiedzi udzielone obecnym klientom od 16 listopada 2022 r. i w uzasadnionych przypadkach zwróci pieniądze najpóźniej do 31 grudnia 2027 r. Byłych klientów, których reklamacje złożone po 15 listopada 2022 r. odrzucono, ma powiadomić o prawie do wniosku o ponowną weryfikację. Komunikat o decyzji ma się pojawić na https://t.co/gRPpJGSInO i w aplikacji mobilnej. Z realizacji obowiązków bank sprawozda Prezesowi UOKiK do 30 kwietnia 2028 r.

Dlaczego to było złe
Ustawa o usługach płatniczych stawia sprawę jasno. Z art. 46 wynika, że po zgłoszeniu nieautoryzowanej transakcji bank ma oddać pieniądze niezwłocznie, najpóźniej do końca następnego dnia roboczego (zasada D+1). Wyjątki są wąskie. Bank może wstrzymać zwrot, gdy ma uzasadnione i udokumentowane podstawy, by podejrzewać oszustwo ze strony samego klienta, i zawiadamia o tym organy ścigania. Zwrot nie przysługuje też, gdy od transakcji minęło więcej niż 13 miesięcy. Z art. 45 wynika, że ciężar dowodu spoczywa na banku. Samo użycie instrumentu płatniczego i prawidłowe uwierzytelnienie (PIN, kod z aplikacji, 3D Secure) nie wystarcza, by wykazać, że klient autoryzował transakcję albo działał umyślnie lub z rażącym niedbalstwem.

W praktyce ofiary spoofingu i phishingu często same wpisują PIN albo zatwierdzają operację w aplikacji, bo oszust podaje się za bank, policję albo inną instytucję. Plus Bank traktował taki ślad uwierzytelnienia jak dowód zgody i odmawiał zwrotu. Klient zostawał bez pieniędzy i słyszał, że odzyskać je można wyłącznie przez organy ścigania. Prezes UOKiK Tomasz Chróstny mówił przy ogłoszeniu decyzji: „Samo wykazanie przez bank, że transakcja została poprawnie uwierzytelniona to za mało, by odmówić zwrotu pieniędzy. Bank musi udowodnić, że to klient samodzielnie i świadomie autoryzował operację lub dopuścił się rażącego niedbalstwa.” W październiku 2026 r. Trybunał Sprawiedliwości UE w wyroku C-70/25 (Tukowiecka) potwierdził to stanowisko: bank nie może odmawiać zwrotu, zasłaniając się „rażącym zaniedbaniem” klienta. Jeśli tak uważa, najpierw oddaje pieniądze, a potem może dochodzić ich przed sądem.

Co to może oznaczać dla wyceny Midas i akcjonariuszy mniejszościowych
Bezpośredniego związku nie ma. Plus Bank kontroluje Zygmunt Solorz, ale sprawa dotyczy bankowości detalicznej, a nie sieci komórkowej ani częstotliwości Midas (900, 1800 i 2600 MHz TDD). Nie daje też argumentu co do wyceny z dnia squeeze-outu w 2016 r. (0,81 zł za akcję). Skutków finansowych dla Plus Banku nie da się dziś oszacować, bo decyzja nie podaje kwot ani kary. W sprawie XXVI GC 619/17 nie ma nowych publicznych informacji.

Źródła: UOKiK, komunikat z 4.11.2026 „Kolejne banki zweryfikują odrzucone reklamacje” (https://t.co/l3fsVABur6); decyzja Prezesa UOKiK nr RWR 8/2026 z 3.11.2026 (https://t.co/lSuGGowOOn); ustawa z 19.08.2011 r. o usługach płatniczych, art. 45 i 46; wyrok TSUE C-70/25 (Tukowiecka).

Plus Bank under a UOKiK decision. A PIN is not enough to refuse a refund
Solorz Business Daily · 15 Nov 2026

On 3 November 2026 the president of UOKiK, Poland's competition and consumer authority, issued commitment decision RWR 8/2026 against Plus Bank, which Zygmunt Solorz controls. The authority found it probable that the bank had refused to refund money after unauthorised transactions, told customers that entering a PIN amounted to their consent, and gave them false limits on complaints. The bank has undertaken to change its procedures and re-examine rejected claims. No financial penalty was imposed. The decision discloses no refund amounts because the authority redacted them.

The ruling was announced on 4 November together with similar decisions against ING Bank Śląski, Bank Ochrony Środowiska and Nest Bank. It is a commitment decision under Article 28 of the competition and consumer protection act: Plus Bank itself offered the undertaking, and the president of UOKiK accepted it. The practices were held to be "probable", not established by a fining decision.

The authority challenged three practices. First, the bank failed to refund unauthorised transactions within the deadline in Article 46(1) of the payment services act, which is the end of the next business day, even though it had no legal basis for withholding the money. Second, in its replies to complaints it told customers that use of a PIN proved the transaction had been authorised. In a template reply quoted in the decision, the bank wrote that "the transaction was authorised after a correct PIN was entered". Third, it falsely told customers that card transactions reported after 120 days could not be treated as unauthorised and that no more than 15 transactions could be disputed. Those limits came from the card processor's chargeback rules, not from Polish law, which gives customers 13 months to report a claim.

Plus Bank must put new procedures in place no later than six months after the decision becomes final. Correct authentication must not be the sole basis for concluding that the customer personally authorised a transaction. The bank must, on its own initiative, re-examine negative replies given to current customers since 16 November 2022 and, where justified, refund the money by 31 December 2027. Former customers whose complaints filed after 15 November 2022 were rejected must be told they may ask for a fresh review. A notice of the decision is to appear on https://t.co/gRPpJGSInO and in the mobile app. The bank must report to the president of UOKiK on how it has met these obligations by 30 April 2028.

Why it was wrong
The payment services act is clear. Article 46 says that once an unauthorised transaction is reported, the bank must return the money promptly, by the end of the next business day (the D+1 rule). The exceptions are narrow. The bank may hold back a refund if it has justified and documented grounds to suspect fraud by the customer and notifies law enforcement. No refund is due if more than 13 months have passed since the transaction. Article 45 places the burden of proof on the bank. Mere use of a payment instrument with correct authentication (a PIN, an app code, 3D Secure) is not enough to show that the customer authorised the transaction or acted intentionally or with gross negligence.

In practice, victims of spoofing and phishing often enter a PIN or approve a transaction in the app themselves, because the fraudster poses as the bank, the police or another institution. Plus Bank treated that authentication trail as proof of consent and refused refunds. Customers were left without their money and were told it could be recovered only through law enforcement. UOKiK president Tomasz Chróstny said when the decisions were announced: "Simply showing that the transaction was correctly authenticated is not enough to refuse a refund. The bank must prove that the customer personally and knowingly authorised the operation or was grossly negligent." In October 2026 the EU Court of Justice confirmed that position in case C-70/25 (Tukowiecka): a bank may not refuse a refund by invoking the customer's "gross negligence". If it takes that view, it must first return the money and may then pursue it in court.

What it may mean for the Midas valuation and minority shareholders
There is no direct link. Zygmunt Solorz controls Plus Bank, but the case concerns retail banking, not the mobile network or Midas's spectrum (900, 1800 and 2600 MHz TDD). It also offers no argument on the valuation as of the 2016 squeeze-out date (PLN 0.81 per share). The financial effect on Plus Bank cannot be quantified, because the decision gives no amounts and no fine. There is no new public information in case XXVI GC 619/17.

We begin from a 15 November 2020 observation by a long-serving corrections professional: empathy and love are necessary but insufficient. Children raised in caring families must also learn to recognize predators and antisocial patterns. In Michigan prisons a formal training, “Anatomy of a Setup,” described coordinated inmate teams that entrap officers through sequences of apparently innocent steps—gifts, sympathy, small favors—until a narrative of leverage is assembled and blackmail or contraband introduction becomes possible. The same logic of incremental narrative construction, the author argued, appears among career politicians.We examine this micro-dynamic and its societal magnification through five analytic lenses, then through the four disciplines.The five lensesSelf-organizing systems. Complex adaptive systems generate coherent global patterns from local interactions without a central designer. In the prison, observers, contacts, turners, and runners self-organize around a target; each step remains locally rational and deniable. On platforms, algorithms and user incentives likewise produce emergent cascades of attention, revenue, and radicalization without a single coordinating authority. Political movements and corporate ESG/CSR regimes can similarly self-organize around status, funding, and moral signaling until the resulting pattern (policing withdrawal, speech norms, hiring preferences) is treated as inevitable.Plausible deniability. The setup works because no single act is damning. Accepting a sketch, expressing sympathy, or sharing a post can be defended as ordinary. The same architecture appears in political rhetoric (“mostly peaceful”), corporate policy (“we are simply following best practice”), and institutional language that separates intent from outcome. Deniability is not merely an alibi; it is a design feature that allows the sequence to continue until the cumulative narrative is irreversible.Murphy’s Law. Systems in which many small failure modes exist will eventually encounter the conjunction that produces large failure. Policy experiments that reduce police capacity while simultaneously elevating narratives that treat law enforcement as illegitimate have, in multiple jurisdictions, been followed by measurable rises in homicide and disorder. Lockdowns, censorship regimes, and certain DEI implementations have likewise produced secondary effects (learning loss, mental-health deterioration, reverse-discrimination litigation, institutional distrust) that were not the stated objectives. The law does not require malice; it requires only that the failure modes remain open.Pandora’s box. Once certain thresholds are crossed—normalization of political violence as a legitimate tool, algorithmic amplification of high-arousal antisocial content, the erosion of shared criteria for predator recognition—the contents cannot be returned to the box by decree. Social media converts local antisocial strategies into scalable revenue streams and status hierarchies. Political narratives that selectively embrace or minimize one form of organized violence while condemning another further lower the threshold. The box, once opened, continues to emit.The butterfly effect. Sensitive dependence on initial conditions means that the acceptance of one gift, the framing of one protest, or the adoption of one hiring rubric can cascade through self-organizing networks into systemic outcomes. The prison setup demonstrates the mechanism at small scale; platform architectures and political narrative markets demonstrate it at large scale. Small differences in early conditions (whether a child is taught discernment, whether a department policy treats a particular sequence as cumulative rather than atomic) produce divergent later trajectories.Disciplinary perspectivesLaw. The classic setup raises questions of entrapment doctrine, conspiracy, and the boundary between protected speech and actionable conspiracy or solicitation. Cumulative narrative construction can convert individually lawful acts into a pattern that satisfies the elements of blackmail or official misconduct. At the societal level, free-speech jurisprudence (Brandenburg and its progeny) must confront coordinated amplification that is not “imminent” in the classic sense yet produces predictable cascades of violence or institutional capture. Corporate ESG and DEI regimes generate parallel questions of fiduciary duty, disparate-impact liability, and the enforceability of viewpoint-neutral rules when private platforms and institutions function as de-facto public squares.Political science. Narrative construction is a core technology of power. Principal–agent problems, institutional trust erosion, and the competitive dynamics of attention markets explain why actors across the spectrum invest in frames that maximize mobilization while preserving deniability. Movements that treat violence as a political tool—whether labeled antifa, other extremist formations, or state-adjacent actors—exploit the same self-organizing and deniability properties. The resulting polarization reduces the shared capacity to name predation when it appears inside one’s own coalition.Psychiatry. Antisocial personality disorder and related spectra are defined by pervasive patterns of deceitfulness, lack of remorse, and exploitation. Prevalence is markedly elevated in incarcerated populations. These traits are not created by politics, yet political and platform environments can selectively amplify individuals who already possess them by supplying larger audiences, status, and revenue. When those mechanisms atrophy or are reframed as “othering,” the cultural repertoire for recognizing setups shrinks. Online tribes recreate totemic identities and ritualized violence; gift economies reappear as attention and revenue. Corporate activism and certain DEI implementations can be read as new prestige economies in which moral signaling substitutes for the older pedagogical function of teaching discernment. ⚡ JUST IN 🇺🇸 | Sarah Huckabee Sanders Admits GOP Took a Beating, and Dodges the 2028 Question

Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders has conceded that the midterm elections were rough for her party, saying there is "no question" Election Night was a bad night for Republicans.

The freshly reelected Republican governor made the remarks Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union" with host Dana Bash, as the GOP reckons with a Democratic sweep that flipped control of Congress.

Bash pressed Sanders, a former White House press secretary in Trump's first term, on whether she might follow her father, Mike Huckabee, into a run for the White House.

Sanders laughed off the question, saying she wasn't sure her dad, who won the Iowa caucuses in 2008, would wish a presidential campaign on her.

"I just got reelected as the Governor of Arkansas. I love what I'm doing," she said, adding that she looks forward to serving the next four years.

When Bash asked if she was committing to a full term, which would effectively rule out a 2028 bid, Sanders noted she will be term-limited out of office in four years anyway.

"The simple answer is I like what I'm doing," she said, stopping short of a firm promise.

Her comments add to a growing chorus of Republicans publicly wrestling with what went wrong for the party this month.

text:
Judges now run Washington State

Democrats just won Yakima Valley's 14th District House seats for the first time in 34 years. On a map a federal judge drew.

Judge Robert Lasnik ruled in 2023 that the Legislature's 2022 lines violated the Voting Rights Act. His replacement map moved 500,000 people across 13 districts.

Then on Oct. 5 the U.S. Supreme Court vacated the Ninth Circuit's ruling and sent the case back for another look under its Louisiana v. Callais decision. So the map that just flipped these seats is still in court. But they did it anyway.

State GOP chair Jim Walsh says "a left-wing Seattle judge won this race." Fair hit on the map. But those same lines elected two Republicans in 2024. This year both incumbents dropped at least 8 points, and both raised more money than the Democrats who beat them.

Both parties love a map right up until it stops working for them.

What to watch:
• The Ninth Circuit's next move on Lasnik's map
• Whether that forces a redraw before the regular one in 2031
• Swearing-in, January

If the courts toss this map, should Washington redraw before 2028 or wait for 2031?

text:
paused subscribers come back 54% of the time. a "please stay" discount at the cancel button keeps 22% (churnkey data across hundreds of cancel flows)

and apple just put retention offers inside the iOS cancel screen (nov 4). the cancel page is the most under-built screen in most products

> why people actually cancel
- churnkey, ~3M cancel sessions: budget 33%, infrequent usage 31%. their read: "budget" often hides product frustration
- prosperstack, jan-oct 2026: pricing 32%, no time 11%, temporary or seasonal 10%, couldn't build a habit 9%
- under 1% of those answers named an AI tool. ask it as its own option or it hides under "pricing"
- recurly: 51% of consumers who canceled said they weren't using it enough. 38% say they'd rather pause

> what each save is worth (churnkey)
- discount: +5.1 months. 11% still paying a year later
- pause: +5.5 months, picked 15 seconds faster than a discount
- plan change: +7-8 months. 30% still active at 12 months
- recurly: when pause is offered, 25% pick it over canceling

> the order that works
- one question first: why are you leaving
- "busy" / "not using it" -> pause. default 1 month, let them extend
- "too expensive" -> downgrade, then a small one-time discount
- pause goes before any discount. cap repeat pauses
- seat removals -> offer a handoff. superhuman cut seat removals 15% this way

> your save rate is probably fake
- retainup audited 8 subscription brands in 2026: median save 10.8%, best 19.3%
- one app dashboard said 62.5%. remove people who just closed the tab: 12.5%
- https://t.co/9ZZcvk02Jo math: 30% take the discount, 40% of them leave when it expires = ~18% real save
- https://t.co/9ZZcvk02Jo test, meditation app: reason-matched flow vs blanket 60% off = ~1.5x acceptance, ~4.5x LTV per save
- count a save once the next invoice pays

> setup
- stripe portal: retention coupon ships OFF. settings > customer portal > cancellations
- stripe retention rules: offer by cancel reason, months subscribed, total spend. one retention coupon per customer. their example: "too expensive" + 6+ months = 30% off for 3 months
- stripe pause: pause_collection + resumes_at. pick void or mark_uncollectible. keep_as_draft leaves invoices you can collect for the paused months later
- apple: retention messages in app store connect (text, image, switch plan, promo offer), shown after "cancel subscription". real-time API by request, answer in 700ms or apple shows your default

> the legal line
- california since jul 2025: save offers are fine online only with a "click to cancel" button shown next to the offer the whole time
- amazon's "iliad" flow: 4 pages, 6 clicks, 15 options vs 1-2 clicks to join. the case ended in a $2.5B ftc settlement
- ftc says uber one took up to 23 screens and 32 actions to cancel. uber disputes it
- federal click-to-cancel rule got vacated in 2025, ftc restarted it march 2026. ~30 states have their own laws

> the fight
one side: save offers pay your most annoyed customers to stay, and deal hunters learn to hit cancel every quarter
other side: no flow means someone who wanted a month off has to fire you
my take: one screen, reason first, one matched offer, cancel button visible the whole time. if it takes 4 screens to keep someone, you kept a hostage

> run this week
- export 90 days of cancel reasons. if budget wins, read the free text
- add pause as the first offer
- recount your save rate with next-invoice-paid only

bookmark this before you touch your cancel button

🇺🇸 🧠 🚀 Elon Musk Invited to Shift Tesla From Blue Texas to Red Florida

Florida Republicans are openly courting Elon Musk to relocate or expand Tesla operations out of Texas after Democrats swept statewide offices there for the first time in a generation.

The 2026 midterms produced a decisive Democratic breakthrough in Texas. Gina Hinojosa unseated longtime Republican Governor Greg Abbott, becoming the first Latina to hold the office and ending a 32-year Democratic drought in statewide races. James Talarico captured a U.S. Senate seat by a double-digit margin, and Democrats flipped the state House while winning the attorney general and lieutenant governor posts. These results reversed years of Republican gains among Hispanic voters in the Rio Grande Valley and delivered unified Democratic control of Texas executive power for the first time since the 1990s.

Against that backdrop, U.S. Representative Carlos Giménez of Florida sent Musk a formal letter dated November 9. The former Miami-Dade mayor urged Tesla to consider moving its headquarters from Austin to Florida or expanding operations there. He pointed to the election of self-described Democratic Socialists and warned of excessive government interference, politically motivated investigations, and policies that punish success. Florida, he wrote, offers lower taxes, responsible regulation, and an environment that rewards rather than targets job creators and innovators. South Florida’s infrastructure, skilled workforce, and position as a gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean were highlighted as practical advantages.

Outgoing Governor Ron DeSantis has already floated the idea of a Tesla gigafactory in the state. Florida itself resisted the national Democratic wave: Republican Byron Donalds defeated Democrat David Jolly to become the state’s first Black governor, preserving nearly three decades of uninterrupted GOP control of the executive branch. Donalds takes office in January 2027 with a mandate to continue the pro-business posture that has defined Florida under DeSantis.

Musk previously relocated Tesla’s headquarters from California to Texas in 2021, citing regulatory hostility. The same dynamic is now reappearing in Texas. Governor-elect Hinojosa has already intervened to pause discussions of selling portions of Boca Chica State Park land adjacent to SpaceX’s Starbase facility, stating that any relationship with Musk’s companies must occur “on our terms.” She has also signaled tighter scrutiny of large-scale data-center projects. Musk has publicly noted that Tesla and SpaceX thrived in Texas precisely because they avoided what he described as an oppressive and extractive state government.

The contrast is straightforward. Texas’s new Democratic leadership is signaling greater intervention in land use, permitting, and private investment. Florida’s incoming Republican administration is explicitly advertising the opposite: a jurisdiction that treats capital formation and technological deployment as assets rather than liabilities. Whether Musk acts on the invitation remains open, but the invitation itself underscores a clear sorting mechanism. States that prioritize regulatory restraint continue to compete for the companies and individuals that generate employment and technological advance, while those that do not risk watching them depart. https://t.co/3a6N059Tga

ENGLAND: DECODING TUCHEL'S SELECTION 🏴

Thomas Tuchel's starting XI suggests an interesting tactical approach. I suspect he wants a side capable of competing physically and tactically in midfield while retaining enough pace, mobility and attacking quality to exploit Spain's defensive vulnerabilities.

The 4-3-3 provides a relatively balanced starting structure, with Declan Rice, Elliot Anderson and Jude Bellingham forming the midfield.

I particularly like the complementary qualities of this midfield combination.

Rice offers positional discipline, defensive protection and ball-winning ability. Anderson brings energy, mobility, aggression in duels and the capacity to cover significant ground. Bellingham, meanwhile, provides carrying power, creativity, physical presence and the ability to arrive in dangerous areas.

My suspicion is that Tuchel wants Bellingham to operate with sufficient attacking freedom while Rice and Anderson provide the necessary balance behind him.

The inclusion of Anthony Gordon is also understandable. His pace, direct running and willingness to attack spaces behind the defensive line could be particularly useful against a Spain side that will naturally commit players forward when building possession.

Morgan Rogers offers something different on the opposite flank. He can carry the ball through congested areas, operate in the half-spaces and combine with Kane and Bellingham. I suspect Tuchel values his ability to create attacking situations without necessarily relying on traditional winger movement.

Harry Kane remains central to the entire structure. Beyond his finishing, his ability to drop into midfield, link play and release runners into space could be crucial. His movement may also create opportunities for Gordon and Rogers to attack the spaces he vacates.

At the back, Ben White's inclusion ahead of Trent Alexander-Arnold is particularly interesting. I suspect Tuchel wants greater defensive reliability and positional discipline against Spain's technical players. Trent offers exceptional passing range and progression, but White provides a different defensive profile.

The Konsa-Quansah partnership also offers mobility and recovery ability. Against Spain's movement and combinations, England will need defenders comfortable defending spaces rather than simply protecting the penalty area.

James Trafford's selection is another notable decision. Tuchel had indicated an intention to rotate his goalkeepers, so this provides an opportunity to assess Trafford in a demanding international environment.

My tactical expectation: England will look to press selectively, disrupt Spain's build-up and attack quickly when possession is recovered. I suspect Tuchel will want his midfield to be aggressive without becoming positionally disorganised.

The bench is also important. Trent Alexander-Arnold can introduce a different passing dimension, Eberechi Eze offers creativity and unpredictability between the lines, while Calvert-Lewin provides a more physical attacking option.

For me, England's biggest challenge will be managing Spain's possession without allowing their midfield and wide players to dictate the rhythm of the game.

If England can disrupt Spain's circulation, win second balls and transition quickly through Bellingham, Gordon and Rogers, they have the attacking personnel to cause serious problems.

Tuchel's selection appears designed to strike a balance between defensive responsibility, midfield intensity and transitional threat. The real test is whether England can execute that balance over the full 90 minutes.

🚨NEW🚨 Britain’s nukes are ‘not up for negotiation', Wes Streeting today declared to Russia as he marked the homecoming of a record-breaking nuclear-armed submarine.

Speaking to the Daily Mail as a tired-looking HMS Vengeance sailed into the Clyde on Sunday, the Defence Secretary insisted he would ‘not abandon’ European allies and cave in to ‘delusional’ demands by Vladimir Putin. 

His comments came after it emerged Kremlin negotiators said Russia would only end its war in Ukraine if Britain agreed to stop protecting Europe with its ultimate weapons. 

But Mr Streeting rejected Moscow’s proposed ceasefire ultimatum, insisting the UK’s commitment to defending its allies with nuclear force was ‘unwavering’ and ‘unshakeable’.  

‘The fact that Putin has made these demands demonstrates what the nuclear deterrent is, and the deterrence effect it is having in the Kremlin,’ he said. 

‘At a dangerous time for our continent, our nuclear deterrent is not up for negotiation, and we will not abandon our allies in Nato.’ 

HMS Vengeance finally returned home after a record-breaking 217 days under the waves. 

No other submarine has completed more than seven months under the water continuously, with Vengeance’s 140-strong crew almost entirely cut off from home for it.  

The Vanguard-class bomber, one of four, can carry up to 16 Trident nuclear missiles, capable of delivering multiple warheads that are strong enough to level a city. 

She is Britain's ultimate insurance with one nuclear-armed submarine always on patrol at any time, ready to strike should it be ordered to do so by the Prime Minister. 

But challenges with maintenance have increased the demands on individual boats and their crews, meaning their patrols have increased from about three months to seven. 

And the strain on Vengeance was clear to see, with barnacles, rust and algae coating the boat’s stealth plating as she crept back towards her base in Faslane. 

For the ship’s company, the homecoming was finally a chance to return home after ‘one of the most stressful jobs’ the Navy can offer. 

One senior submariner said the strain crews faced was immense. ‘Anyone who says this would be easy is lying, it is hard,’ they said. ‘But we’re proud to do it.’

When they set off in April, Sir Keir Starmer was still Prime Minister and the World Cup in America was still months away. 

She had been due home last week, but her relief boat needed to return home for spare parts. 

In a message to the crew delivered to the crew, Prime Minister Andy Burnham praised them for their steadfast dedication and for protecting the nation. 

Speaking to Mail as the submarine sailed home, Mr Streeting said he was immensely proud of the crew. 

‘For the time they have been at sea, there is literally no one else, in any part of the country, in the UK or overseas, who has done more to keep our country safe,’ he added. 

‘The nuclear deterrent has been the cornerstone of our national defence and security since its inception, and it is just as - if not more - important today, with the sort of threat environment we have. 

‘So, for the UK, for our country and for our continent, these people can be exceptionally proud of their service.’

🇺🇸🇪🇺 Europe is diligently weaning itself off its dependence on Russian gas - only to find itself gravitating toward a new one. According to Forbes, Russia accounted for 45% of the EU’s gas imports before the war. By 2025, that share had dropped to 12%, and Brussels has pledged to phase out Russian gas entirely by the end of 2027. It sounds like a victory - except that Washington has already stepped into the spot once occupied by Moscow.

In the first half of 2026, the U.S. supplied 59% of Europe’s total liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports, a figure that could climb to 80% by 2028. In effect, Europe is simply swapping one supplier for another, all while suffering the consequences of high prices. And this is where things get interesting. While the EU makes a show of turning its back on Russian energy, Trump is moving in the opposite direction, easing sanctions pressure on Moscow. This means that the very leverage Europe worked so hard to wrest from the Kremlin has quietly shifted into the hands of the White House. 

Forbes offers a candid warning: Trump could wield this leverage - not just to pressure allies, but as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Putin. Gas-based blackmail hasn’t disappeared; it has simply changed its address.

A Classical Catholic High School has been proposed in honor of Blessed Fulton Sheen in downtown Springfield; and the Diocese of Springfield in Illinois is considering the possibility of its opening in fall 2027. The school proposed to be erected at the former Cathedral School building is named ‘Fulton Sheen Academy’ and it will offer a Catholic liberal arts education rooted in the great intellectual tradition of the Church, emphasizing the formation of students in faith, virtue, wisdom, and the pursuit of truth.

The proposal has been made in the wake of the interest expressed by families in the Springfield area for having a Catholic classical academy for high school students. Now the Diocese is assessing whether there is sufficient interest and commitment among families to make the school a reality.

Dr. Mark Newcomb, director of the Diocese’s Department for Catholic Education said that families have asked Bishop Thomas John Paprocki and other dignitaries of the diocese to have a Catholic classical academy for high school students. “We have decided that it is time to explore these conversations in earnest to see if there are enough families to commit to the work it would take to make such an academy a reality,” he added.

Fulton Sheen Academy, different from a traditional high school curriculum, would approach learning through the lens of historical periods, integrating literature, mathematics, art, and science into the study of different eras.

Courtney Clenney, the former OnlyFans model who pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter in the killing of her boyfriend Christian Obumseli, has been transferred to a minimum-security prison in Florida with a projected release date of July 20, 2028, less than two years away.

Clenney, 30, was initially charged with second-degree murder in Obumseli's April 2022 death but took a plea deal in August that gave her a six-year sentence. She was given credit for nearly four years already spent behind bars while her case worked through the courts.

Prosecutors say the plea deal includes a provision barring Clenney from profiting from the killing, and they pledged to back any action by the Florida Attorney General's Office to enforce it.

text:
Yesterday was another reminder of why I don’t judge college football teams by their records alone.

Georgia scored on its first five possessions and beat Missouri 48–21.

Utah had 500 yards of offense but committed three turnovers and needed a late 70-yard touchdown to escape Arizona 40–39.

LSU led Texas 21–10 and still lost 22–21, with Sam Leavitt throwing three interceptions.

Three very different performances.

There’s a difference between dominating a game, overcoming your own mistakes, and failing to finish one you had control of.

Winning matters, but so does how you win. Execution, turnovers, consistency, and situational awareness tell you far more about a team than its record alone.

If we’re evaluating the best teams in college football, why aren’t we putting more weight on how they actually play?

WEEK IN GEOPOLITICS: TRUMP-XI-PUTIN SUMMIT LOOMS AS UKRAINE TALKS AND IRAN CLASHES INTENSIFY

Overview
The week of November 9–15, 2026, centered on high-stakes great-power diplomacy ahead of Asian summits, persistent high-intensity conflict in Ukraine and the US-Iran theater in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, US-China economic maneuvering, and the aftershocks of the November 3 US midterm elections that delivered both chambers of Congress to Democrats. Preparations accelerated for a first-ever trilateral meeting of US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen. US-mediated Ukraine-Russia talks resumed in Abu Dhabi with limited progress, while Iran claimed drone strikes on US-linked targets in Bahrain amid ongoing Hormuz disruptions. Technology and trade issues, including a leadership crisis at Nvidia, added layers to US-China rivalry. Domestic US politics shifted sharply toward divided government.

Key International Specifics:
Historic Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral confirmed for November 19 in Shenzhen: The White House and Kremlin confirmed the first three-way leaders’ meeting of the world’s top nuclear powers, on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting (November 18–19). Agenda items include nuclear arms reductions (following the February 2026 expiry of New START, with no extension) and the Iran conflict; Ukraine is not expected on the trilateral agenda. Expectations for major breakthroughs are low, with the meeting framed as an “entry point” or symbolic step. Trump is also scheduled for bilateral talks with Xi. China had earlier confirmed it was in communication about the possibility.

Ukraine-Russia war and diplomacy: 
US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine resumed in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11 (first direct talks in nine months), yielding an agreement in principle on a major prisoner exchange but no resolution of core territorial disputes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that US envoys (including Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff) floated the idea of Ukraine withdrawing from remaining parts of Donbas in exchange for NATO membership—the first time this linkage was raised. Zelenskyy said he would only consider putting territorial concessions to a national referendum if Ukraine received a comprehensive package of security guarantees (modeled at minimum on NATO Article 5), a strong military, and reconstruction funding. Fighting continued intensely, with Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets. Europe sought a larger role in subsequent talks.

US-Iran conflict and Hormuz: 
Tensions remained elevated in the ongoing conflict. Iran’s IRGC claimed drone attacks targeting a US air-defense radar at a base in Bahrain (including claims on November 13/Friday and November 15/Sunday of six drones); Bahraini defenses intercepted the attacks with no reported damage or casualties, and US CENTCOM stated it shot down Iranian drones in the earlier incident. Iran asserted the Strait of Hormuz remained restricted and warned of stronger responses to US actions. US forces had conducted limited strikes in the area (including on Qeshm). Oil prices reflected disruption risks (Brent near $95–96). Trump has signaled possible restraint on further strikes absent new provocations, while Iran maintains demands related to the blockade and sanctions.

US-China trade and technology: 
On November 13, the two sides held their first meeting under a bilateral economic and trade consultation mechanism, discussing a proposed package of reciprocal tariff cuts worth roughly $60 billion ($30 billion each side), including US agricultural products. No final agreement was announced. China extended the suspension of certain expanded rare-earth export controls until January 2027. Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 (with CFO Colette Kress named interim CEO); the move followed reports of personal relationships, including one involving a woman US authorities had identified as a possible Chinese intelligence-linked individual (claims remain under investigation and disputed in parts). The episode intensified scrutiny of AI chip export controls to China.

Other developments:
 COP31 opened in Antalya, Turkey, with WMO warnings that 2026 ranks among the warmest years and El Niño is intensifying. Houthis gained ground around Bab al-Mandab in Yemen. ASEAN extended restrictions on Myanmar’s leaders over the stalled 2021 peace plan. Estonia announced border closures with Russia from December 1 following a suspected sabotage incident. IAEA concerns over Iran’s nuclear activities continued.

Most Notable Events in the USA:
The November 3 midterm elections produced a decisive Democratic victory, flipping control of both the House and Senate. Democrats are projected to hold roughly 55 Senate seats (Alaska still unresolved in some counts) and a House majority around 255–169 (some races pending). Notable flips and firsts included Texas, Ohio, Georgia (first Black female governor), Michigan (first Muslim senator), and others. President Trump’s approval stood near historic lows for his second term (around 32% in one poll), with the White House and Trump attributing losses to factors other than his policies.

In the aftermath, House Republicans selected Jim Jordan as minority leader. An impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth (led by Rep. Thomas Massie and supported by some Democrats) failed on a procedural vote. A nationwide FAA ground stop on November 13 (linked to a router/communications issue during maintenance) caused widespread flight disruptions before being lifted. The Supreme Court agreed to hear a case on the administration’s asylum restrictions at the southern border. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was relocated for security reasons amid reports of an Iranian plot. Judicial confirmations faced internal Republican resistance before the new Congress. These events set up a period of divided government starting in January.

Geopolitical Predictions:
The Shenzhen meetings (bilateral Trump-Xi and the trilateral) will likely prove more symbolic than transformative. Limited or no concrete progress is expected on nuclear arms control or a durable Iran de-escalation, though the format itself advances multipolar optics and could create narrow diplomatic channels. Ukraine negotiations will continue on a separate track; the Donbas-for-NATO idea faces steep obstacles from Russian rejection of NATO expansion, Ukrainian domestic resistance, and European caution—breakthrough remains unlikely in the near term amid ongoing fighting.  

In the Middle East, the Hormuz/Bahrain theater carries elevated escalation risk if provocations persist, but a temporary pause remains possible given summit timing and reported US restraint signals. Oil markets will stay sensitive to shipping incidents.

Domestically, the incoming Democratic Congress will increase oversight of Iran policy, Ukraine support, and export controls, constraining White House flexibility and raising the prospect of gridlock or veto battles. China will use APEC hosting to project influence and test the durability of any trade truce. Overall, the period ahead favors managed competition and transactional diplomacy over broad institutional resolutions, with persistent risks of localized flare-ups in Ukraine and the Gulf.

🧭 A DAY OF UNION, REBELLION & REINVENTION

════════════════ ❧ ════════════════

ANNALS OF THE DAY 🪔

════════════════ ❧ ════════════════

A HISTORICAL CHRONICLE • NOVEMBER 15 EDITION

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

⏱️ READING TIME: APPROXIMATELY 9–11 MINUTES

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🪔 EPIGRAPH

“We carry yesterday like a lantern—not to light the road behind us, but to see how far we’ve already come, and how much farther we need to go.” — Hodgepodgery, 2026

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🧭 CALENDAR OVERVIEW ♏️

November 15 is the 319th day of 2026 (≈87.40% completed), with 46 days remaining (≈12.60%). Today is Sunday, in ISO week 46. Observances include the World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims, National Philanthropy Day, and America Recycles Day, which promotes recycling and waste reduction. 🌍

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

📑 TABLE OF CONTENTS

🪔 Epigraph — A thought to frame the day.

🧭 Calendar Overview — The date, its place in the year, and its observances.

🔎 Intro — The stories and contradictions behind November 15.

🏛️ Major Historical Events — Five consequential moments that changed the course of events.

🔬 Scientific, Technological & Cultural Milestones — Discoveries and innovations that changed how we see the world.

🎂 Famous Birthdays — Notable people born on this date.

🥀 Memoriam — Remembering those whose lives ended on November 15.

🏟️ Sports Highlights — Records, milestones, and extraordinary sporting moments.

❓ History Quiz — A question to test your historical instincts.

🌎 Closing — A final reflection on the lessons of the past.

📣 There's More History Waiting! — Today's publication schedule.

🦉 The Stoic Mind — One thought from the Stoic tradition.

✅ Quiz Answer — The answer and its historical explanation.

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🔎 INTRO

November 15 brings political reinvention, military consequence, and technological ambition. A young nation tried to define its government, an empire gave way to a republic, and an international organization opened with hopes of preventing another world war.

A military campaign exposed civilians to conflict's costs, while a mass protest carried the names of the war dead into the American capital. Elsewhere, broadcasting and spaceflight were changing how people understood distance and possibility.

Today's history asks what it takes to build something new—and what happens when ambition outruns the institutions meant to sustain it.

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🏛️ MAJOR HISTORICAL EVENTS

From the birth of a new American union and the fall of an empire to a sweeping Civil War campaign and a global movement for peace, November 15 has repeatedly marked moments when nations, governments, and the course of history stood on the brink of change.

—— ❦ ——

1777 — The Articles of Confederation Are Adopted 🇺🇸

On November 15, 1777, the Second Continental Congress adopted the Articles of Confederation, the first written constitution of the United States. It created a national framework while preserving substantial state authority—a deliberate response to British rule.

Congress could conduct diplomacy and manage the war, but could not tax citizens directly or compel states to provide money and troops. The Articles took effect in 1781, after Maryland became the final state to ratify them. Their weaknesses helped prompt the Constitutional Convention of 1787.

🧩 TRIVIA: Each state had one vote in the Confederation Congress, regardless of population or economic size.

🌀 OBSCURE: Maryland delayed ratification partly because of disputes over western land claims. It feared that states with expansive colonial charters would gain an unfair advantage from territory won during the Revolution.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Winning independence and building a workable government are two very different achievements.

—— ❦ ——

1864 — Sherman’s March to the Sea Begins 🔥

On November 15, 1864, Union Major General William Tecumseh Sherman led his army out of Atlanta, Georgia, beginning the March to the Sea. Rather than pursue Confederate forces conventionally, he took approximately 60,000 soldiers across Georgia toward the Atlantic.

His troops destroyed railroads, supplies, and other resources supporting the Confederacy. The campaign weakened the South's ability to fight but brought hardship to civilians. Savannah fell on December 21.

🧩 TRIVIA: Sherman divided his army into separate wings, making it harder for Confederate forces to predict its route and concentrate against it.

💡 INSIGHT: The campaign illustrated how warfare could extend beyond armies in the field to the economic and civilian foundations supporting them.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Strategic success does not erase the suffering inflicted on people who never chose to fight.

—— ❦ ——

1889 — Brazil Becomes a Republic 🇧🇷

On November 15, 1889, a military-led movement overthrew Emperor Pedro II and ended the Brazilian Empire, established after independence from Portugal in 1822. The provisional government proclaimed a federal republic.

Military discontent, republican ideas, and the political consequences of slavery's abolition in 1888 weakened the monarchy. Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca headed the provisional government, and Decree No. 1 established the republic. Pedro II went into exile.

🧩 TRIVIA: Pedro II died in Paris in 1891, less than two years after the monarchy was overthrown.

🐶 SPOT: November 15 remains Republic Day in Brazil.

⚠️ IRONY: The end of the monarchy did not immediately produce broad democratic participation; political power remained concentrated among influential groups.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Replacing a political system is easier than ensuring that the new one fulfills its promises.

—— ❦ ——

1920 — The League of Nations Holds Its First Assembly 🌐

On November 15, 1920, the first Assembly of the League of Nations convened in Geneva. Created after World War I, the organization aimed to prevent another catastrophe through diplomacy and collective security.

Representatives of 41 states attended. The League pursued peaceful dispute resolution and international cooperation, but its authority was limited. The United States never joined: the Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, despite Wilson's advocacy.

🧩 TRIVIA: Wilson received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1919 for his work toward establishing the League.

⚠️ IRONY: The country whose president had been among the League's strongest advocates remained outside the organization.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: An ambitious vision for peace cannot succeed without the sustained participation of those expected to uphold it.

—— ❦ ——

1969 — The Vietnam Moratorium Draws a Massive Crowd ✌️

On November 15, 1969, hundreds of thousands gathered in Washington, D.C., to protest the Vietnam War as part of the nationwide Moratorium movement.

In the March Against Death, participants processed silently with placards bearing the names of Americans killed in Vietnam. Students, veterans, religious groups, and other citizens turned individual losses into a public act of remembrance and protest.

The demonstration did not end the war, but made opposition impossible for leaders to dismiss.

🧩 TRIVIA: The March Against Death began on November 13 and continued into November 15.

🐶 SPOT: The silent procession gave individual identities to casualties who might otherwise have appeared only as numbers in official reports.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Questioning the decisions of leaders is essential, especially when those decisions cost human lives.

The pages of history turn. The lessons remain. 📜

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🔬 SCIENTIFIC, TECHNOLOGICAL & CULTURAL MILESTONES

November 15 also witnessed artistic revelations, scientific advances, and technological achievements that expanded humanity's understanding of its world.

—— ❦ ——

1867 — The Stock Ticker Speeds Up Wall Street 📈

On November 15, 1867, Edward A. Calahan's stock ticker was unveiled in New York. Connected by telegraph, it printed abbreviated stock quotations on paper strips, moving market information faster than messengers could.

It linked financial offices and helped create expectations for continuously updated prices.

🧩 TRIVIA: The machine's name came from the clicking sound it made while printing quotations.

🌀 OBSCURE: The paper strips later inspired the expression “ticker-tape parade,” when shredded tape was thrown from office windows during celebrations.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A device that speeds up information can transform an industry—and the behavior of the people who depend on it.

—— ❦ ——

1926 — NBC Begins Nationwide Radio Broadcasting 📻

On November 15, 1926, the National Broadcasting Company began its first nationwide radio broadcast, linking 25 stations in 21 cities. Distant audiences could hear the same programming at nearly the same time.

The network model helped shape radio and television.

🧩 TRIVIA: NBC's inaugural nationwide broadcast connected 25 stations in 21 cities.

🏆 FIRST: The broadcast marked a major early step in establishing a nationwide American radio network.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Communication technology can unite people through shared experiences, even when they are physically far apart.

—— ❦ ——

1966 — Gemini XII Completes NASA’s Gemini Program 🚀

On November 15, 1966, James Lovell and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin splashed down in the Atlantic, completing Gemini XII, the final crewed Gemini mission.

Gemini developed skills needed for Apollo, including rendezvous, docking, and spacewalking. Aldrin completed three spacewalks.

🧩 TRIVIA: Gemini XII completed 59 orbits of Earth during a mission lasting approximately four days.

🌀 OBSCURE: Aldrin practiced spacewalking techniques underwater, where neutral buoyancy helped simulate some conditions of weightlessness.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Exploration advances through preparation and repeated experimentation, not daring alone.

—— ❦ ——

1971 — Intel Introduces the 4004 Microprocessor 🖥️

On November 15, 1971, Intel advertised its 4004 microprocessor in Electronic News. Developed for Japanese calculator maker Busicom, the chip placed a computer's central processing functions on a single piece of silicon.

It contained about 2,250 transistors and became the first commercially available single-chip microprocessor. Its development involved engineers at Intel and Busicom.

🧩 TRIVIA: The original design was created for a Japanese calculator, not a personal computer.

🌪️ TWIST: A chip designed for a specialized calculator became part of the technological foundation for a vast range of later devices.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: World-changing technologies can begin as solutions to seemingly modest problems.

—— ❦ ——

1988 — The Soviet Buran Shuttle Makes Its First Flight 🛰️

On November 15, 1988, the Soviet Buran spacecraft made its first and only orbital flight. Launched by Energia, the uncrewed shuttle circled Earth twice and landed automatically at Baikonur.

Buran demonstrated automated orbital return and landing, but the program was canceled amid the Soviet Union's collapse.

🧩 TRIVIA: Buran's first orbital mission was entirely uncrewed and included two orbits of Earth.

🏆 FIRST: Buran became the first space shuttle to complete an uncrewed orbital flight and automatic landing.

⚠️ IRONY: A program capable of an extraordinary technological achievement could not survive the political and economic conditions surrounding it.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Innovation needs more than engineering brilliance; it also needs the resources and commitment to continue.

Here's to curious minds, bold ideas, and discoveries that move humanity forward. 🚀

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🎂 FAMOUS BIRTHDAYS

November 15 gave the world statesmen, astronomers, artists, actors, and musicians whose influence reached far beyond their own lifetimes.

—— ❦ ——

1708 — William Pitt the Elder 🏛️

William Pitt the Elder was a British statesman whose leadership during the Seven Years’ War helped expand Britain’s power. He later opposed policies that heightened tensions with the American colonies. He was born in Westminster, England.

🧩 TRIVIA: Pitt was elevated to the peerage as Earl of Chatham in 1766, after years of prominence in the House of Commons.

—— ❦ ——

1738 — William Herschel 🔭

William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer. He discovered Uranus in 1781 and made important observations of nebulae, star clusters, and the Milky Way. His sister Caroline was also a distinguished astronomer. He was born in Hanover, in the Electorate of Hanover, in what is now Germany.

🧩 TRIVIA: Herschel initially named Uranus Georgium Sidus, or George's Star, in honor of King George III.

—— ❦ ——

1887 — Georgia O’Keeffe 🎨

Georgia O’Keeffe became a leading American modernist, known for large-scale flower paintings, skyscrapers, and Southwestern landscapes. She was born in Sun Prairie, Wisconsin.

🧩 TRIVIA: O'Keeffe's home and studio in Abiquiú, New Mexico, became a major source of inspiration and is now preserved as a historic site.

—— ❦ ——

1891 - Erwin Rommel 🪖

Erwin Rommel, born in Heidenheim an der Brenz, Württemberg, German Empire, was a German military commander known as the “Desert Fox” for his leadership of German forces in North Africa during World War II. Implicated in the aftermath of the July 20, 1944, plot against Hitler, he was forced by the Nazi regime to take his own life.

🧩 TRIVIA: Rommel wrote Infantry Attacks, based on his World War I experiences, which became influential in military circles.

—— ❦ ——

1929 — Ed Asner 🎭

Ed Asner was an American actor best known as Lou Grant on The Mary Tyler Moore Show and its dramatic spin-off Lou Grant. He later voiced Carl Fredricksen in Pixar’s Up. He was born in Kansas City, Missouri.

🧩 TRIVIA: Asner won seven Primetime Emmy Awards.

—— ❦ ——

1932 — Petula Clark (age 94) 🎤

Petula Clark is a British singer and actress, born in Ewell, Surrey, England, whose career began during World War II. She became an international recording star in the 1960s with “Downtown,” “I Know a Place,” and “Don’t Sleep in the Subway.”

🧩 TRIVIA: “Downtown” reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in January 1965.

—— ❦ ——

1940 — Sam Waterston (age 86) 🎬

Sam Waterston is an American actor known for playing District Attorney Jack McCoy on Law & Order. His films include The Great Gatsby and The Killing Fields. He was born in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

🧩 TRIVIA: Waterston received an Academy Award nomination for playing journalist Sydney Schanberg in The Killing Fields.

—— ❦ ——

1942 — Daniel Barenboim (age 84) 🎹

Daniel Barenboim is an acclaimed pianist and conductor who helped establish the West-Eastern Divan Orchestra. He was born in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

🧩 TRIVIA: Barenboim became an Israeli citizen in 1956 while continuing an international musical career.

—— ❦ ——

1945 — Anni-Frid Lyngstad (age 81) 🎶

Anni-Frid “Frida” Lyngstad is a Swedish singer, best known as one of the four members of ABBA. Her voice helped define “Dancing Queen,” “Fernando,” and “The Winner Takes It All.” She was born in Bjørkåsen, Ballangen, Norway.

🧩 TRIVIA: Lyngstad was born in Norway to a Norwegian mother and German father and moved to Sweden with her grandmother as a young child.

—— ❦ ——

1952 — Randy “Macho Man” Savage 🤼

Born Randy Poffo in Columbus, Ohio, Savage became a wrestling icon known for his flamboyant style, raspy voice, and flying elbow drop. His rivalry with Hulk Hogan helped define wrestling’s golden era.

🧩 TRIVIA: Before wrestling, he played minor-league baseball as a catcher in the St. Louis Cardinals organization.

—— ❦ ——

Happy birthday to all those born on November 15! 🎂

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🥀 MEMORIAM

Today we remember notable individuals whose lives ended on November 15. Their work and ideas continue to shape the world.

—— ❦ ——

1630 - Johannes Kepler (Aged 58) 🌌

Johannes Kepler was a German mathematician and astronomer whose laws of planetary motion transformed astronomy. Using Tycho Brahe's observations, he showed that planets travel in elliptical rather than circular orbits. He died of a fever while traveling back to Prague.

🧩 TRIVIA: Kepler's first two laws of planetary motion appeared in his 1609 work Astronomia Nova.

—— ❦ ——

1787 — Christoph Willibald Gluck (aged 73) 🎼

Christoph Willibald Gluck, a German composer, reshaped European opera by favoring dramatic coherence over distracting ornamentation, as in Orfeo ed Euridice. He died of a stroke in Vienna.

🧩 TRIVIA: Orfeo ed Euridice, first performed in 1762, became one of the best-known works associated with Gluck's operatic reforms.

—— ❦ ——

1908 — Empress Dowager Cixi (Aged 72) 🏯

Empress Dowager Cixi, one of late imperial China’s most powerful figures, dominated the Qing dynasty through an era of foreign pressure, rebellion, and attempted modernization. Her legacy remains controversial. She died in Beijing one day after Emperor Guangxu, with whom she had a strained relationship.

🧩 TRIVIA: Cixi exercised political authority across the reigns of several Qing emperors, although she was never formally crowned emperor herself.

—— ❦ ——

1917 — Émile Durkheim (aged 59) 📚

Émile Durkheim, a French sociologist, helped establish sociology as an academic discipline, arguing that social forces shape individual behavior. His books include The Division of Labor in Society and Suicide. He died in Paris of a stroke, weakened by grief over his son André’s death in World War I.

🧩 TRIVIA: His 1897 study Suicide used comparative statistical analysis to examine the relationship between social integration, regulation, and suicide rates.

—— ❦ ——

1978 — Margaret Mead (aged 76) 🧭

Margaret Mead was an American cultural anthropologist whose studies of adolescence, gender, and social behavior challenged assumptions about human universals. Her book Coming of Age in Samoa made her widely known. She died of pancreatic cancer in New York City.

🧩 TRIVIA: Mead served as president of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 1975.

In fond remembrance of them all. 🕯️

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🏟️ SPORTS HIGHLIGHTS

November 15 has also produced pioneering achievements, remarkable performances, and unforgettable sporting moments.

—— ❦ ——

1898 — Pat O’Dea’s Extraordinary 62-Yard Drop Kick 🏈

On November 15, 1898, Wisconsin football star Pat O'Dea made a celebrated 62-yard drop kick against Northwestern, an extraordinary feat in the sport's early years.

🧩 TRIVIA: O'Dea was born in Australia and became known as the “Kangaroo Kicker.”

🐶 SPOT: Before becoming a celebrated American football player, O'Dea had played Australian rules football.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Sporting greatness can come from bringing an unusual skill and background into a developing game.

—— ❦ ——

1960 — Elgin Baylor Scores 71 Points Against the Knicks 🏀

On November 15, 1960, Elgin "Rabbit" Baylor scored 71 points and collected 25 rebounds in the Lakers' 123–108 victory over the Knicks, setting a new NBA single-game scoring record.

🧩 TRIVIA: Baylor's 71-point record lasted until Wilt Chamberlain scored 100 points in 1962.

💡 INSIGHT: Baylor's 25 rebounds made the performance more than a scoring exhibition; he dominated multiple dimensions of the game.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Greatness is often revealed by the range of things an athlete can do, not just one statistic.

—— ❦ ——

1973 — Bobby Orr Records Seven Points in One NHL Game 🏒

On November 15, 1973, Boston Bruins defenseman Bobby "the Godfather" Orr recorded three goals and four assists in a 10–2 win over the Rangers, becoming the first NHL defenseman to score seven points in one game.

🧩 TRIVIA: Orr remains the only defenseman to win the NHL scoring title, accomplishing the feat twice.

🌪️ TWIST: A player in a position traditionally associated with stopping opponents became one of hockey's most dangerous offensive forces.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Progress begins when someone demonstrates that a familiar role has possibilities others had not recognized.

—— ❦ ——

1980 — Dale Earnhardt Wins His First NASCAR Cup Championship 🏁

On November 15, 1980, Dale "The Intimidator" Earnhardt clinched his first of seven NASCAR premier-series titles with a fifth-place finish at Ontario Motor Speedway, beating Cale Yarborough by 19 points.

🧩 TRIVIA: Earnhardt won his first championship driving for Rod Osterlund; his other six Cup titles came with Richard Childress Racing.

🐶 SPOT: The championship came in only his second full season in NASCAR's premier division.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A first championship can mark the beginning of a legacy rather than its culmination.

November 15 has produced records, breakthroughs, and performances that helped redefine what athletes could accomplish. 🏆

✅ QUIZ ANSWER: [B] — The Articles of Confederation.

The Articles of Confederation were adopted by the Second Continental Congress on November 15, 1777. They established the first national framework of government for the United States after independence from Great Britain.

The document reflected the states' determination to preserve their individual authority. It created a national Congress but did not give that body the power to tax citizens directly or reliably compel states to meet national obligations.

Those weaknesses helped lead to the Constitutional Convention of 1787 and the adoption of the United States Constitution. The Articles were imperfect, but they gave the new nation its first experience with a written national framework—and helped its leaders understand what the next one would need to accomplish.

STELLANTIS $STLA FELL 5 DAYS AS EUROPE SET 3 RECORDS:

Stellantis (STLA) at $3.82, -$0.04 / -1.04% on Friday.

Stellantis, the maker of Jeep, Ram, Peugeot and Fiat, is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es, and its shares closed lower on every day of the week that ended Friday. Europe's broad stock index set a record close on three of those days, and carmakers were the only one of its 20 industry groups to lose ground for the week. Friday's close was Stellantis's lowest since a merger created the company in January 2021. On Thursday Antonio Filosa, its chief executive, warned of costlier raw materials and chips in 2027, and Canada's government formally accused the company of breaking an aid agreement. Europe's stock markets are shut on Sundays and reopen at 3am ET Monday, when Stellantis trades in Milan. Asia ended Friday split, and US stock futures settled Friday with the technology contract down the most.

Momentum wants gains over one, three and six months and a price near its high; Stellantis is down 14.2%, 28.9% and 49.7% over those spans in New York and closed Friday 68.5% under December 10's $12.12, its highest close of the past year. What would put Stellantis on the Momentum Len5: gains over all three spans, with closes climbing back toward $12.12.

Europe's last prices are Friday's closes:
- Stoxx Europe 600, Europe's broad index: 664.14, +0.13 points / +0.02% on Friday, its third record close in a row.
- Stoxx Europe 600 Automobiles and Parts, an index of Europe's carmakers and parts makers: 430.92, +0.50 points / +0.12% on Friday.
- FTSE 100 (UK): 10,903, +39.46 points / +0.36% on Friday.
- DAX (Germany): 26,750, -21.95 points / -0.08% on Friday.
- CAC 40 (France): 8,368.91, +7.55 points / +0.09% on Friday.
For the week the broad index gained 2.44% and the carmakers' index lost 1.57%. The other 19 industry groups all gained, from 0.27% for real estate to 3.95% for banks.

Stellantis fell on all five days in New York and in Milan.
- New York: $4.43 on November 6 to Friday's close, -13.8% for the week.
- Milan, in euros: 4.02 to 3.518, -12.5% for the week.
- New York, since December 31: -64.9%.
- New York on October 28, the day Stellantis reported July-September revenue of 37.6B euros: +13.0%, to $4.68.
- New York, October 28's close to Friday's: -18.4%.
Friday's close is the lowest in either city since Fiat Chrysler and Peugeot's owner, PSA, merged to form Stellantis in January 2021.

Thursday brought two reports about Stellantis.
- Filosa told Anfia, the Italian car-parts makers' association, in Milan that Stellantis and its suppliers face "significant raw material inflation" in 2027 and probably 2028, along with higher costs for memory chips, circuit boards and semiconductors, Reuters reported. "For us, Stellantis, this is inflation that we measure in billions of euros," he said. Stellantis later said he was referring to its total cost base of billions of euros a year.
- Melanie Joly, Canada's industry minister, sent Stellantis a second notice of default, after one in December 2025. The notice is a formal claim that Stellantis broke a 2022 agreement under which Canada committed up to C$529M, in Canadian dollars, to retool its plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ontario. Stellantis moved production of the Jeep Compass from Brampton to Illinois, and on November 9 it announced the sale of the Brampton plant. Joly said Canada is ready to sue to recover hundreds of millions of dollars. Stellantis has 30 days to fix the breaches, the financial news site 24/7 Wall St. reported.
The New York shares lost 6.1% on Thursday, their biggest fall of the week. Three of the week's five falls came before that day.

Asia ended its week before Europe did. Friday's closes:
- Nikkei 225 (Japan): 61,142, +323 points / +0.53% on Friday.
- Hang Seng (Hong Kong): 23,638, -371 points / -1.55% on Friday.
- Shanghai Composite: 3,634.35, -21.48 points / -0.59% on Friday.
Tokyo reopens at 7pm ET Sunday, Hong Kong and Shanghai at 8:30pm.

US stock futures, contracts that track the stock indexes, settled Friday at these official end-of-day prices, measured from Thursday's:
- S&P 500 futures: 7,583.00, -32.25 points / -0.42%.
- Nasdaq-100 futures: 28,034.75, -350 points / -1.23%.
- Dow futures: 52,418.00, +28.00 points / +0.05%.
The technology-heavy contract fell about three times as far as the broad one, and the Dow contract rose. At those prices large technology stocks were set to open Monday lower than the broad market. Futures trade again from 6pm ET Sunday, and whatever they do overnight can reverse before New York's 9:30am ET open on Monday.

Stellantis's New York shares lost 13.8% in a week when every European industry group except carmakers gained. Its Milan shares trade from 3am ET Monday, six and a half hours before its New York shares. Thirty days from Thursday's notice puts Canada's deadline near December 12.
