text:
🎮 100 Facts About Nintendo

🎴 ORIGINS

𝟏. Nintendo was founded on 23 September 1889 in Kyoto, Japan 🇯🇵, by Fusajiro Yamauchi.

𝟐. That makes it the same age as the Eiffel Tower, which opened in 1889 🗼.

𝟑. It started out making hanafuda, traditional Japanese flower playing cards 🎴.

𝟒. The name is usually translated as 'leave luck to heaven', though its exact meaning is debated.

𝟓. Nintendo still makes hanafuda and playing cards today.

𝟔. In 1959 it signed a deal to print playing cards featuring Disney characters.

𝟕. Hiroshi Yamauchi took over in 1949, in his early twenties, and ran the company until 2002.

𝟖. In the 1960s it reportedly tried a taxi company, instant rice and a love hotel chain.

𝟗. Gunpei Yokoi's Ultra Hand, an extending grabber toy from 1966, sold more than a million units 🦾.

𝟏𝟎. Yokoi also created the Love Tester (1969), a gadget that claimed to measure romance ❤️.

𝟏𝟏. In the 1970s Nintendo built Laser Clay Shooting ranges in old bowling alleys 🔫.

🕹️ ARCADES & HANDHELDS

𝟏𝟐. Its first home video game systems, the Color TV-Game series, arrived in Japan in 1977 📺.

𝟏𝟑. Game & Watch (1980) was reportedly inspired by Yokoi seeing a commuter play with a calculator.

𝟏𝟒. The Game & Watch version of Donkey Kong (1982) popularised the cross-shaped D-pad ✚.

𝟏𝟓. Nintendo of America was set up in 1980 and later moved to Redmond, Washington 🇺🇸.

𝟏𝟔. Donkey Kong (1981) was Shigeru Miyamoto's first game as lead designer 🦍.

𝟏𝟕. Its hero was called Jumpman and was a carpenter, not a plumber 🔨.

𝟏𝟖. Jumpman was renamed Mario, reportedly after Mario Segale, the landlord of Nintendo's US warehouse.

𝟏𝟗. Universal sued Nintendo, claiming Donkey Kong copied King Kong, and lost in 1983 ⚖️.

𝟐𝟎. Nintendo's lawyer in that case, John Kirby, is often cited as the namesake of Kirby 🩷.

𝟐𝟏. Luigi made his debut in the arcade game Mario Bros. (1983).

📺 FAMICOM & NES

𝟐𝟐. The Family Computer, or Famicom, launched in Japan on 15 July 1983.

𝟐𝟑. It reached North America in 1985 as the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES).

𝟐𝟒. The NES is widely credited with reviving the US games market after the 1983 crash 📈.

𝟐𝟓. Nintendo bundled R.O.B., a little robot, to sell the NES as a toy rather than a games console 🤖.

𝟐𝟔. The 'Official Nintendo Seal of Quality' was introduced to fight low-quality games.

𝟐𝟕. The NES Zapper light gun came with Duck Hunt 🦆.

𝟐𝟖. The Famicom and NES sold about 61.9 million units worldwide.

𝟐𝟗. Super Mario Bros. (1985) sold more than 40 million copies 🍄.

𝟑𝟎. Mario's cap and moustache helped avoid drawing hair and a mouth in tiny pixel art.

𝟑𝟏. Koji Kondo composed the iconic music of Super Mario Bros. and The Legend of Zelda 🎵.

𝟑𝟐. The Legend of Zelda (1986) was one of the first console games with battery-backed saving 💾.

𝟑𝟑. Metroid (1986) revealed at the end that its armoured hero, Samus, was a woman 👩‍🚀.

𝟑𝟒. Nintendo Power magazine ran in North America from 1988 to 2012 📖.

📟 GAME BOY

𝟑𝟓. The Game Boy launched in 1989, designed by Gunpei Yokoi's team.

𝟑𝟔. In North America it came bundled with Tetris 🧱.

𝟑𝟕. Game Boy and Game Boy Color together sold about 118.7 million units.

𝟑𝟖. A Game Boy that survived a bombing in the Gulf War still works and has been displayed at Nintendo's New York store.

𝟑𝟗. Yokoi's motto 'lateral thinking with withered technology' meant using cheap, proven tech in new ways.

𝟒𝟎. Pokémon Red and Green launched on Game Boy in Japan in 1996 ⚡.

𝟒𝟏. Pokémon is often cited as the highest-grossing media franchise of all time.

𝟒𝟐. Nintendo co-owns The Pokémon Company with Game Freak and Creatures.

𝟒𝟑. The Game Boy Camera (1998) was listed by Guinness as the world's smallest digital camera 📷.

𝟒𝟒. The Game Boy Advance (2001) sold about 81.5 million units.

🎮 SNES, N64 & VIRTUAL BOY

𝟒𝟓. The Super Famicom launched in Japan in 1990 and as the SNES in North America in 1991.

𝟒𝟔. The SNES family sold about 49.1 million units.

𝟒𝟕. Yoshi made his debut in Super Mario World (1990) 🦖.

𝟒𝟖. Star Fox (1993) used the Super FX chip inside the cartridge to draw 3D polygons 🚀.

𝟒𝟗. A planned Nintendo and Sony CD add-on fell apart in 1991; Sony went on to make the PlayStation.

𝟓𝟎. In Japan, the Satellaview add-on beamed games to the Super Famicom by satellite 🛰️.

𝟓𝟏. The Virtual Boy (1995) reportedly sold fewer than 800,000 units, one of Nintendo's biggest flops.

𝟓𝟐. The Nintendo 64 (1996) sold about 32.9 million units.

𝟓𝟑. Super Mario 64 set the template for 3D platform games.

𝟓𝟒. The N64's Rumble Pak (1997) helped make controller vibration standard 📳.

𝟓𝟓. Ocarina of Time (1998) holds a 99 on Metacritic, among the highest scores ever 🗡️.

𝟓𝟔. GoldenEye 007 (1997), made by Rare, became a landmark console shooter.

💿 GAMECUBE, DS, WII & 3DS

𝟓𝟕. The GameCube (2001) used small 8 cm discs and sold about 21.7 million units.

𝟓𝟖. Satoru Iwata became president in 2002, the first from outside the Yamauchi family.

𝟓𝟗. The Nintendo DS (2004) sold about 154 million units, with two screens and a touchscreen ✍️.

𝟔𝟎. Brain Age and Nintendogs drew millions of people who had never played games 🐶.

𝟔𝟏. The Wii (2006) brought motion controls to living rooms and sold about 101.6 million units.

𝟔𝟐. Wii Sports sold nearly 83 million copies, mostly bundled with the console 🎳.

𝟔𝟑. Miis, the customisable avatars, debuted on the Wii.

𝟔𝟒. Wii Fit and its Balance Board turned a games console into a home gym 🧘.

𝟔𝟓. The 3DS (2011) offered glasses-free 3D and sold about 76 million units.

𝟔𝟔. The Wii U (2012) sold only about 13.6 million units, one of Nintendo's weakest home consoles.

𝟔𝟕. Iwata launched the Nintendo Direct video presentations in 2011.

𝟔𝟖. amiibo figures, which unlock in-game content, arrived in 2014.

𝟔𝟗. Iwata died in 2015, aged 55, and is still widely mourned by players.

𝟕𝟎. Splatoon (2015) showed Nintendo could still launch brand-new hit series 🦑.

🔀 THE SWITCH ERA

𝟕𝟏. The Nintendo Switch, a home and handheld hybrid, launched on 3 March 2017.

𝟕𝟐. It has overtaken the DS to become Nintendo's best-selling console ever 🏆.

𝟕𝟑. Switch game cards are coated with a bitter substance to stop children swallowing them 🤢.

𝟕𝟒. Breath of the Wild (2017) reinvented Zelda as an open world 🏔️.

𝟕𝟓. Mario Kart 8 Deluxe has sold more than 60 million copies, the Switch's top seller 🏎️.

𝟕𝟔. Animal Crossing: New Horizons (2020) sold more than 45 million copies 🏝️.

𝟕𝟕. Super Smash Bros. Ultimate has 89 playable fighters 🥊.

𝟕𝟖. Nintendo Labo (2018) let players build cardboard accessories for the Switch 📦.

𝟕𝟗. Nintendo Switch Online includes classic NES, SNES, N64 and other retro libraries.

𝟖𝟎. The Switch 2 launched on 5 June 2025.

𝟖𝟏. It sold 3.5 million units in four days, Nintendo's fastest-selling hardware ever 🚀.

𝟖𝟐. Its Joy-Con 2 controllers attach magnetically and can work like a mouse 🖱️.

𝟖𝟑. Shuntaro Furukawa has been Nintendo's president since 2018.

🍄 CHARACTERS & CREATORS

𝟖𝟒. Mario has appeared in more than 200 games.

𝟖𝟓. Charles Martinet voiced Mario for decades before Kevin Afghani took over in 2023 🎙️.

𝟖𝟔. Miyamoto has said Princess Zelda was named after the writer Zelda Fitzgerald.

𝟖𝟕. Link's name reportedly reflects his role linking the past and the future.

𝟖𝟖. Pikachu became the official mascot of Pokémon.

𝟖𝟗. Miyamoto has said exploring caves and countryside as a child inspired Zelda 🌲.

𝟗𝟎. The Mario series has reportedly sold well over 800 million games across all its spin-offs.

🏢 BUSINESS & BEYOND

𝟗𝟏. From 1992 until 2016, Yamauchi and then Nintendo were majority owners of the Seattle Mariners ⚾.

𝟗𝟐. Nintendo Tokyo, its first official store in Japan, opened in Shibuya in 2019 🛍️.

𝟗𝟑. Nintendo's New York store at Rockefeller Center first opened as Nintendo World in 2005 🗽.

𝟗𝟒. Super Nintendo World opened at Universal Studios Japan in Osaka in 2021 🎢.

𝟗𝟓. Super Nintendo World has since opened in Hollywood (2023) and Orlando (2025) 🎡.

𝟗𝟔. The Nintendo Museum opened in Uji, Kyoto, in 2024, in a former playing-card factory 🏛️.

𝟗𝟕. The Super Mario Bros. Movie (2023) grossed more than $1.3 billion worldwide 🎬.

𝟗𝟖. A sequel, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, was slated for 2026 🌌.

𝟗𝟗. A live-action Legend of Zelda film is in the works.

𝟏𝟎𝟎. After more than 135 years, Nintendo is still headquartered in Kyoto, the city where it began 🇯🇵.

📸 Super Nintendo World at Universal Studios Japan, Osaka, at dusk. Photo: https://t.co/IQ5AcxLqSC, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Then came the real argument. “𝘍𝘪𝘵𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘴 𝘩𝘢𝘴 𝘣𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘶𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘶𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘥𝘦𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘦 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘪𝘴 𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘥𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘪𝘴 𝘭𝘢𝘻𝘺.” And the professor’s verdict: “𝘞𝘦 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘢𝘯 𝘰𝘱𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘩𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘭 𝘳𝘦𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴𝘩𝘪𝘱 𝘵𝘰 𝘧𝘪𝘵𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘴.”

on the following thoughts.

Use as a lens for your lecture

Yes, it is important to teach empathy and love. 
However, if a child lives in a loving, caring family 
it becomes more important 
to teach them how to deal with antisocial personalities and predators. 
I have been working in prisons since 1987 and I have seen many such adults exploited by predators and antisocial personalities because their loving parents neglected to teach them how to recognize predators. 

The Michigan Prisons used to have a 40 hour training program "Anatamy of a Setup." Prisoners will work in teams to entrap Correctional Officers. 
Once entrapped Correctional Officers were blackmailed to engage in sex and bring drugs into the prison. 
I have collected many sad stories over the years. 
I have been lucky.
 I was never setup. 
I was offered beautiful sketches 
and always refused because accepting a gift is an initial step in the setup. 
Each step seems innocent enough.
 But when a number of steps are put together 
by a number of prisoners 
it creates a narrative. 
They are just as evil in creating narratives as Careeer Politicians.

📷📷📷34 sources
Thought for 31s

Lecture: 
Predators, Narratives, and Cascades 
— An Interdisciplinary Inquiry 
into Antisocial Emergence

Graduate seminar framing for 
Law, 
Political Science, 
Psychiatry, and 
Social Anthropology. 

We begin from a 
15 November 2020 observation 
by a long-serving corrections professional: 

empathy and love 
are necessary 
but insufficient. 

Children raised in caring families 
must also learn 
to recognize predators 
and antisocial patterns. 

In Michigan prisons a formal training, 
“Anatomy of a Setup,” 
described coordinated inmate teams t
hat entrap officers 
through sequences of 
apparently innocent steps
—gifts, 
sympathy, 
small favors
—until a narrative of leverage 
is assembled 
and blackmail 
or contraband introduction 
becomes possible. 

The same logic of 
incremental narrative construction, 
the author argued, 
appears among career politicians.

We examine this micro-dynamic 
and its societal magnification 
through five analytic lenses, 
then through the four disciplines.

The five lenses
Self-organizing systems. 
Complex adaptive systems 
generate coherent global patterns from local interactions without a central designer.
 
In the prison, 
observers, 
contacts, 
turners, 
and runners 
self-organize 
around a target; 
each step 
remains locally rational and deniable. 

On platforms, 
algorithms 
and user incentives 
likewise produce emergent cascades 
of attention, 
revenue, 
and radicalization 
without a single coordinating authority. 

Political movements a
nd corporate ESG/CSR regimes 
can similarly self-organize around 
status, 
funding, and 
moral signaling 
until the resulting pattern 
(policing withdrawal, 
speech norms, 
hiring preferences) 
is treated as inevitable.

Plausible deniability. 
The setup works 
because no single act is damning. 
Accepting a sketch, 
expressing sympathy,
or sharing a post 
can be defended as ordinary. 

The same architecture 
appears in political rhetoric 
(“mostly peaceful”), 
corporate policy 
(“we are simply following best practice”), 
and institutional language 
that separates intent from outcome. 

Deniability is not merely an alibi; 
it is a design feature 
that allows the sequence 
to continue 
until the cumulative narrative 
is irreversible.

Murphy’s Law. 
Systems in which 
many small failure modes exist 
will eventually meet
the conjunction t
hat produces large failure. 

Policy experiments 
that reduce police capacity 
while simultaneously elevating narratives 
that treat law enforcement 
as illegitimate 
have, in multiple jurisdictions,
 been followed by 
measurable rises in 
homicide and disorder. 

Lockdowns, 
censorship regimes, 
and certain DEI implementations 
have likewise 
produced secondary effects 
(learning loss, mental-health deterioration, reverse-discrimination litigation, institutional distrust) 
that were not the stated objectives. 

The law does not require malice; 
it requires only 
that the failure modes remain open.

Pandora’s box. 

Once certain thresholds are crossed
—normalization of political violence 
as a legitimate tool, 
algorithmic amplification 
of high-arousal antisocial content, 
the erosion 
of shared criteria for predator recognition
—the contents 
cannot be returned to the box by decree. 

Social media 
converts local antisocial strategies 
into scalable revenue streams 
and status hierarchies. 

Political narratives 
that selectively embrace 
or minimize one form of organized violence 
while condemning another 
further lower the threshold. 

The box, once opened, 
continues to emit.

The butterfly effect. 

Sensitive dependence 
on initial conditions 
means that the acceptance of one gift, 
the framing of one protest, 
or the adoption of one hiring rubric 
can cascade 
through self-organizing networks 
into systemic outcomes. 

The prison setup 
demonstrates the mechanism 
at small scale; 
platform architectures
 and political narrative markets 
demonstrate it at large scale. 

Small differences 
in early conditions 
(whether a child is taught discernment, 
whether a department policy 
treats a particular sequence 
as cumulative rather than atomic) 
produce divergent later trajectories.

Disciplinary perspectives

Law. 
The classic setup
 raises questions 
of entrapment doctrine, 
conspiracy, 
and the boundary 
between protected speech 
and actionable conspiracy 
or solicitation. 

Cumulative narrative construction 
can convert individually lawful acts 
into a pattern 
that satisfies the elements 
of blackmail 
or official misconduct. 

At the societal level, 
free-speech jurisprudence 
(Brandenburg and its progeny) 
must confront 
coordinated amplification 
that is not “imminent” 
in the classic sense 
yet produces 
predictable cascades 
of violence or institutional capture. 

Corporate ESG and DEI regimes 
generate parallel questions 
of fiduciary duty, 
disparate-impact liability, 
and the enforceability 
of viewpoint-neutral rules 
when private platforms 
and institutions 
function as de-facto public squares.

Political science. 
Narrative construction 
is a core technology of power.

Principal–agent problems, 
institutional trust erosion, 
and the competitive dynamics 
of attention markets 
explain why actors 
across the spectrum 
invest in frames
that maximize mobilization 
while preserving deniability. 

Movements 
that treat violence as a political tool
—whether labeled antifa, 
other extremist formations, 
or state-adjacent actors
—exploit the same 
self-organizing and deniability properties. 

The resulting polarization 
reduces the shared capacity 
to name predation 
when it appears 
inside one’s own coalition.

Psychiatry. 
Antisocial personality disorder 
and related spectra 
are defined 
by pervasive patterns of 
deceitfulness, 
lack of remorse, 
and exploitation. 

Prevalence
 is markedly elevated 
in incarcerated populations. 

These traits 
are not created by politics, 
yet political and platform environments 
can selectively amplify 
individuals 
who already possess them 
by supplying larger audiences, 
status, 
and revenue. 

Empathy training 
without concurrent 
training in boundary recognition 
and pattern detection 
leaves the empathically oriented 
especially vulnerable
—the precise failure mode 
described in the 2020 observation.

Radicalization literature
further shows 
that incremental commitment sequences 
(foot-in-the-door) 
operate similarly 
in ideological and criminal domains.

Social anthropology. 
Societies historically 
used rites, 
gift protocols, 
and explicit pedagogy 
to teach the difference 
between reciprocity and predation. 

When those mechanisms atrophy 
or are reframed 
as “othering,” 
the cultural repertoire 
for recognizing setups shrinks. 

Online tribes 
recreate totemic identities 
and ritualized violence; 
gift economies reappear 
as attention and revenue. 

Coporate Activism 
and certain DEI implementations 
can be read as 
new prestige economies 
in which moral signaling 
substitutes 
for the older pedagogical function 
of teaching discernment. 

The ethnographic question 
is whether any large-scale society 
can sustain high levels 
of generalized trust 
without also sustaining 
explicit, non-partisan training 
in predator recognition.

Synthesis 
and the listed proof-of-concept phenomena

Defund-the-police campaigns, 
selective corporate activism, 
globalist institutional pressures, 
DEI and 
affirmative-action regimes, 
ESG/CSR frameworks, 
censorship architectures, 
and lockdown policies 
can each be analyzed 
as instances 
in which self-organizing incentives, 
deniable incrementalism, 
open failure modes,
 irreversible thresholds, 
and sensitive dependence
produced outcomes 
divergent from stated aims. 

Social media 
functions as the principal amplifier, 
into scalable ones. 

The same lenses 
apply symmetrically: 
any political or institutional project 
that lowers the cost of predation 
or raises the cost of naming it 
will generate parallel cascades. 

The empirical record since 2020 
supplies multiple natural experiments; 
the analytic task 
is to measure the cascades 
rather than to defend or indict 
any single narrative in advance.

The gaps that remain 
are precisely those 
the lecture has circled: t
he distance 
between plausible deniability 
and enforceable transparency 
or accountability; 
the distance between 
self-organizing emergence 
and reliable predictability; 
the distance between 
the release of harms 
and the design of cures; 
and the distance 
between butterfly cascades 
of harm and interventions 
capable of interrupting them 
before they become irreversible.

Poem (in the style of Flash Ki / Muse, 
“Dead Inside (Mix Edit)”)

Dead inside
(Dead inside)

You taught the child only love
And left the predator’s grammar untaught

Each sketch, each post, each small gift
Seems pure enough to keep

But when the steps assemble
There’s nothing there

Light only shines 
from those who name the pattern

Unleash a million feeds
And confine the wary, 
erase the boundary, babe

Do the systems have no soul?
It’s like it died
when deniability became the design
Your metrics feel warm to the touch

You can bring the numbers back to life
On the outside you’re ablaze with virtue
But you’re dead inside
You’re free to touch the sky of narrative

Whilst the cascade is crushed and pulverised
Because the gap needs plausible cover
Now the sequence 
is the one that’s letting go

You like to give an inch of empathy
Whilst the setup is giving infinity
But now the trust has nothing left

You have no ledger 
and the harmed are bereft

Your skin of policy feels warm to caress
I see magic in the stated aims
On the outside you’re ablaze and alive

But you’re dead inside
Feel the gap now, 
hold the account please

I need the system 
to see what the steps become
Open the record to me, 
stop hiding the cumulative

It’s hurting, 
the cascade 
only naming can stop the pain

Don’t leave the pattern out in the cold
Don’t leave the next child out to die
We gave the platforms everything
We can’t give the predators any more

Now the culture has become just like the setup
Our lips feel warm with the correct phrase
Our words seem so alive with solidarity
Our metrics are warm to the brand caress
We’ll control the frame and hypnotise

You’ve taught the feed to lie without a trace
And to amplify with no remorse
On the outside
We’re the greatest moral architecture
Now we’re dead inside

(The cure for the gaps 
is the refusal of the first gift
the insistence that sequences be named 
before they cohere
the restoration of predictability 
where self-organization meets predation
the design of interruption 
before the box stays open
the mapping of the butterfly’s path 
while the wings are still small.)
Dead inside.

text:
Kirk Cousins starts for the Vikings at Green Bay today, a week after starting for the Raiders, and three different NFL teams are paying him this season. Adam Schefter says he's the first QB to start back-to-back weeks for two teams since starts became an official stat in 1950. And the team paying him the most this year is the one that cut him.

Here's the money. The Falcons released Cousins in March but still owed him a $10 million guaranteed bonus for 2026. The deal had offset language, so what the Raiders paid him came off Atlanta's bill, leaving the Falcons owing about $8.7 million. The Raiders paid his $1.3 million base salary, and after Tuesday's trade they're splitting it with the Vikings, about $650,000 each. Minnesota also takes on a $10 million guaranteed bonus due in March. So Atlanta, the team that let him go, is paying the most by a mile.

The Raiders got a steal. Cousins started their first nine games, they won the first three, and he was the NFL's 11th-rated passer at the trade, all for about $650,000 in salary this season. Then Vegas flipped him to Minnesota for a 2027 third-rounder and handed the job to rookie Fernando Mendoza, who makes his first start today.

The Vikings needed him. Kyler Murray is out with a hamstring injury, and Carson Wentz struggled in Monday night's loss to Buffalo. Minnesota's defense is No. 1 in scoring defense, so a steady QB could make the 6-3 Vikings a real contender. Cousins already knows Kevin O'Connell's offense and Justin Jefferson from his first run in Minnesota.

Then there's the career number. Cousins was a fourth-round pick in 2012, 102nd overall. He's made more than $341 million in the NFL, passing Tom Brady's roughly $333 million and trailing only Matthew Stafford. Brady won seven Super Bowls. Cousins has won one playoff game.

If Minnesota makes the playoffs, Schefter says Cousins could be the first QB ever to start a playoff game for a team after starting for another team that same season. Nobody in NFL history has been signed, cut, traded and paid quite like Kirk Cousins. Say what you want about his playoff record, but the man has never lost a negotiation.

text:
Individual freedom is not one value among others.

It is the mother of all the others.

I'll own it: I have an almost sacred view of consent. And I believe that if we rebuilt everything from first principles, we would design systems where consent is axiom number one. Not an ideal. An axiom. The starting point for everything else.

Everything good humanity has ever produced rests on the same thing: two people saying yes. Trade, trust, friendship, love, business, innovation. Everything terrible it has produced rests on the opposite: someone deciding for you.

Take taxation.

On a huge range of issues, forced taxation is theft. If an individual took half of what you produce under threat, we'd have a word for it. When the State does it, we call it solidarity. The irony: Article 14 of the French Declaration of the Rights of Man of 1789 literally speaks of citizens "consenting" to taxation. The word is right there. We just emptied it of meaning.

And we all accept this because of two axioms almost nobody questions.

Axiom one: a State can't make money, so it has to take it. Wrong. From first principles, nothing stops us from imagining a State that runs a surplus, funding what it does by selling services people choose to buy, competing with private companies, with no legal monopoly and no abuse of dominant position. If your service is good, people pay. If it's bad, they leave. That's exactly what we demand of every company. And ultimately, I think we'll have to go all the way: a complete separation of economy and State, the way we separated Church and State.

Axiom two: without coercion, nothing holds together. History says the opposite. Mises proved it in 1920: without free prices born of free exchange, an economy can't calculate. It flies blind. Hayek took it further in 1944 in The Road to Serfdom: once you plan the economy, you end up planning people, and the least scrupulous rise to the top. East Germany vs West Germany. North Korea vs South Korea. Venezuela. Every system that breaks consent ends up dysfunctional. Then totalitarian. It's not a drift. It's the natural slope.

Now follow the logic all the way.

When you're convinced you know better than individuals what's good for them, you always end up crossing the most sacred lines. Including this one: a child cannot consent.

A child cannot consent to sex with an adult. Ever. A child is not responsible for their decisions until adulthood, and that is exactly why we must protect them. This principle must be sacred, and violating it must be punished with the utmost severity.

It wasn't always obvious. On January 26, 1977, Le Monde published an open letter written by Gabriel Matzneff and signed by Sartre, Beauvoir, Barthes, Deleuze, Guattari, Aragon, Kouchner and Jack Lang, defending three men prosecuted for sexual relations with minors under 15. In the name of liberation. In the name of progress. The left-wing intelligentsia of the day, in all its glory.

In Germany it was worse, because it was the State. In Berlin, psychologist Helmut Kentler had abandoned children placed in the homes of pedophile men, with the approval and funding of youth welfare services. For nearly thirty years. They called it a pedagogical experiment. A University of Hildesheim report documented the network in 2020.

These weren't the excesses of an era. These were deviants who used the language of emancipation to erase the one boundary that protects a child: their inability to consent.

The same principle applies today to the medicalization of children questioning their gender. A 12-year-old can't vote, sign a contract or buy a beer. How could they consent to an intervention that commits their body for life, when nobody knows the effects? The Cass Review concluded in 2024 that the evidence was remarkably weak. The UK banned puberty blockers for minors. And now it's launching a trial on 226 children under 16. I believe history will judge this period as one of the great medical scandals of our time.

Consent is violated everywhere, every day. And every time, the outcome is net negative.

Forced taxation: they take it before you even see your paycheck. Value moves from those who create to those who redistribute, and some of it gets lost along the way.

Mandatory pay-as-you-go pensions: you're not allowed to choose where your savings go. A system that only works if every generation is bigger than the last.

Public debt: we bind people who haven't been born yet. The purest form of non-consent: they can't even say no.

Inflation: the tax nobody voted for. They print, your savings melt, in silence.

School zoning: someone else decides where and how your child will learn.

Public monopolies: when you can't leave, the service has no reason to improve.

Why is it always net negative? Because a consensual exchange creates value on both sides, otherwise it wouldn't happen. A forced exchange destroys value on at least one side. And above all, it erases the most valuable information there is: what people actually want. No consent, no signal. No signal, no correction. No correction, and the error grows until it becomes a crisis.

So let me go all the way: a State should have no power whatsoever to dictate to individuals what they must do.

None.

Its role fits in one sentence: protect the people and enforce the law. Protect the nation and its borders. Protect every person's life, property and given word. And the law must be chosen by the people, for the people, with one limit no majority should ever be able to cross: the law protects your freedom. It doesn't confiscate it.

Everything else is a matter of consent. An economic service? You choose it or you don't. A vaccine? Your body, your choice. Insurance, retirement, school? Same thing. The State can offer. It must never impose.

We got the full-scale demonstration during Covid.

For two years, we saw what happens when a State decides it knows better than you what you're allowed to do with your body, your days, your social life. Permission slips to leave your own home. A QR code to drink a coffee. A French president explaining in January 2022 that he "really wanted to piss off" part of his own citizens.

And hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets, Saturday after Saturday. People who had never protested in their lives. Nurses, tradesmen, retirees. In Canada, truckers shut down Ottawa for three weeks.

That wasn't irrationality. It was a signal.

When you mess with individual freedom, you're playing with forces that always end badly. You fracture a society. You turn people against each other. You create a hatred that doesn't disappear when the decree is lifted. Trust doesn't come back by decree.

We should have learned the lesson: never build coercive systems again.

Instead, we're accelerating.

Chat Control: scanning the private messages of 450 million Europeans, in the name of protecting children. The European Parliament had asked for targeted investigations authorized by a judge. The permanent version is still being negotiated behind closed doors.

The DSA: giving Brussels leverage of up to 6% of platforms' global revenue to get them to moderate whatever is inconvenient.

The digital euro: a currency issued by the ECB that merchants won't be allowed to refuse, with a cap on how much you'll be allowed to hold. They promise privacy. But centralized monetary infrastructure doesn't need to be abused today to be dangerous. It only needs to exist on the day someone decides to use it.

I think it's pure madness.

Not because the people designing these tools are all malicious. Because every control tool built by people who believe they're benevolent ends up in the hands of people who aren't. That's Hayek again: in a centralized system, the worst get on top.

And if these tools aren't scrapped outright, they will generate enormous negativity. Distrust, anger, division. What we lived through during Covid, only worse. Because it's permanent.

And yet I believe the 21st century will be the century of individual freedom.

The century of private property. The century when bureaucrats, and those who extract rent without building anything, lose their power over the people who actually create value: entrepreneurs.

AI will accelerate this. When one person with a few agents can do what used to take a ministry, the argument "we need the State for that" collapses, line by line.

A State that protects, yes. A State that imposes, never.

The 20th century tried coercion. It filled cemeteries.

The 21st will be the century of yes.

text:
Why Are Cats So Irresistibly Cute?

They ignore our commands, steal our beds, knock expensive things off tables, and sometimes stare at us as though we are the least intelligent creatures in the house. Yet millions of people adore them. From ancient Egyptian temples to modern neuroscience laboratories, the remarkable story of cats reveals something extraordinary about evolution, affection, and the mysterious connections between humans and animals.

Why does a kitten stretching its paws make us feel happier? Why do we forgive cats for behavior that would drive us crazy in almost any other animal?
Most importantly, do cats actually love us—or have we simply fallen for one of evolution's most successful little opportunists?
The answers involve ancient history, brain chemistry, genetics, animal psychology, and a surprisingly profound truth about human relationships.
Cats didn't need to become human to win our hearts. They succeeded, in large part, by remaining unmistakably themselves.

The Science of Cuteness: Why Your Brain Finds Kittens Almost Impossible to Resist
Look closely at a kitten.
Its head is relatively large. Its eyes are prominent. Its face is rounded, its nose small, and its movements occasionally awkward.
Now imagine a human baby.
Notice anything familiar?

In the twentieth century, Austrian zoologist Konrad Lorenz described a collection of infant-like characteristics known as Kindchenschema, or the baby schema.
The idea was remarkably simple.
Certain physical features—large eyes, rounded cheeks, a prominent forehead, and a relatively small mouth—tend to evoke tenderness and caregiving responses in humans.
From an evolutionary perspective, that makes sense.
Human infants are extraordinarily dependent on adults. A predisposition to respond positively to infant-like features can encourage protection and care.
But our brains do not always restrict this response to human babies.
Kittens, puppies, and numerous other young animals possess some of the same features.

Even animated characters are designed around them.
In 2009, researchers at the University of Pennsylvania published a study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences examining how exaggerated baby-like facial features affected the human brain.
They found that images with stronger baby-schema characteristics increased activity in brain regions associated with reward and motivation in the women studied.
The experiment involved human infant faces, not cats. It therefore cannot prove that every cute kitten produces precisely the same neural response.
Nevertheless, it helps explain why certain animal features are so appealing.
And kittens have another advantage.
They move.
A kitten misjudging a jump, cautiously investigating a shoelace, or falling asleep halfway through grooming combines appealing appearance with unpredictable behavior.
That unpredictability matters.
Our attention is especially sensitive to movement, novelty, and surprising events.
A kitten attempting to intimidate a cardboard box is a small comedy built around an enormous contradiction: the animal behaves like a fearsome predator while looking like a fluffy toy.
The result is irresistible.
Of course, not everyone experiences cuteness in the same way. Personal experience, culture, temperament, and familiarity with animals all influence our responses.
And cuteness should never become the only criterion for selecting a pet.
Some cats bred for extremely flattened faces may suffer respiratory, dental, or eye problems associated with their anatomy.
A face that humans find adorable is not necessarily a face that allows an animal to live comfortably.
Real affection begins when we care about the creature behind the appearance.

 Do Cats Actually Love Us? Scientists Finally Put the Question to the Test

Every cat owner knows this argument.
One person insists cats are affectionate.
Another says cats only care about food.
A dog lover points out that dogs greet their owners enthusiastically, while cats sometimes barely acknowledge their arrival.
But absence of dramatic behavior is not evidence of absence of attachment.

In 2019, researchers at Oregon State University published a study in Current Biology examining attachment between cats and human caregivers.
The researchers used a modified version of a test commonly employed in studies of attachment.
A kitten entered an unfamiliar room with its caregiver.
The caregiver left briefly and then returned.
The researchers observed how the animal responded to the separation and reunion.
Of the 70 kittens whose behavior could be classified, approximately 64 percent displayed patterns categorized as secure attachment.
These kittens tended to use their caregiver as a source of reassurance and then resume exploring their environment.
The researchers also studied adult cats and found broadly similar proportions.
The findings challenged the popular idea that cats are inherently indifferent to their humans.
However, attachment classifications developed for human children do not necessarily map perfectly onto feline relationships.
Other researchers have raised questions about how such behaviors should be interpreted across different species and experimental settings.
The study does not establish that cats experience love in exactly the same subjective way humans do.
What it does demonstrate is that many cats form selective, behaviorally meaningful bonds with their caregivers.

And that distinction matters.
A cat who follows you between rooms may be seeking company.
A cat who sleeps near you may regard your presence as reassuring.
A cat who rubs its face against your leg may be engaging in friendly social contact, scent communication, or both.
Not every affectionate cat is a lap cat.
Some prefer physical contact.
Others prefer remaining nearby.
A cat's affection is not measured by how enthusiastically it performs for an audience.
Sometimes, trust looks like a small animal falling asleep peacefully in the same room.

The Secret Language of Cats: A Slow Blink Can Say More Than a Meow

Cats communicate through a sophisticated combination of posture, movement, sound, and scent.
Unfortunately, humans often misunderstand the conversation.
Consider the tail.
A tail held upright during a relaxed approach is often associated with friendly greeting.
A rapidly thrashing tail may indicate agitation, frustration, or heightened arousal.
A puffed-up tail can signal fear or defensive excitement.
Ears matter too.
Forward-facing ears often accompany interest.
Flattened or rotated ears may indicate discomfort or defensiveness.
And the belly?
A cat lying on its back may feel safe enough to expose a vulnerable part of its body.
That does not automatically mean it wants a belly rub.
Many people have learned this lesson through direct contact with four sets of claws.
One of the most fascinating discoveries concerns slow blinking.
In 2020, researchers at the University of Sussex published experiments in Scientific Reportsexamining how cats respond when humans deliberately narrow and slowly close their eyes.
Cats were more likely to produce similar eye-narrowing movements after owners performed slow blinks.
In another experiment, cats were more likely to approach an unfamiliar experimenter after a slow-blink interaction than after a neutral expression.
The results suggest that slow blinking can function as positive social communication between cats and humans.
But it is not a magical love spell.
Some cats rarely slow-blink.
Others may show affection through proximity, playful interaction, gentle head rubbing, or relaxed resting.
A thoughtful 2025 Reddit discussion captured this beautifully.
One cat owner described a ragdoll who followed her, slept nearby, and appeared comfortable in her company—but almost never returned her slow blinks.
Was something missing from their relationship?
The most useful answer is that animal behavior should be interpreted as a whole.
No single gesture can measure the depth of a bond.
Love does not need to look identical in every individual, even within the same species.
8. The Strange Science of Purring: Your Cat's Tiny Motor Is More Mysterious Than You Think
There are few sounds more comforting than a relaxed cat purring nearby.
The soft vibration seems almost mechanical.
But how do cats produce it?
For years, one leading explanation emphasized rapid, rhythmic contractions of muscles in the larynx.

Then, in 2023, a study published in Current Biology complicated the picture.
Researchers examined eight excised domestic-cat larynges.
Surprisingly, the structures were able to produce vibrations at typical purring frequencies without active neural control.
The researchers identified specialized connective tissue within the vocal folds that could help generate these unusually low-frequency sounds.
The findings suggested that the physical properties of the larynx play a larger role in purring than previously recognized.
The study did not eliminate the possibility that neural and muscular control also contribute in living cats.
It showed that an apparently familiar sound still contains unanswered biological questions.
There is another popular misconception.
Purring does not always mean happiness.
Cats may also purr during stressful, painful, or medically difficult situations.
A sick cat that purrs while hiding or refusing food should not automatically be considered comfortable.
And claims that cat purring can reliably heal human fractures or cure disease remain unsupported as clinical treatments.
A purring cat may feel wonderful to hold.
But a cat is a companion, not a medical device.
Its behavior deserves interpretation in context.

Why Cats Have Become the Companions of the Modern World

In September 2026, the American Pet Products Association released striking figures.
According to its latest cat-owner survey, approximately 53 million US households owned at least one cat in 2025.
That represented around 39 percent of American households.
The report also documented growth in multi-cat households and highlighted changing ownership patterns among younger adults and men.
Cats have clearly become central to modern companion-animal culture.
Why now?

One explanation involves lifestyle.
Cats can adapt to indoor environments and do not generally require the same daily outdoor exercise arrangements as dogs.
They often fit into smaller homes and households with demanding schedules.
But "lower maintenance" should never be confused with "no maintenance."
Cats require appropriate nutrition, veterinary attention, physical activity, mental stimulation, clean litter facilities, and opportunities to perform natural behaviors.
A cat left alone without stimulation in a barren apartment is not necessarily happy simply because it is quiet.
Still, the relationship offers something distinctive.
A dog frequently seeks active cooperation with humans.
Many cats are more selective about the timing and type of interaction.
This difference makes feline companionship attractive to people who appreciate shared space without constant activity.
Imagine working late at your computer.
A cat settles on the desk beside your keyboard.
It has no useful suggestions about your presentation.
It does not care about your unfinished emails.
It simply remains there.
For some people, that quiet presence is deeply reassuring.
Yet there is an important warning against turning this comfort into a medical promise.

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis examined 21 observational studies involving more than 159,000 people.
Overall, pet ownership was not associated with a statistically significant reduction in depression risk.
The researchers even found a small association between cat ownership and higher reported depression risk in their subgroup analysis.
That result does not mean cats cause depression.
People experiencing loneliness or emotional difficulties may be more likely to seek animal companionship. Many other social and lifestyle factors could influence the results.
The broader research literature is mixed.
Individual people may experience substantial emotional benefits from living with cats, while others experience stress, financial burden, or little change.
A cat cannot replace professional mental-health care or supportive human relationships.
But companionship does not become meaningless simply because its benefits cannot be guaranteed in a population study.
Sometimes the value of an animal is intensely personal.

The Internet's Most Honest Cat Stories Are Often About Misunderstanding

One of the most revealing things about online cat communities is how often their stories involve small misunderstandings.
In September 2026, a Reddit user described believing that their cat did not want to sleep beside them.
The animal usually rested elsewhere on the bed.
Then, one evening, it fell asleep nearby.
When it woke and began moving away, the owner gently invited it to remain.
According to the post, the cat subsequently began approaching the same sleeping place more often.
The story attracted thousands of reactions.
We cannot independently verify every detail of a social-media anecdote, nor can we know what the cat thought.
But the account resonated because it described something familiar.

Humans and cats frequently misunderstand each other's signals.
A person interprets distance as rejection.
The cat may simply prefer a particular resting position.
An owner wants to hug.
The cat wants to remain close without being restrained.
A cat rubs against someone's legs.
The person assumes it is asking for food, when the behavior may also involve greeting or scent exchange.
In another discussion, a cat owner worried that their affectionate pet rarely returned slow blinks.
Other owners pointed out that cats express comfort in different ways.
The underlying lesson applies well beyond pet ownership.
We tend to evaluate affection according to the behavior we want to receive.
But meaningful relationships require learning how the other individual actually communicates.
There is a difference between being loved and being loved in precisely the manner we expect.
Cats offer us frequent reminders of that distinction.

What Cats Teach Us About Love, Independence, and the Art of Doing Nothing

Dogs have often been celebrated as symbols of loyalty.
Cats have become symbols of independence.
Neither stereotype fully describes either species.

Dogs can be independent.
Cats can be deeply social.

Both possess individual temperaments shaped by biology and experience.
Nevertheless, the feline relationship has a distinctive philosophical appeal.
A cat can seek your company without needing to remain beside you constantly.
It can enjoy physical affection while rejecting it at another moment.
It can rest quietly in the same room without demanding an activity.
For people accustomed to measuring relationships through constant communication, these behaviors can be unexpectedly instructive.
Consider the strange modern contradiction.
We live in an age of instant messaging, constant notifications, and virtually unlimited entertainment.
Yet many people find it increasingly difficult simply to remain still.

A cat does not seem troubled by that problem.
It can sit by a window for half an hour, watching sunlight move across a wall.
It can investigate an ordinary cardboard box with complete concentration.
It can fall asleep without checking whether anyone has responded to its last message.

Of course, we should not romanticize this as superior feline wisdom.
Cats are responding to their needs, senses, routines, and environment.
They are not practicing a philosophical discipline.
But observing them can nevertheless encourage reflection.
Perhaps companionship does not always require conversation.
Perhaps attention is valuable precisely because it cannot be divided infinitely.
Perhaps affection becomes more meaningful when it respects boundaries.
And perhaps a good life includes moments that produce no measurable achievement at all.

In a culture obsessed with productivity, the domestic cat offers a delightfully unproductive presence.
The cat does not know your salary.
It does not care how many followers you have.
It has no opinion about your professional reputation.
It is mainly concerned with whether the environment is safe, whether its needs are met, and whether this particular human is worth approaching.
That can be strangely liberating.

The Responsibility Behind the Cuteness

There is, however, a final complication.
Our affection for cats has consequences.
Uncontrolled outdoor hunting can harm wildlife, particularly in ecosystems where native animals evolved without similar predators.
Abandoned and unsterilized cats can contribute to expanding free-roaming populations.
Some breeds are selected for extreme physical characteristics that compromise health.
And viral kitten videos can sometimes encourage impulsive purchases from irresponsible breeders.
The same emotional response that makes us want to protect a kitten can be exploited commercially.
Responsible ownership begins before adoption.
It means considering whether you can provide appropriate housing, veterinary care, enrichment, and long-term commitment.

Cats may live well into their teens, and some beyond twenty years.
A kitten is not a temporary decoration for an apartment.
It is a living animal whose needs will change through adulthood and old age.
Older cats deserve particular attention.
Changes in behavior that owners dismiss as laziness, stubbornness, or aging may sometimes indicate pain, dental disease, arthritis, thyroid disorders, or other medical problems.
A cat suddenly hiding, avoiding jumps, eating less, or becoming unusually vocal deserves careful observation and potentially a veterinary examination.
Caring properly for an animal requires more than enjoying its company.
It requires noticing when something is wrong, even when the animal cannot explain it.
And it requires recognizing that our relationship with cats extends beyond our homes to the ecological systems around them.
We should protect the animal we love without ignoring the other animals affected by our decisions.

For the human, a cat may represent comfort, routine, humor, memory, and companionship.
For the cat, a trusted person may represent safety, familiarity, resources, and an important social connection.
These experiences need not be identical to be meaningful.
And perhaps that is the deepest lesson of living with another species.

Love does not require two beings to understand the world in exactly the same way. It requires them to find a way to share it.
One day, the kitten that once chased your shoelaces will grow old.
It may move more slowly.
It may stop jumping onto the highest shelf.
You may find yourself remembering the days when it knocked pens onto the floor, stole your chair, or woke you before sunrise demanding breakfast.
The very behaviors that once irritated you may become memories you treasure.
Because what we love about cats is not merely their beauty.
It is their individuality.
Their habits.
Their peculiar preferences.
The way they transform an ordinary house into a place filled with small, unexpected encounters.
Some people say cats are mysterious.
Perhaps they are.
But there is something wonderfully straightforward about a creature that can lie in a patch of sunlight and appear completely absorbed in the experience of being alive.

We spend so much of our lives searching for happiness in extraordinary achievements.
A cat occasionally reminds us to notice the ordinary moment already in front of us.
So the next time your cat settles beside you, resist the temptation to interpret every movement.
Put down your phone.
Let the room become quiet.
And enjoy the company.
The world may see only a cat. But sometimes, to one human being, that small creature becomes the warmest part of home.
And perhaps the most remarkable thing is that neither species planned for this relationship.
Thousands of years ago, a wildcat followed a mouse toward a human settlement.
Today, its descendants sleep on our pillows.
Somewhere along the way, an unlikely partnership became an enduring affection.
Cats didn't simply move into our houses. They found a place in the human heart—and, for all their independence, many have chosen to stay. https://t.co/7dnx7e5Iky

text:
When Tim Cook was about 12, he rode his bike past a burning cross outside a Black family's home in Alabama.

He yelled at the men in white robes to stop. One of them lifted his hood.

It was a deacon from a local church.

When Cook took over from Steve Jobs, Apple was worth $350 billion. When he handed it off this September, it was worth about $4 trillion.

Here's what usually gets left out.

Cook grew up in Robertsdale, a small town near the Gulf Coast. His dad was a foreman at a shipyard. His mom worked at a pharmacy.

At 12, he had a paper route. Later, he flipped burgers for about $1.10 an hour. He was the first in his family to go to college.

He has said the image of that burning cross stayed with him for the rest of his life.

He studied industrial engineering at Auburn, the kind of engineering nobody makes movies about. It's about factories, warehouses and moving products efficiently. Then 12 years at IBM. Then Compaq, at the time the biggest PC maker in the world.

In 1998, Apple kept calling. He kept saying no.

Apple was losing money, and Michael Dell had famously said that if he ran Apple, he'd shut it down and give the money back to shareholders. One CEO told Cook he'd be a fool to leave Compaq.

He finally agreed to meet Steve Jobs.

Five minutes in, he wanted the job.

He has said that if he'd made a pros-and-cons list, Apple would have lost every time.

At Apple, he went to war with inventory. He called it "fundamentally evil" and compared it to milk: the longer it sits, the worse it gets. He closed warehouses and factories. Within months, Apple went from about a month of unsold computers to a few days.

He was quiet. He wasn't easy.

In one meeting, he said someone needed to be in China fixing a supply problem. Thirty minutes later, he looked at one of his executives and asked, "Why are you still here?"

The executive got up, drove to the airport and flew to China without going home to pack.

In 2009, Jobs was dying and needed a liver transplant. Cook found out their blood types were compatible and offered him part of his own liver.

Jobs refused. Cook later said it was one of the few times Jobs ever yelled at him.

Before Jobs died in 2011, he gave Cook one piece of advice: never ask what Steve would have done. Just do what's right.

So Cook didn't try to be Steve Jobs.

He built the Apple Watch, AirPods and Apple's own chips. He turned services into a $100 billion business. This September, he handed Apple to John Ternus.

In 2014, he publicly came out as gay, the first openly gay CEO of a Fortune 500 company. He said he did it for kids who were writing to him about being bullied and alone.

And he's still a little bit of a normal guy. He wakes up before 5 a.m. to read emails. In 2024, a reporter asked him about naming group chats, and he didn't know you could. He went and named one with his college roommates. He called it "Roommates."

The kid who yelled at the Klan grew up to run one of the most valuable companies in the world.

He just never forgot that night.

Jobs built Apple. Cook turned it into a $4 trillion company.

Who was the better CEO?

text:
Jeffery Simmons does not play in Nashville anymore, and he spent part of his bye week this month inside a juvenile detention facility there anyway.

His foundation put the pictures out. He is sitting at a round table in a room with painted cinder block walls, arms folded, talking to a group of young men in grey.

Chicago traded for him in late October, so this was his first week off since. He could have gone anywhere and done nothing, which is what a bye week is for.

He went back to Tennessee and walked into that building.

None of this is new for him. The Nashville Juvenile Detention Center, the one that sits next to the stadium he played in for seven years, is listed as a partner of his foundation. He has been going in there for years.

In November of 2024 he went with about twenty other people from the Titans. They ate lunch with the kids, walked the building, saw the cells and the classrooms and the showers. Jelly Roll organised it, because he had been held in that same facility himself as a teenager.

One of the kids recorded a song in a studio Jelly Roll had paid to put in the building. One of the Titans got into a push up contest with another one.

Simmons spent about thirty minutes of it sitting with one teenager.

Jim Wyatt of the Titans website asked him about it afterward. He said it was heart touching and that it had left him close to speechless. Then he said the other thing.

"One decision can change your whole life."

He has been the Titans nominee for the Walter Payton Man of the Year award three years running. The list of what he does is long enough to be tedious. A football camp and a mental health session for about sixty students from the Martha O'Brien Center. A campaign where he pledged 980 dollars of his own money for every sack he recorded, to fund students in a program called HERO. Fishing days and suit fittings through Big Brothers Big Sisters. Turkey drives. Christmas shopping sprees. Honorary chair of a pediatric cancer fundraiser. Visits to the children's hospital.

Asked about the award in December, he did not seem interested in it.

"I don't do this for the publicity, and the awards that come with it."

He is 29 years old, in the middle of his first season with a new team, in a new city, learning a new defense, with two first round picks worth of expectation sitting on him.

He got one week off in the middle of all that, and he gave a piece of it to a room full of kids in a city that is not his job anymore.

text:
Brad Pitt at 62: The Fitness Philosophy Behind Staying Strong and Athletic

Brad Pitt has spent decades impressing audiences with his on-screen performances and athletic appearance. From the lean physique he displayed in Fight Club to the powerful build he developed for Troy, his fitness journey has reflected the demands of different roles and stages of life.

For Troy in 2004, Pitt transformed his body to portray the legendary warrior Achilles. 

His preparation involved months of strength training, disciplined nutrition, and extensive sword-fighting practice. The result was a muscular, athletic look that became one of the film's most memorable features.

As the years pass, fitness naturally becomes less about pushing the body to its limits and more about maintaining strength, mobility, and overall health. 

A balanced approach to exercise, proper nutrition, cardiovascular activity, and adequate recovery can help support those goals at any age.

The real lesson isn't about following a celebrity's supposed secret routine. It's about building habits that last:

•Strength training: Resistance exercises help preserve muscle and support everyday movement.

•Cardiovascular fitness: Regular activity helps maintain endurance and heart health.

•Balanced nutrition: Adequate protein, whole foods, and proper hydration support an active lifestyle.

•Recovery: Rest, quality sleep, and consistency are just as important as exercise.

•Long-term discipline: Sustainable habits matter far more than extreme diets or punishing workouts.

Brad Pitt's changing screen roles offer a reminder that fitness evolves throughout life. The goal isn't to look exactly as you did at 30. 

It's to stay healthy, strong, capable, and confident at every age.

True fitness isn't a quick transformation. It's a lifelong commitment to taking care of yourself.

text:
This essay is part of MIT Technology Review’s 2023 Innovators Under 35 package. Meet this year’s honorees.

Innovation is a powerful engine for uplifting society and fueling economic growth. Antibiotics, electric lights, refrigerators, airplanes, smartphones—we have these things because innovators created something that didn’t exist before. MIT Technology Review’s Innovators Under 35 list celebrates individuals who have accomplished a lot early in their careers and are likely to accomplish much more still. 

Having spent many years working on AI research and building AI products, I’m fortunate to have participated in a few innovations that made an impact, like using reinforcement learning to fly helicopter drones at Stanford, starting and leading Google Brain to drive large-scale deep learning, and creating online courses that led to the founding of Coursera. I’d like to share some thoughts about how to do it well, sidestep some of the pitfalls, and avoid building things that lead to serious harm along the way.

AI is a dominant driver of innovation today

As I have said before, I believe AI is the new electricity. Electricity revolutionized all industries and changed our way of life, and AI is doing the same. It’s reaching into every industry and discipline, and it’s yielding advances that help multitudes of people.

AI—like electricity—is a general-­purpose technology. Many innovations, such as a medical treatment, space rocket, or battery design, are fit for one purpose. In contrast, AI is useful for generating art, serving web pages that are relevant to a search query, optimizing shipping routes to save fuel, helping cars avoid collisions, and much more. 

The advance of AI creates opportunities for everyone in all corners of the economy to explore whether or how it applies to their area. Thus, learning about AI creates disproportionately many opportunities to do something that no one else has ever done before.

For instance, at AI Fund, a venture studio that I lead, I’ve been privileged to participate in projects that apply AI to maritime shipping, relationship coaching, talent management, education, and other areas. Because many AI technologies are new, their application to most domains has not yet been explored. In this way, knowing how to take advantage of AI gives you numerous opportunities to collaborate with others. 

Looking ahead, a few developments are especially exciting.

  • Prompting: While ChatGPT has popularized the ability to prompt an AI model to write, say, an email or a poem, software developers are just beginning to understand that prompting enables them to build in minutes the types of powerful AI applications that used to take months. A massive wave of AI applications will be built this way. 
  • Vision transformers: Text trans­formers—language models based on the transformer neural network architecture, which was invented in 2017 by Google Brain and collaborators—have revolutionized writing. Vision transformers, which adapt transformers to computer vision tasks such as recognizing objects in images, were introduced in 2020 and quickly gained widespread attention. The buzz around vision transformers in the technical community today reminds me of the buzz around text transformers a couple of years before ChatGPT. A similar revolution is coming to image processing. Visual prompting, in which the prompt is an image rather than a string of text, will be part of this change.
  • AI applications: The press has given a lot of attention to AI’s hardware and software infrastructure and developer tools. But this emerging AI infrastructure won’t succeed unless even more valuable AI businesses are built on top of it. So even though a lot of media attention is on the AI infrastructure layer, there will be even more growth in the AI application layer. 

These areas offer rich opportunities for innovators. Moreover, many of them are within reach of broadly tech-savvy people, not just people already in AI. Online courses, open-source software, software as a service, and online research papers give everyone tools to learn and start innovating. But even if these technologies aren’t yet within your grasp, many other paths to innovation are wide open.

Be optimistic, but dare to fail 

That said, a lot of ideas that initially seem promising turn out to be duds. Duds are unavoidable if you take innovation seriously. Here are some projects of mine that you probably haven’t heard of, because they were duds: 

  • I spent a long time trying to get aircraft to fly autonomously in formation to save fuel (similar to birds that fly in a V formation). In hindsight, I executed poorly and should have worked with much larger aircraft.
  • I tried to get a robot arm to unload dishwashers that held dishes of all different shapes and sizes. In hindsight, I was much too early. Deep-learning algorithms for perception and control weren’t good enough at the time.  
  • About 15 years ago, I thought that unsupervised learning (that is, enabling machine-learning models to learn from unlabeled data) was a promising approach. I mistimed this idea as well. It’s finally working, though, as the availability of data and computational power has grown.

It was painful when these projects didn’t succeed, but the lessons I learned turned out to be instrumental for other projects that fared better. Through my failed attempt at V-shape flying, I learned to plan projects much better and front-load risks. The effort to unload dishwashers failed, but it led my team to build the Robot Operating System (ROS), which became a popular open-source framework that’s now in robots from self-driving cars to mechanical dogs. Even though my initial focus on unsupervised learning was a poor choice, the steps we took turned out to be critical in scaling up deep learning at Google Brain.

Innovation has never been easy. When you do something new, there will be skeptics. In my younger days, I faced a lot of skepticism when starting most of the projects that ultimately proved to be successful. But this is not to say the skeptics are always wrong. I faced skepticism for most of the unsuccessful projects as well.

As I became more experienced, I found that more and more people would agree with whatever I said, and that was even more worrying. I had to actively seek out people who would challenge me and tell me the truth. Luckily, these days I am surrounded by people who will tell me when they think I’m doing something dumb! 

While skepticism is healthy and even necessary, society has a deep interest in the fruits of innovation. And that is a good reason to approach innovation with optimism. I’d rather side with the optimist who wants to give it a shot and might fail than the pessimist who doubts what’s possible. 

Take responsibility for your work

As we focus on AI as a driver of valuable innovation throughout society, social responsibility is more important than ever. People both inside and outside the field see a wide range of possible harms AI may cause. These include both short-term issues, such as bias and harmful applications of the technology, and long-term risks, such as concentration of power and potentially catastrophic applications. It’s important to have open and intellectually rigorous conversations about them. In that way, we can come to an agreement on what the real risks are and how to reduce them.

Over the past millennium, successive waves of innovation have reduced infant mortality, improved nutrition, boosted literacy, raised standards of living worldwide, and fostered civil rights including protections for women, minorities, and other marginalized groups. Yet innovations have also contributed to climate change, spurred rising inequality, polarized society, and increased loneliness. 

Clearly, the benefits of innovation come with risks, and we have not always managed them wisely. AI is the next wave, and we have an obligation to learn lessons from the past to maximize future benefits for everyone and minimize harm. This will require commitment from both individuals and society at large. 

At the social level, governments are moving to regulate AI. To some innovators, regulation may look like an unnecessary restraint on progress. I see it differently. Regulation helps us avoid mistakes and enables new benefits as we move into an uncertain future. I welcome regulation that calls for more transparency into the opaque workings of large tech companies; this will help us understand their impact and steer them toward achieving broader societal benefits. Moreover, new regulations are needed because many existing ones were written for a pre-AI world. The new regulations should specify the outcomes we want in important areas like health care and finance—and those we do not want. 

But avoiding harm shouldn’t be just a priority for society. It also needs to be a priority for each innovator. As technologists, we have a responsibility to understand the implications of our research and innovate in ways that are beneficial. Traditionally, many technologists adopted the attitude that the shape technology takes is inevitable and there’s nothing we can do about it, so we might as well innovate freely. But we know that’s not true. 

When innovators choose to work on differential privacy (which allows AI to learn from data without exposing personally identifying information), they make a powerful statement that privacy matters. That statement helps shape the social norms adopted by public and private institutions. Conversely, when innovators create Web3 cryptographic protocols to launder money, that too creates a powerful statement—in my view, a harmful one—that governments should not be able to trace how funds are transferred and spent. 

If you see something unethical being done, I hope you’ll raise it with your colleagues and supervisors and engage them in constructive conversations. And if you are asked to work on something that you don’t think helps humanity, I hope you’ll actively work to put a stop to it. If you are unable to do so, then consider walking away. At AI Fund, I have killed projects that I assessed to be financially sound but ethically unsound. I urge you to do the same. 

Now, go forth and innovate! If you’re already in the innovation game, keep at it. There’s no telling what great accomplishment lies in your future. If your ideas are in the daydream stage, share them with others and get help to shape them into something practical and successful. Start executing, and find ways to use the power of innovation for good. 

This essay is part of MIT Technology Review’s 2023 Innovators Under 35 package. Meet this year’s honorees.

Andrew Ng is a renowned global AI innovator. He leads AI Fund, https://t.co/rYB64c7qZ0, and Landing AI.

                Beware Socialism’s Moderate Makeover
                                The Wall Street Journal 

Several large U.S. cities will soon be under the leadership of DSA mayors selling a softer version of the radical ideology.

The mayors of America’s two most populous cities and the nation’s capital will soon be members of the Democratic Socialists of America. Nithya Raman won her election in Los Angeles, and Janeese Lewis George won hers in Washington. They join a string of recently elected socialist mayors, including Zohran Mamdani in New York, Katie Wilson in Seattle and David Morales in Providence, R.I.

At first blush, it appears the American electorate has swung far to the left. The truth is that many of the victorious democratic socialists have built big coalitions by cloaking radical policies in the language of moderation and pragmatism.

Ms. Raman attracted disparate factions by downplaying her ties to democratic socialism. She wrangled an endorsement from the DSA’s L.A. chapter, though it took months to make it official due to concerns she wasn’t sufficiently outspoken against Israel or dogmatically committed to their party agenda. She also appeared alongside DSA-aligned influencers, comedians and podcasters. Yet, at least in Ms. Raman’s public messaging, she’s tempered her stances on public safety, homelessness enforcement and local tax policy, while emphasizing practical issues such as fixing streetlights and potholes. This moderation was part of her appeal to labor unions, undecided voters and the Democratic establishment aligned with her opponent, Mayor Karen Bass. Ms. Raman described herself weeks before the November election as both a “democratic socialist” and a “capitalist.”

This rhetorical straddle feeds into existing uncertainty among the electorate about what the politicians who identify as socialists really stand for. When asked, voters struggle to define democratic socialism. Nobody really knows whether it means Soviet-style collectivism, cold-blooded Maoism or a Nordic model of cradle-to-grave welfare. The confusion may be the point. It invites voters to ignore specifics and focus on vibes. Ms. Raman seems nice. She couldn’t be that crazy.

Other left-wing candidates camouflaged their whackier ideas to help secure victory. Ms. Lewis George blended her progressive activism with traditional D.C. Democratic Party governance through a “sewer socialism” agenda focused on improving public services, housing and affordability. “I’ll be the mayor of the corner store,” she said in an acceptance speech, “and the corner office.” Echoing Mr. Mamdani, her plans include universal affordable child care, free buses for certain residents and ending the Metropolitan Police Department’s cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. In her 2020 City Council run she called to defund the police and decriminalize drugs and sex work, though she has since distanced herself from those statements.

Texas’ Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa defines herself as a “left-populist” while rejecting the label “progressive,” explaining that the latter has been associated with culture wars, “and I don’t think culture wars are the fight of 2026.” Ms. Hinojosa’s track record tells a different story. She’s a member of the Texas Legislative Progressive Caucus, and her voting history in the Texas House puts her among the most liberal Democrats on issues ranging from universal healthcare to environmental policy.

All politicians alter their messages to win elections. But socialism has a particularly ugly history of hiding the ball for politically expedient reasons. Fidel Castro publicly denied being a communist on a visit to the U.S. in 1959, instead describing his political ideal as a form of “humanism.” After the Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961, he declared himself a Marxist-Leninist, explaining he’d previously hid from this label to avoid alienating middle-class allies and the bourgeoisie. Vladimir Lenin used the slogan “Peace, Land, and Bread” to build broad public support among the devastated postwar population. His Bolsheviks quickly transitioned from populist promises to centralized control after seizing power in 1917.

Those examples are certainly more extreme than anything happening on America’s ascendant far-left, yet certain elements of the DSA do take them as inspiration.

The DSA mayors leading socialism’s current rebrand are priming the American electorate for the 2028 presidential race, which may feature Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as a candidate for the Democratic nomination. Yet much rests on what happens in the cities they run during the next two years. Since socialism is being pitched not definitionally but through the pledge of results-oriented governance, its makeover will succeed or fail on a performance basis. The rising crop of left-wing leaders will have to deliver policy successes if they want voters to believe their promises.
