White Workers Claiming Discrimination Complicates Shell’s DEI Drive [Bloomberg]

In October, Shell Plc held a “DE&I in Action and World Mental  Health” day, focused on inclusion and mental wellbeing. Staff in the  U.S. and elsewhere were encouraged to reflect on their experiences at  work, to “practice care, courage and curiosity” and to use a special  video-conference background to mark the occasion.

For an oil major that does business with the U.S. government, the mere existence of the event is notable.

At a time when many global companies are downplaying diversity  measures, London-headquartered Shell — which counts the U.S. as its  biggest country market — is vocal in its commitment to diversity, equity  and inclusion, calling it “a key driver for our winning performance  culture.” That stance helps Shell comply with global diversity  regulations that are non-negotiable for businesses based outside of the  U.S. But it also increases the risk of scrutiny from the Trump  administration and conservative activists.

Shell’s DEI commitment has become central to legal challenges filed  by three current or former employees represented by an activist group  co-founded by President Donald Trump’s new Chief of Staff, Stephen  Miller. The workers claim to have been discriminated against because  they are White, describing a team restructure that favored  ethnic-minority colleagues and foreign nationals, as well as a manager  who they say gave them “tear jars” as jokey leaving gifts, which they  found insensitive.

The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — whose  Trump-appointed chair has urged White men to report workplace  discrimination — did not take up the case but gave the trio notice of  the right to sue, an administrative step. In March, a judge will review  whether one of the cases is ready to proceed to trial, according to  court filings.

Shell strongly rebuts the allegations, a company spokesperson said,  adding that it does not tolerate discrimination and makes employment  decisions based on merit and business needs. The business complies with  local laws and regulations in countries where it operates, the  spokesperson added. Shell also said in a legal filing that the unit the  plaintiffs worked for has a long-standing practice of giving departing  employees iconic blue-and-white Dutch pottery in recognition of their  time at the company.

Employment discrimination lawsuits don’t typically threaten large  corporations’ core operations or business viability. And people with  knowledge of the oil and gas sector said that firms like Shell broadly  have good relationships with the Trump administration and more pressing  concerns than DEI.

Nonetheless, these cases can cause reputational damage, incur legal  costs and soak up managers’ time and attention. They also show how  Trump’s DEI pushback is being pursued.

“We’re seeing more enforcement activity where we hadn’t seen  enforcement activity before,” said Samia Kirmani, a Boston-based  attorney at Jackson Lewis PC, which focuses on employment law.

The EEOC has already stepped up its pursuit of DEI-related cases  through policy statements and guidance; notified Fortune 500 companies  that it’s prepared to litigate over DEI; filed a lawsuit against a  Coca-Cola Co. distributor over a women’s-only retreat and this month  settled with Lockheed Martin Corp. over alleged discrimination against  White employees related to performance and compensation decisions. While  the Democrats’ landslide victory in the midterm elections this month  has altered the political landscape, the implications for government  actions on DEI remain to be seen.

Of the 32 workplace DEI-discrimination lawsuits ongoing across the  country right now, most concern White people claiming discrimination,  according to New York University’s Meltzer Center for Diversity,  Inclusion and Belonging.

In addition to the EEOC’s growing appetite for enforcement, there are  President Trump’s own executive orders and directives from the  Department of Justice to consider, Kirmani said, meaning businesses  across the board can’t ignore the prospect of future legal action.

Scaling Back

In the American workforce, White people hold about 80% of all  management roles and have one of the lowest unemployment rates of any  cohort. The Trump administration has prioritized fighting what it  describes as racism against White workers, barring federal contractors  from engaging in “illegal DEI.” In response, companies like McDonald’s  Corp. and Ford Motor Co. have scaled back their inclusion efforts.

Meanwhile, Shell, which is among the world’s largest energy companies  and is enjoying healthy financial growth after several years of  cost-cutting, has continued to set measurable global diversity targets,  although it does not target specific numbers in the U.S. It aims for  women to hold 40% of global senior leadership positions by 2030. It  maintains a Global Council for Race — a group of senior Shell leaders  aiming to advance workforce diversity, who do not make individual  employment decisions — and supports employee groups focused on race and  ethnicity, as well as LGBTQ+ and disability inclusion.

In the U.K. and European Union, where diversity rules mainly focus on  gender rather than race, companies are required to meet targets and  follow disclosure rules around things like board diversity, gender pay  gaps and pay transparency. Countries including Japan and Australia also  impose diversity regulations on corporations. To operate in these  jurisdictions, U.S. companies must meet these requirements too,  regardless of their approach at home.
Thomas Hutt holds the tear jar he says was given to him by his former boss at Shell.
Measures like holding DEI events aren’t specifically covered by these  regulations. But the oil and gas industry often struggles to bring in  women and needs to maintain a balanced global workforce to do business  in many countries, said Alison Taylor, a clinical associate professor at  New York University who focuses on corporate responsibility and  business ethics. “They tend to operate via moving people around,” she  said.

In lawsuits filed in Texas, the most recent of them in August, three  people who work or have worked in Shell’s U.S. corporate security unit  allege that the company violated employment laws. They are seeking back  pay, compensation for future lost earnings, benefits and damages from  Shell, without specifying a figure.

The plaintiffs allege that the oil company favored minority workers  at their expense during a restructuring of their division in January  2025 — just as Trump was beginning his second term and when many  companies were already scaling back their DEI efforts.

Miller’s America First Legal, which lists dismantling DEI as a  priority on its website, is also representing White people in cases  against corporations including TV network CBS, Meta Platforms Inc. and  International Business Machines Corp.

“Federal civil rights laws protect every American, and America First  Legal is fighting to hold Shell accountable for violating those  protections in the name of ‘DEI,’” AFL spokeswoman Alexa Vance said in  an emailed statement. “Shell touts its commitment to ‘diversity’ while  simultaneously showing high-performing, longtime employees the door  because they are White.”

Complaints like those against Shell are victories for right-wing  groups because they support their broader media campaign and narrative,  said Jonathan Feingold, a law professor at Boston University. “Large  corporations often have actually pretty shallow commitments to reckon  with the way in which misogyny or racism manifest in their  institutions,” he said.

In his complaint, Thomas Hutt, a former manager in Shell’s corporate  security unit, said he was forced to reapply for his role after almost  15 years at the company, during which he received strong performance  reviews. Hutt said his manager Wayne Hunt, a defendant in the case, had  said he was looking to “diversify the talent.”

Hutt said he was ultimately replaced by a Black colleague who, in his  view, lacked experience in corporate security, having previously worked  in fraud investigations. When he left the job, Hutt said that Hunt gave  him a “tear jar” — a small, decorative vessel, supposedly for  collecting tears — to mock him.

Two of Hutt’s colleagues, Kevin Taylor and Michelle Romak, jointly  filed a similar complaint in August last year. They said they were told  to reapply for their roles during the 2025 reorganization, while  minority employees weren’t. They allege that some minority applicants  for jobs within the team got preferential treatment, such as interview  coaching. In a formal written response to the allegations dated Oct. 16,  2025, Shell said that a coaching session was to help an employee join  its corporate security group, not to prepare them for interviews.

Taylor, who still works at Shell, said in the complaint that he was  demoted and forced to transfer from company headquarters to another  state, while a Hispanic contractor, who Taylor said was  under-performing, was given his preferred role. In its response, Shell  denied the allegations but accepted that Hunt had approved Taylor’s  transfer. Romak was ultimately laid off and said Hunt also gave her a  tear jar.

The EEOC declined to comment, while the White House didn’t respond to emails seeking comment.

Polarized Views

During an internal company webcast around the time of Trump’s January  2025 inauguration, Shell Chief Legal Officer Philippa Bounds was asked  how Trump’s policies may affect its contracts and said the company was  not turning its back on DEI, according to a former employee who declined  to be identified discussing internal communications. Shell did not  comment on the matter.

On employee-review website Glassdoor, Shell ranks 4.1 out of 5 for  its DE&I measures. Some employees have also praised the company’s  efforts on platforms like LinkedIn, where one employee wrote earlier  this year that she was proud to work with “everyone who makes diversity,  equity and inclusion real.”

But for some former employees in the U.S., Shell’s approach has been a frustration.

One ex-supervisor who worked offshore said he believed staff  reductions disproportionately affected White, male workers and that he  was compelled to give presentations on LGBTQ issues that he felt  conflicted with his Christian faith. The supervisor declined to be  identified, citing a non-disclosure agreement.

Another former offshore worker, who also asked not to be named, said  he believed Shell aimed to make its Whale production platform the most  diverse in the Gulf of Mexico and that managers actively sought Black  and other minority employees for leadership-development programs.

In his view, DEI impacted morale among White, male employees who felt overlooked and unable to voice criticism.

As Americans’ perspectives on DEI have become more polarized, the workload for international companies has only increased.

“Whenever the wind blows one way, we have one kind of lawsuit, and  then when the wind blows the other way, we have another kind of  lawsuit,” said Katie Mehnert, who is chief executive officer of  Houston-based workforce development company Ally Energy and has also  worked at Shell.

“It’s just a very disruptive approach to how to do business.”

text:
$VICR $FPS $INIO deep dive + valuation comp:

$VICR, $FPS, and $INIO still sit on $11.4B in combined backlog to fix a grid bottleneck that takes years to clear. I compared them across four areas:

• Growth
• Margins & Cash Flow
• Valuation
• AI Slowdown Risk

Company Overviews:

1. On-site power: INNIO ($INIO · $10.9B Market Cap)

What they do: Builds industrial natural-gas engines that let data centers generate electricity right on site instead of waiting years for a utility hookup. Unlike traditional power turbines, these engines use almost no water, making permits much easier in dry states like Texas.

Latest quarter: Q3 backlog rose 142% YoY to $8.0B, and Free Cash Flow hit $201M. Recurring service and parts generate 33% of sales and 62% of trailing EBITDA.

Risks Still carries $1.4B in net debt (~1.8x EBITDA), local gas plants need air permits, and its private-equity backer still holds a large stake from the June IPO.

2. Campus power gear: Forgent ($FPS · $6.7B Market Cap)

What they do: Builds custom electrical gear and factory-wired power rooms that distribute and regulate electricity safely across a data center campus into the server racks.

Latest quarter: Q1 revenue jumped 69% YoY to $479M, management raised full-year guidance to $2.55B (+80% YoY), and Free Cash Flow flipped positive to $104M, doubling unrestricted cash to $200M.

Risks: Quarter-over-quarter growth slowed, gross margin dipped to 33.1% from new-plant startup costs, and full-year guidance requires a steep second-half ramp.

3. Last-inch chip power: Vicor ($VICR · $7.3B Market Cap)

What they do: Builds tiny, high-density power modules placed right underneath the AI chip rather than feeding power across the circuit board, cutting wasted heat and saving space for memory.

Latest quarter: Q3 revenue grew 78.5% YoY to $197M, boosted by patent royalties surging 207% to $67M as new licenses and a U.S. import case pushed server makers toward Vicor's tech. Gross margin hit 68.3%, Free Cash Flow hit $54M, and Vicor holds $506M net cash with zero bank debt.

Risks: High-margin royalties do a lot of heavy lifting right now, and patent timelines or settlements can slip, leaving less room for error at a higher valuation.

Investment Ranking

To keep myself objective, I compared all three purely against each other on Growth, Margins & Cash Flow, and Valuation (scored out of 10 per category), plus a standalone slowdown risk check.

1. Growth ($FPS 10 · $VICR 6 · $INIO 4)
Forgent leads with 56% expected annual revenue growth through 2028, ahead of Vicor at 36% and INNIO at 25%.

2. Margins & Cash Flow ($VICR 10 · $FPS 6 · $INIO 4)
Vicor wins on profitability and balance sheet strength (68% gross margin, 27% FCF margin, $506M net cash). Forgent flipped FCF positive (22% margin) and brought net debt way down. INNIO prints the largest raw cash ($201M/qtr) alongside $1.4B in net debt.

3. Valuation ($FPS 9 · $INIO 8 · $VICR 3)
Forgent trades at 10.8x 2028E consensus earnings and 2.05x EV/2028E Sales (Enterprise Value includes debt and cash). INNIO is slightly cheaper on EV/Sales at 1.99x (13.5x 2028E earnings). Vicor commands a quality premium at 18.8x 2028E earnings and 5.78x EV/Sales.
(Combined score out of 30: Forgent 25 · Vicor 19 · INNIO 16.)

4. AI Slowdown Risk (10 = most exposed to U.S. permitting delays)

This needs to be factored in because its real. 

Forgent ($FPS): 9/10 risk (~59% North America data center sales; customers can delay or cancel orders)

Vicor ($VICR): 8/10 risk (~70% AI/data center exposure on a $406M backlog)

INNIO ($INIO): 4/10 risk (33% recurring global service sales plus an $8.0B non-cancellable backlog)

My POV

Forgent ($FPS) is the best mix of growth and valuation if its second-half factory ramp stays on track.

Vicor ($VICR) has the cleanest balance sheet and highest margins if its licensing flywheel keeps scaling.

INNIO ($INIO) looks like the steadier downside bet with non-cancellable backlog and recurring service cash flow. Also most insulated from AI slowdown

text:
If you like your private plan, this bill is not a supplement. It is a replacement.
The price tag, in studies of Medicare for All-style plans, is not a rounding error. A Mercatus Center analysis of the Act put the added federal commitment at about $32.6 trillion over the first ten years of full implementation. The Urban Institute estimated that a comprehensive single-payer plan covering everyone, including undocumented immigrants, would raise federal spending by about $34 trillion over ten years. The Congressional Budget Office, in an options analysis, found that a comprehensive single-payer design with long-term care would add about $3 trillion in federal costs in a single year, 2030. Those are not new scores of this exact Congress's budget. They are the best independent estimates of the model they keep reintroducing.

If you want a preview of the immigrant piece, look at California. When the state finished expanding full-scope Medi-Cal to income-eligible residents regardless of immigration status, the Los Angeles Times reported the 2024–25 price at $9.5 billion — more than $3 billion above the prior estimate of $6.4 billion, with $8.4 billion coming from the state's general fund. California later froze new enrollment for undocumented adults. That is not a talking point. It is a budget.

They are not against "voter ID." They are against the bill that would actually require it.

Democrats will tell you they do not oppose voter identification. Schumer has said, "Our objection as Democrats is not to a photo ID." He points to the Freedom to Vote Act and "commonsense" standards. Then he helped bury the SAVE America Act, which would have required proof of citizenship to register and a photo ID to vote in federal elections, as a "voter suppression" bill. The House passed it. The Senate did not. Some of that failure belongs to Republicans who would not touch the filibuster. That does not wash the Democratic position clean. They fought the citizenship proof.

Noncitizen voting in federal elections is already illegal. Some Democratic jurisdictions have already invited noncitizens into local elections. The District of Columbia allows noncitizens to vote in local races. San Francisco allows certain noncitizen parents and guardians to vote for the Board of Education. That is not a mass theft of the presidency. It is a principle — the ballot as a residency perk, not a citizenship right. If you think that stays in city hall forever, you have not been paying attention.

In Texas, the first deliverable is already named.

On Nov. 18, 2025, Gov. Greg Abbott designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations and the Muslim Brotherhood as foreign terrorist organizations and transnational criminal organizations under Texas law, barring them from acquiring real estate in the state and authorizing heightened enforcement. The federal government has never designated CAIR as a foreign terrorist organization. CAIR calls itself a civil-rights group and denies the accusations. The record that prompted Abbott is not imaginary. Federal prosecutors named CAIR an unindicted co-conspirator in the 2008 Holy Land Foundation terrorism-financing case — they did not charge the organization — and the United Arab Emirates listed CAIR as a terrorist organization in 2014.
Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who defeated Abbott on Nov. 3, told The Washington Post she will remove the CAIR designation. "We have to use public safety measures for public safety," she said, dismissing what she called "nonsense happening with power that should be used for public safety." The published interview did not establish that she will also lift the Muslim Brotherhood label. Pulling the proclamation would not, by itself, repeal the underlying statutes or automatically end investigations already underway. It would still be a political act with a beneficiary: an organization Texas had labeled a security risk. Hinojosa takes office in January.

Quick & Easy Explanation (for sharing with a friend)
In the 2026 midterms, Republicans suffered a major defeat. Democrats took control of both the House and Senate, including surprising wins in traditional Republican strongholds like Texas.
Trump initially said on election night that he would accept the results. A few days later, he posted on Truth Social questioning whether anyone really believes the election was honest, pointing to massive early-vote dumps, voting machines, and how polls could be so wrong.
This reignited fraud suspicions and created a split inside MAGA:

Accept side: Figures like Steve Bannon said people should stop complaining that the election was stolen and accept the outcome.
Skeptics side: Hardcore supporters called for recounts and investigations (similar energy to 2020).

Anomalies noted by skeptics: In Texas, the Democratic Senate candidate got roughly 5.4 million votes (about 600k more than Harris in 2024), while overall statewide turnout dropped compared to 2024. Similar patterns in other places raised eyebrows for people who still question 2020.
Right-wing takeaway:
Election integrity remains a core issue. Heavy reliance on early voting, mail-in ballots, and voting machines reduces transparency. Democrats controlling election administration in key states is seen as a major risk for 2028. While official investigations found no widespread hacking or foreign interference, many on the right still view these results as suspicious and believe full audits are necessary. The internal MAGA split could affect cohesion heading into 2028.

One-line summary: Trump flipped from “I’ll accept the results” to raising fraud claims again → MAGA is now divided between “move on” and “investigate.” Suspicious numbers in red strongholds + control of election offices are the big talking points on the right.

China Report is MIT Technology Review’s newsletter about technology developments in China. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Tuesday.

If you saw these images pop up on your timeline, would you be able to tell if they were real photographs of the southwestern city of Chongqing in the 1990s?

In fact, none of them are real. Zhang Haijun, a street photographer in Chongqing, generated these images with Midjourney, an image-making artificial-intelligence program. 

A number of artists and creators are generating nostalgic photographs of China with the help of AI. Even though these images still get some details wrong, like the number of fingers that humans have or what Chinese characters look like, they are realistic enough to trick and impress many social media followers, including me.

Retro AI artwork like Zhang’s has also caught the attention of Tong Bingxue, a collector of Chinese historical photographs. He reposted some of them to his popular Twitter account China in Pictures last week. 

These generated photos are indeed aesthetically pleasing, Tong says. They look sophisticated in terms of standard photography metrics, like definition, sharpness, saturation, and color tone. “When people look at things on social media, these [attributes] are the first things that catch the eye. The authenticity of the photo comes second,” he says. Real historical photos, on the other hand, sometimes look amateur or come with material imperfections.

Zhang, the creator of the AI images above, was born in Chongqing in 1992. He grew up near the Chongqing Iron and Steel Company, one of the oldest and largest steel factories in China, and remembers watching the workers when he was about seven years old. “When I was little, I would often watch them come out of the factory during their break, sit on the ground, smoke a cigarette, and look into the distance. There were stories in their eyes,” he says.

When he turned that experience into an image-generating prompt for Midjourney, he was amazed by the results. “What the AI generated—the look of resilience in their eyes and the way they are dressed—it looks exactly the same as what I described to it,” he says.

Now, Zhang pays more than $200 a year for Midjourney, and uses it to generate new retro photographs with different themes: rural weddings in the ’90s, physical laborers for hire waiting in the market, and Chongqing street fashion. Each time, he writes the prompts in Chinese, uses machine translation tools to convert them to English, feeds them into Midjourney, and spends about 20 minutes tweaking them to get the ideal result. 

Some artists working with AI are inspired by the discovery of real photos. Diaspora youth in the West have been forming communities on Instagram where they crowdsource and curate historical photos in order to rebuild memories free from a Western framing. 

Kim Wang, a 28-year-old UI designer and photographer in Hangzhou, was inspired by Beijing Silvermine, a project by the French artist Thomas Sauvin, who rescued 850,000 discarded color negatives, dating from around 1985, from a recycling factory in Beijing.

She used Midjourney to create photos of China in the 1980s and ’90s. 

“For our generation, I feel like there’s a massive leap from 1995 to 2023,” says Wang. “Now is a completely different era, but I kind of want to go back to that era.” In particular, she wanted to re-create what Hangzhou looked like before it became a tech hub and home to multiple Chinese tech companies, including Alibaba, Hikvision, and NetEase. “I want to restore it to the era when it was not so involuted,” she says, using a word that has become popular in recent years to describe the widespread feeling of burnout in China.

In one photo she generated, a young couple are sharing fast food by Hangzhou’s famous West Lake. She wanted the McDonald’s logo to appear on the packaging of the soft-serve ice cream. Instead, Midjourney placed the logo on a crimson-colored traditional Chinese pillar, giving it a surprising twist. Wang liked the accidental result and decided to post this picture along with seven others on the social media app Xiaohongshu, where she got nearly 9,000 likes.

These AI-generated photos are making waves right now mostly because of a recent major update of Midjourney that was released in mid-March. Wang says the new version, Version 5, is better not only at generating human hands but also at simulating various photography styles. In the previous version, generated photographs often look like illustrations because of incorrect lighting. The same new version of Midjourney is also behind a few AI images that have gone viral in the past week, including some featuring a fashionable pope and others purporting to show Donald Trump being arrested.

Another important upgrade with the new version, according to Wang, is that the software has started to move beyond rendering stereotypes of Asian faces. “The photographs generated by Version 4,” she says, “looked more like the model faces that would appear in Western fashion advertisements: almond eyes, slit eyes, and monolids.” 

Even so, it’s still relatively easy even for untrained eyes to tell that the photos are generated by an AI (in the photograph of the bride above, for example, the woman behind in red pants is missing a leg).

As with other applications of Midjourney or other similar AI tools, there are concerns about intellectual-property theft, because the software mimics the styles of certain artists, often without permission or credit.

“It steals data from photographers and uses it to make money or send messages in ways they don’t necessarily support,” Rui Zhong, a policy researcher and artist, commented under a tweet by Tong Bingxue showing the AI-generated retro photo of Chongqing. On Chinese social media, the recent popularity of image-making AIs has set some illustrators on high alert, and they are going around looking for and exposing AI-generated artwork that wasn’t properly labeled.

Tong says the retro images don’t have much value outside of being pleasing to the eye. “The most important attribute of a historical photo is its archival value. Its sharpness, color tone, artistic value—these are all secondary,” he says. 

There are things to learn from old photos, he says—not just about the subject of the image, but also from what can be seen in the background, details that could have been captured just by accident. The photographs themselves are artifacts too: they’re material media, whether silver film, glass negatives, or pieces of paper, and they document their own trip through time. AI retro photography, by contrast, offers nothing more than a good-looking image.

Do you think AI-generated nostalgic photographs will be good or bad for the photography profession? Let me know your thoughts at zeyi@technologyreview.com.

Catch up with China

1. TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew was grilled by US House lawmakers for five hours on Thursday about the app, which has raised concerns over national security and the mental health of teenagers. (Washington Post $)

  • Meanwhile, TikTok paid a group of influencers on its platform to come to Washington, DC, and advocate against banning the app that has made their careers. (New York Times $)
  • Hours before the meeting, China’s Commerce Ministry said it strongly opposes a sale of TikTok. Any deal that involves transferring technology outside the country would require government approval. (Wall Street Journal $)
  • Perhaps the most unexpected result is how Chew himself became a social media darling for his good looks and calm demeanor during the hearing. (Insider $)

2.  Satellite images show the origin and route of the Chinese high-altitude balloon that flew over the US and grabbed the whole country’s attention in early February. (New York Times $)

3. To boost the marriage rate and address population decline, one city in China launched a matchmaking platform, using data on single residents. (The Guardian)

4. Top US corporate executives, including Apple CEO Tim Cook, attended a business meeting in Beijing over the weekend and met with Chinese officials. (Wall Street Journal $)

5. After rejecting Western mRNA vaccines for over two years, China finally approved its first homegrown mRNA vaccine for covid last week. (BBC)

6. Nvidia modified H100, one of its flagship chips, in order to continue to be able to sell it to Chinese companies without triggering US export controls. (Reuters $)

7. Seventy-three years before the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to three scientists who worked on quantum entanglement, it was Chien-Shiung Wu, a Chinese-American physicist, who conducted the first experiment to document evidence of entanglement in photons. (Scientific American)

Lost in translation

In China, cyberbullying is still claiming lives. 

After the suicide of a Chinese woman who was cyberbullied last year for dying her hair pink, a group of college students at Fudan University’s Fushu data journalism lab set out to gather data illustrating the severity of online harassment in China. 

Having sorted through thousands of news articles, they ended up with a database of 311 documented cases of cyberbullying that happened in 2022. Over 40% of the victims are ordinary people—they don’t have any public-facing occupation but merely became targets when strangers online decided they wanted to chime in on their personal life. The students found that women are more likely to be bullied for their appearance, relationships, and family morals, while men are more likely to be bullied for ideological differences, discourse about the news, or professional performance.

In 2022, many Chinese social media platforms pledged to introduce new mechanisms that filter out harmful information and to enable self-protection restrictions for victims of bullying. To test the effectiveness of these new rules, the students simulated cyberbullying comments on four Chinese platforms. They found that almost all fell under the platforms’ detection thresholds for self-harm, sarcastic insults, and explicit images, particularly when it came to private messages. 

One more thing

It’s time to turn that male gaze back toward men. Coconut Palm, a wildly popular Chinese beverage brand, is known for head-scratching advertisements full of sexual innuendo and risqué photos of women. But facing increasing market competition, the brand wants to remake itself to attract more young female customers. So during the last International Women’s Day, on March 8, it broadcast a livestream of muscular men working out in tight outfits while holding a can of the signature beverage. Unfortunately, it didn’t work. The male models sold less than $150 worth of products online during the livestream.

China Report is MIT Technology Review’s newsletter about technology developments in China. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Tuesday.

If you saw these images pop up on your timeline, would you be able to tell if they were real photographs of the southwestern city of Chongqing in the 1990s?

In fact, none of them are real. Zhang Haijun, a street photographer in Chongqing, generated these images with Midjourney, an image-making artificial-intelligence program. 

A number of artists and creators are generating nostalgic photographs of China with the help of AI. Even though these images still get some details wrong, like the number of fingers that humans have or what Chinese characters look like, they are realistic enough to trick and impress many social media followers, including me.

Retro AI artwork like Zhang’s has also caught the attention of Tong Bingxue, a collector of Chinese historical photographs. He reposted some of them to his popular Twitter account China in Pictures last week. 

These generated photos are indeed aesthetically pleasing, Tong says. They look sophisticated in terms of standard photography metrics, like definition, sharpness, saturation, and color tone. “When people look at things on social media, these [attributes] are the first things that catch the eye. The authenticity of the photo comes second,” he says. Real historical photos, on the other hand, sometimes look amateur or come with material imperfections.

Zhang, the creator of the AI images above, was born in Chongqing in 1992. He grew up near the Chongqing Iron and Steel Company, one of the oldest and largest steel factories in China, and remembers watching the workers when he was about seven years old. “When I was little, I would often watch them come out of the factory during their break, sit on the ground, smoke a cigarette, and look into the distance. There were stories in their eyes,” he says.

When he turned that experience into an image-generating prompt for Midjourney, he was amazed by the results. “What the AI generated—the look of resilience in their eyes and the way they are dressed—it looks exactly the same as what I described to it,” he says.

Now, Zhang pays more than $200 a year for Midjourney, and uses it to generate new retro photographs with different themes: rural weddings in the ’90s, physical laborers for hire waiting in the market, and Chongqing street fashion. Each time, he writes the prompts in Chinese, uses machine translation tools to convert them to English, feeds them into Midjourney, and spends about 20 minutes tweaking them to get the ideal result. 

Some artists working with AI are inspired by the discovery of real photos. Diaspora youth in the West have been forming communities on Instagram where they crowdsource and curate historical photos in order to rebuild memories free from a Western framing. 

Kim Wang, a 28-year-old UI designer and photographer in Hangzhou, was inspired by Beijing Silvermine, a project by the French artist Thomas Sauvin, who rescued 850,000 discarded color negatives, dating from around 1985, from a recycling factory in Beijing.

She used Midjourney to create photos of China in the 1980s and ’90s. 

“For our generation, I feel like there’s a massive leap from 1995 to 2023,” says Wang. “Now is a completely different era, but I kind of want to go back to that era.” In particular, she wanted to re-create what Hangzhou looked like before it became a tech hub and home to multiple Chinese tech companies, including Alibaba, Hikvision, and NetEase. “I want to restore it to the era when it was not so involuted,” she says, using a word that has become popular in recent years to describe the widespread feeling of burnout in China.

In one photo she generated, a young couple are sharing fast food by Hangzhou’s famous West Lake. She wanted the McDonald’s logo to appear on the packaging of the soft-serve ice cream. Instead, Midjourney placed the logo on a crimson-colored traditional Chinese pillar, giving it a surprising twist. Wang liked the accidental result and decided to post this picture along with seven others on the social media app Xiaohongshu, where she got nearly 9,000 likes.

These AI-generated photos are making waves right now mostly because of a recent major update of Midjourney that was released in mid-March. Wang says the new version, Version 5, is better not only at generating human hands but also at simulating various photography styles. In the previous version, generated photographs often look like illustrations because of incorrect lighting. The same new version of Midjourney is also behind a few AI images that have gone viral in the past week, including some featuring a fashionable pope and others purporting to show Donald Trump being arrested.

Another important upgrade with the new version, according to Wang, is that the software has started to move beyond rendering stereotypes of Asian faces. “The photographs generated by Version 4,” she says, “looked more like the model faces that would appear in Western fashion advertisements: almond eyes, slit eyes, and monolids.” 

Even so, it’s still relatively easy even for untrained eyes to tell that the photos are generated by an AI (in the photograph of the bride above, for example, the woman behind in red pants is missing a leg).

As with other applications of Midjourney or other similar AI tools, there are concerns about intellectual-property theft, because the software mimics the styles of certain artists, often without permission or credit.

“It steals data from photographers and uses it to make money or send messages in ways they don’t necessarily support,” Rui Zhong, a policy researcher and artist, commented under a tweet by Tong Bingxue showing the AI-generated retro photo of Chongqing. On Chinese social media, the recent popularity of image-making AIs has set some illustrators on high alert, and they are going around looking for and exposing AI-generated artwork that wasn’t properly labeled.

Tong says the retro images don’t have much value outside of being pleasing to the eye. “The most important attribute of a historical photo is its archival value. Its sharpness, color tone, artistic value—these are all secondary,” he says. 

There are things to learn from old photos, he says—not just about the subject of the image, but also from what can be seen in the background, details that could have been captured just by accident. The photographs themselves are artifacts too: they’re material media, whether silver film, glass negatives, or pieces of paper, and they document their own trip through time. AI retro photography, by contrast, offers nothing more than a good-looking image.

Do you think AI-generated nostalgic photographs will be good or bad for the photography profession? Let me know your thoughts at zeyi@technologyreview.com.

Catch up with China

1. TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew was grilled by US House lawmakers for five hours on Thursday about the app, which has raised concerns over national security and the mental health of teenagers. (Washington Post $)

  • Meanwhile, TikTok paid a group of influencers on its platform to come to Washington, DC, and advocate against banning the app that has made their careers. (New York Times $)
  • Hours before the meeting, China’s Commerce Ministry said it strongly opposes a sale of TikTok. Any deal that involves transferring technology outside the country would require government approval. (Wall Street Journal $)
  • Perhaps the most unexpected result is how Chew himself became a social media darling for his good looks and calm demeanor during the hearing. (Insider $)

2.  Satellite images show the origin and route of the Chinese high-altitude balloon that flew over the US and grabbed the whole country’s attention in early February. (New York Times $)

3. To boost the marriage rate and address population decline, one city in China launched a matchmaking platform, using data on single residents. (The Guardian)

4. Top US corporate executives, including Apple CEO Tim Cook, attended a business meeting in Beijing over the weekend and met with Chinese officials. (Wall Street Journal $)

5. After rejecting Western mRNA vaccines for over two years, China finally approved its first homegrown mRNA vaccine for covid last week. (BBC)

6. Nvidia modified H100, one of its flagship chips, in order to continue to be able to sell it to Chinese companies without triggering US export controls. (Reuters $)

7. Seventy-three years before the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to three scientists who worked on quantum entanglement, it was Chien-Shiung Wu, a Chinese-American physicist, who conducted the first experiment to document evidence of entanglement in photons. (Scientific American)

Lost in translation

In China, cyberbullying is still claiming lives. 

After the suicide of a Chinese woman who was cyberbullied last year for dying her hair pink, a group of college students at Fudan University’s Fushu data journalism lab set out to gather data illustrating the severity of online harassment in China. 

Having sorted through thousands of news articles, they ended up with a database of 311 documented cases of cyberbullying that happened in 2022. Over 40% of the victims are ordinary people—they don’t have any public-facing occupation but merely became targets when strangers online decided they wanted to chime in on their personal life. The students found that women are more likely to be bullied for their appearance, relationships, and family morals, while men are more likely to be bullied for ideological differences, discourse about the news, or professional performance.

In 2022, many Chinese social media platforms pledged to introduce new mechanisms that filter out harmful information and to enable self-protection restrictions for victims of bullying. To test the effectiveness of these new rules, the students simulated cyberbullying comments on four Chinese platforms. They found that almost all fell under the platforms’ detection thresholds for self-harm, sarcastic insults, and explicit images, particularly when it came to private messages. 

One more thing

It’s time to turn that male gaze back toward men. Coconut Palm, a wildly popular Chinese beverage brand, is known for head-scratching advertisements full of sexual innuendo and risqué photos of women. But facing increasing market competition, the brand wants to remake itself to attract more young female customers. So during the last International Women’s Day, on March 8, it broadcast a livestream of muscular men working out in tight outfits while holding a can of the signature beverage. Unfortunately, it didn’t work. The male models sold less than $150 worth of products online during the livestream.

China Report is MIT Technology Review’s newsletter about technology developments in China. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Tuesday.

If you saw these images pop up on your timeline, would you be able to tell if they were real photographs of the southwestern city of Chongqing in the 1990s?

In fact, none of them are real. Zhang Haijun, a street photographer in Chongqing, generated these images with Midjourney, an image-making artificial-intelligence program. 

A number of artists and creators are generating nostalgic photographs of China with the help of AI. Even though these images still get some details wrong, like the number of fingers that humans have or what Chinese characters look like, they are realistic enough to trick and impress many social media followers, including me.

Retro AI artwork like Zhang’s has also caught the attention of Tong Bingxue, a collector of Chinese historical photographs. He reposted some of them to his popular Twitter account China in Pictures last week. 

These generated photos are indeed aesthetically pleasing, Tong says. They look sophisticated in terms of standard photography metrics, like definition, sharpness, saturation, and color tone. “When people look at things on social media, these [attributes] are the first things that catch the eye. The authenticity of the photo comes second,” he says. Real historical photos, on the other hand, sometimes look amateur or come with material imperfections.

Zhang, the creator of the AI images above, was born in Chongqing in 1992. He grew up near the Chongqing Iron and Steel Company, one of the oldest and largest steel factories in China, and remembers watching the workers when he was about seven years old. “When I was little, I would often watch them come out of the factory during their break, sit on the ground, smoke a cigarette, and look into the distance. There were stories in their eyes,” he says.

When he turned that experience into an image-generating prompt for Midjourney, he was amazed by the results. “What the AI generated—the look of resilience in their eyes and the way they are dressed—it looks exactly the same as what I described to it,” he says.

Now, Zhang pays more than $200 a year for Midjourney, and uses it to generate new retro photographs with different themes: rural weddings in the ’90s, physical laborers for hire waiting in the market, and Chongqing street fashion. Each time, he writes the prompts in Chinese, uses machine translation tools to convert them to English, feeds them into Midjourney, and spends about 20 minutes tweaking them to get the ideal result. 

Some artists working with AI are inspired by the discovery of real photos. Diaspora youth in the West have been forming communities on Instagram where they crowdsource and curate historical photos in order to rebuild memories free from a Western framing. 

Kim Wang, a 28-year-old UI designer and photographer in Hangzhou, was inspired by Beijing Silvermine, a project by the French artist Thomas Sauvin, who rescued 850,000 discarded color negatives, dating from around 1985, from a recycling factory in Beijing.

She used Midjourney to create photos of China in the 1980s and ’90s. 

“For our generation, I feel like there’s a massive leap from 1995 to 2023,” says Wang. “Now is a completely different era, but I kind of want to go back to that era.” In particular, she wanted to re-create what Hangzhou looked like before it became a tech hub and home to multiple Chinese tech companies, including Alibaba, Hikvision, and NetEase. “I want to restore it to the era when it was not so involuted,” she says, using a word that has become popular in recent years to describe the widespread feeling of burnout in China.

In one photo she generated, a young couple are sharing fast food by Hangzhou’s famous West Lake. She wanted the McDonald’s logo to appear on the packaging of the soft-serve ice cream. Instead, Midjourney placed the logo on a crimson-colored traditional Chinese pillar, giving it a surprising twist. Wang liked the accidental result and decided to post this picture along with seven others on the social media app Xiaohongshu, where she got nearly 9,000 likes.

These AI-generated photos are making waves right now mostly because of a recent major update of Midjourney that was released in mid-March. Wang says the new version, Version 5, is better not only at generating human hands but also at simulating various photography styles. In the previous version, generated photographs often look like illustrations because of incorrect lighting. The same new version of Midjourney is also behind a few AI images that have gone viral in the past week, including some featuring a fashionable pope and others purporting to show Donald Trump being arrested.

Another important upgrade with the new version, according to Wang, is that the software has started to move beyond rendering stereotypes of Asian faces. “The photographs generated by Version 4,” she says, “looked more like the model faces that would appear in Western fashion advertisements: almond eyes, slit eyes, and monolids.” 

Even so, it’s still relatively easy even for untrained eyes to tell that the photos are generated by an AI (in the photograph of the bride above, for example, the woman behind in red pants is missing a leg).

As with other applications of Midjourney or other similar AI tools, there are concerns about intellectual-property theft, because the software mimics the styles of certain artists, often without permission or credit.

“It steals data from photographers and uses it to make money or send messages in ways they don’t necessarily support,” Rui Zhong, a policy researcher and artist, commented under a tweet by Tong Bingxue showing the AI-generated retro photo of Chongqing. On Chinese social media, the recent popularity of image-making AIs has set some illustrators on high alert, and they are going around looking for and exposing AI-generated artwork that wasn’t properly labeled.

Tong says the retro images don’t have much value outside of being pleasing to the eye. “The most important attribute of a historical photo is its archival value. Its sharpness, color tone, artistic value—these are all secondary,” he says. 

There are things to learn from old photos, he says—not just about the subject of the image, but also from what can be seen in the background, details that could have been captured just by accident. The photographs themselves are artifacts too: they’re material media, whether silver film, glass negatives, or pieces of paper, and they document their own trip through time. AI retro photography, by contrast, offers nothing more than a good-looking image.

Do you think AI-generated nostalgic photographs will be good or bad for the photography profession? Let me know your thoughts at zeyi@technologyreview.com.

Catch up with China

1. TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew was grilled by US House lawmakers for five hours on Thursday about the app, which has raised concerns over national security and the mental health of teenagers. (Washington Post $)

  • Meanwhile, TikTok paid a group of influencers on its platform to come to Washington, DC, and advocate against banning the app that has made their careers. (New York Times $)
  • Hours before the meeting, China’s Commerce Ministry said it strongly opposes a sale of TikTok. Any deal that involves transferring technology outside the country would require government approval. (Wall Street Journal $)
  • Perhaps the most unexpected result is how Chew himself became a social media darling for his good looks and calm demeanor during the hearing. (Insider $)

2.  Satellite images show the origin and route of the Chinese high-altitude balloon that flew over the US and grabbed the whole country’s attention in early February. (New York Times $)

3. To boost the marriage rate and address population decline, one city in China launched a matchmaking platform, using data on single residents. (The Guardian)

4. Top US corporate executives, including Apple CEO Tim Cook, attended a business meeting in Beijing over the weekend and met with Chinese officials. (Wall Street Journal $)

5. After rejecting Western mRNA vaccines for over two years, China finally approved its first homegrown mRNA vaccine for covid last week. (BBC)

6. Nvidia modified H100, one of its flagship chips, in order to continue to be able to sell it to Chinese companies without triggering US export controls. (Reuters $)

7. Seventy-three years before the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to three scientists who worked on quantum entanglement, it was Chien-Shiung Wu, a Chinese-American physicist, who conducted the first experiment to document evidence of entanglement in photons. (Scientific American)

Lost in translation

In China, cyberbullying is still claiming lives. 

After the suicide of a Chinese woman who was cyberbullied last year for dying her hair pink, a group of college students at Fudan University’s Fushu data journalism lab set out to gather data illustrating the severity of online harassment in China. 

Having sorted through thousands of news articles, they ended up with a database of 311 documented cases of cyberbullying that happened in 2022. Over 40% of the victims are ordinary people—they don’t have any public-facing occupation but merely became targets when strangers online decided they wanted to chime in on their personal life. The students found that women are more likely to be bullied for their appearance, relationships, and family morals, while men are more likely to be bullied for ideological differences, discourse about the news, or professional performance.

In 2022, many Chinese social media platforms pledged to introduce new mechanisms that filter out harmful information and to enable self-protection restrictions for victims of bullying. To test the effectiveness of these new rules, the students simulated cyberbullying comments on four Chinese platforms. They found that almost all fell under the platforms’ detection thresholds for self-harm, sarcastic insults, and explicit images, particularly when it came to private messages. 

One more thing

It’s time to turn that male gaze back toward men. Coconut Palm, a wildly popular Chinese beverage brand, is known for head-scratching advertisements full of sexual innuendo and risqué photos of women. But facing increasing market competition, the brand wants to remake itself to attract more young female customers. So during the last International Women’s Day, on March 8, it broadcast a livestream of muscular men working out in tight outfits while holding a can of the signature beverage. Unfortunately, it didn’t work. The male models sold less than $150 worth of products online during the livestream.

Another example— DC judge frees teen who shot man on Metrobus, sparking outrage from interim US Attorney for the District of Columbia:

“The Youth Rehabilitation Act gives judges broad discretion when sentencing defendants who were under 24 when their crimes were committed, angering prosecutors:

A 19-year-old former college football player who shot a man in the chest on a crowded Metrobus in March walked free from court this month after a judge suspended his entire prison sentence under Washington, D.C.’s Youth Rehabilitation Act.

Javarry Peaks pleaded guilty to felony counts of aggravated assault while armed and possession of a firearm during a crime of violence after video showed him pulling out an unregistered handgun and shooting the victim on the bus. The victim survived after being treated by EMS at the scene.

But D.C. Superior Court Judge Rainey Branch stunned prosecutors by suspending Peaks’ entire four-year prison sentence and three years of supervised release, instead sentencing him only to probation under the Youth Rehabilitation Act.

The YRA gives judges broad discretion when sentencing defendants who were under 24 when their crimes were committed, allowing for alternatives to incarceration except in the most serious cases like murder. Defendants sentenced under the act can also have their crimes shielded from public view and potential employers if they meet court conditions...

In her ruling, Judge Branch cited Peaks’ age, lack of prior criminal record and strong family support as reasons for the suspended sentence. The judge also noted that Peaks’ cousin had been robbed on public transportation five months earlier, causing ‘anxiety and paranoia’ while using transit…”

text:
📊 Weekly Wrap | Gold · Oil · Crypto | November 9–13

🥇 Gold — hot CPI, a 50bp hint, and a new 52-week low
Started well. Monday opened near $4,053 and rallied to $4,126 as Brent fell 4% — cheaper oil, cooler inflation, fewer reasons to hike. It touched $4,157 Monday. That was the top.
Tuesday's October CPI broke it: headline +0.4% MoM, core +0.3%, with shelter alone doing over 30% of the increase. Waller then hinted at 50bp. Gold fell below $4,000 and never recovered — Thursday alone it dropped ~3% to $3,866, a 52-week low, while the 10-year topped 5%. Friday's PPI was tamer than feared (+0.3% MoM, 6.5% YoY, slightly below consensus) and gold steadied.
Markets now price an 88% chance of a 25bp December hike, with 12% on a 50bp move. Silver has now fallen 59% from its January all-time high.
That's the whole story: real rates, not demand.

🛢️ Oil — second straight weekly loss, and the narrative has flipped to surplus
Brent (January) settled Friday at $98; WTI (December) at $89.
Inside the week it was anything but orderly: Monday took Brent down 5.85% on the Qatari peace proposal, then it clawed back as talks stalled. Houthis claimed fresh attacks on the Saudi East-West pipeline and Yanbu. Mossad's director was in Washington Friday for talks on the Iran war.
The structural shift is the real news. The IEA said Friday the oil market will be in surplus this quarter for the first time since the war began — roughly 2M bpd of Q4 oversupply. OPEC+ output is back to ~90% of pre-war levels. US crude and fuel stocks built in the week to Nov 6 on weaker refined-product demand. Brent is down ~18% on the month.
Trump has pivoted from military escalation to economic pressure — blockade plus sanctions. Hormuz tanker traffic remains well below pre-war levels even as flows recover.

🪙 Crypto — below $70k for the first time in three months
Brutal. BTC closed Friday at $70k, — lowest close in at least three months and 19.7% below its September 21 high of $86k. ETH closed $1,970, breaking $2,000.
Thursday into Friday saw ~$1.47B in leveraged liquidations, $1.31B of it longs.
Flows are the problem, not price. Crypto ETFs lost $1.53B across Nov 9-13 — BTC funds $1.065B of it, with BlackRock's IBIT posting outflows on all five sessions. ETH funds shed $398.9M. BTC and ETH together were 95.6% of the total. BTC ETFs had already flipped negative for 2026 the prior week after a $1.28B outflow.

👀 Key levels — week ahead
🥇 Gold: $3,850 is where WisdomTree sees solid support; below that $3,800. Reclaiming $3,937 flips the near-term bias, then $4,000. The 50-day crossed below the 100-day Monday. December hike at 88% is already priced — what isn't is a 50bp move, and Waller put that on the table. Watch FOMC minutes Wednesday Nov 18 for whether 50bp has real support. Central bank demand is unchanged (Goldman sees 60t/month through 2027), so this remains a positioning washout, not a thesis break.
🛢️ Brent $95.84 / WTI $88.56, spread $7.28 (narrowed sharply from $13.52 three weeks ago — that compression is itself a de-escalation signal). The IEA surplus call changes the frame: for the first time since February, the bear case has fundamentals behind it rather than just diplomacy. $91 is the downside, $98 the cap. Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure remain the only thing that reverses this quickly.
🪙 BTC: $69,556 with the 12-month low at $58,559 — the cushion is thinner than it's been all year. $70,000 is now resistance, not support. ETH: $1,970, with $1,900 the next test. Nvidia earnings Tuesday Nov 17 and FOMC minutes Wednesday are the macro catalysts — crypto is trading as pure risk beta right now, and the correlation to tech is tight. Until ETF outflows stop, nothing else matters.

Rates up, inflation hot, oil in surplus, crypto bleeding. Only one of those is good news for anyone. 📉

text:
JUST IN: Lula Says Brazil Found New Buyers Instead of 'Crying' Over Trump Tariffs 🇧🇷🇺🇸💼🌏

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva says his country chose to find new trading partners rather than beg Washington after the US slapped heavy tariffs on Brazil.
Lula spoke to reporters on Sunday in Manila, where he attended the 49th ASEAN summit.
He said that instead of crying or pleading with the American government, Brazil went looking for other countries to buy from and sell to.
According to Lula, the United States now accounts for 9.2 percent of Brazil's foreign trade.
He said Brazil's trade with China has grown by about 20 percent, with Germany by 15.8 percent, Indonesia by about 15 percent and Vietnam by 13 percent.
Lula said he wants to double trade with ASEAN countries, which stood at 38.4 billion dollars in 2025.
Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira said Brazil hopes to become a full ASEAN dialogue partner in 2027, when Singapore takes over the bloc's chair.
On the sidelines, Lula met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to discuss wrapping up the Mercosur-Canada trade deal.
He also said he wants foreign investment to mine and process critical minerals and rare earths inside Brazil for chips and batteries.
Looking ahead to his fourth term, Lula pledged to invest in science, technology, the digital industry and the green economy.
He said Brazil must stop being a country that is forever developing and become a developed nation.

text:
As the clock hit  0:0 last night, my family and I just stood there. Nobody said a word.

Four hours of feeling everything. In the last ten minutes alone, we went from the highest of highs to the lowest of lows. We were stunned, heartbroken, and still trying to process what we’d just watched. And somehow, underneath all of that, I felt at peace.

I saw Noah and Dash afterward. I could see how much they were carrying. My wife and Noah’s fiance, Faith, saw it too. They walked in the training room and just sat with them after media. 

When we got back to the house, we prayed before we ate like we always do. I shared something I’d heard Wednesday at the funeral for my cousin’s wife, Ronnie.

“Faith does not eliminate questions, but faith knows where to take them.”
I needed those words as much as much as i was hoping my boys would heed it. 

From Big Noon Kickoff to the catwalk, zona zoo,  to the final snap, the whole day felt surreal. This was the Arizona we used to hear about. These were the fans we always knew we had. If I’d been a recruit in that stadium last night, I would’ve committed to Arizona on the spot.

We talk a lot about building a football culture here. Tucson showed us what the fans can do to make Arizona a place where nights like that are expected. The whole stadium felt like it had a stake in every snap.

We’ve got four more years here with Dash. I told Noah last night, you’re just starting this chapter of Arizona football for our family. Dash and Uhila will help write the next ones. And through it all, God is still writing our whole story, 

Thank you, Tucson, for showing up the way you did for our sons, for this team, and for your city. I wish the score had gone our way. We’ll still remember that night for the rest of our life. 3 more to go, no matter what. 

Love y’all. 🥤➡️🐻⬇️
